Name that bit from the spray is a drug-work snag. Mark pools lack most bits, so lookup oft fails. Their 2026 preprint, SpecBridge, joins scans and bit forms in one shared space. Past tools built bits atom by atom, a slow road.

The bridge learns from both modes at once. It does not start that shared space from nil. Fast true names speed drug and chem work. Untouched samples can then yield their bits.
arxiv-2601-17404:
Anke Fischer-Janzen, Thomas M. Wendt, and Kristof Van Laerhoven study eye control for assistive robot arms. Shared control splits work between user and robot. The user guides, and the robot helps with hard parts. Eye tracking is a key input for users with limited motion. It still faces real flaws. Three-dimensional gaze can be off target.

Gaze is also hard to read when many tasks are in view. The study tackles daily task help with those flaws in mind. Better gaze use could give users more freedom at home. It could cut the load on carers too. The work speaks to design of arms that serve meals, doors, and tools.
arxiv-2601-17704:
Kazuki Ezumi, Min-Ruei Lin, and Takeshi Miura study a variant of Tingley's problem. The problem asks if maps that preserve distance on unit spheres must be linear. They work with positive parts of unit spheres. The spaces are continuous functions that vanish at infinity. X and Y are locally compact Hausdorff spaces in their setup.

Positive spheres fit ordered function spaces used in analysis. A positive answer would extend isometries to full linear maps. That gives strong rigidity for such spaces. Rigidity results simplify classification across functional analysis. The variant is a focused test of how far Tingley phenomena reach. Each new space type settled adds to the map.
arxiv-2601-17804:
Arman and Prasanta K. Panigrahi study how to measure slow damage in quantum systems with very fine tools. Their 2026 preprint is about a bosonic channel that spreads and blurs quantum states. The damage in view is dephasing, a loss of phase links caused by noise. The team asks which probe states can sense that loss most sharply, using a finite store of non-Gaussian states.

They find the best probes by a score called quantum Fisher information. Two states stand out: the squeezed cat state and a symmetric squeezed compass state. To judge them, the team views the noisy system as part of a larger clean one. Their results match what numeric tests show. The work guides sensing where noise must be tracked with care.
arxiv-2601-19104:
Ryo Koshikawa and three co-authors trace cause and effect inside moving air. Airflow over wings and bodies forms swirls that push and pull on each other over time. The team reads snapshot data with a method that splits the flow into modes that change over time, guided by information theory.

Their convolutional causal learning pulls out the swirl structures that carry the most news about what comes next. Knowing which structures drive the flow, not just which are big, can guide control of drag and noise. The work ties machine learning to a classic physics question: what makes the flow do what it does?
arxiv-2601-19204:
Zhixi Cai and five co-authors give visual reasoning a visible structure with a team of automata. New vision language models see well, but their reasoning is hidden and they often make up facts on hard queries. Older compositional methods are clearer, yet they use one agent or a fixed hand built pipeline.

Their system, MATA, is a trainable layered automaton that can call in partner agents when skills overlap or compete. It decides when teamwork helps and when agents should vie. Clear, structured reasoning that still adapts could make visual answers safer to trust in real tools.
arxiv-2601-19304:
Sneha Shashidhara and four co-authors study voice chatbots that help Indian schoolchildren practice spoken English. Fluency in spoken English strongly lifts earning chances for low income youth in India. Yet chances to practice speaking are scarce in their schools, most of all in low resource, multilingual settings.

The team deployed a voice based chatbot and heard from the many parties involved: students, teachers, and others. A multi stakeholder study catches what a lab test cannot: how a tool fits real classrooms. Findings like these guide speech tools that must work where bandwidth, devices, and languages all vary.
arxiv-2601-19504:
Varun Narayan Kannan Pillai, Akshay Ajith, and Sumesh K J blend three crafts into one trading system. Markets move under fundamental, technical, and psychological forces at once. Their hybrid system joins technical analysis, machine learning, and financial sentiment reading into a single strategy engine.

The design adapts its equity strategies to the market regime, trending or choppy, rather than forcing one style on all weather. A full version of the work was accepted at a computing systems conference. Regime aware hybrids are a popular answer to a known failure: strategies that shine in one market mood and bleed in another.
arxiv-2601-19604:
William J. Huddie and Rembert A. Duine build a theory of a diode made from single atoms. A diode lets a current pass one way but not the other. Here the current carries spin, the magnetic property of electrons, rather than just charge. Their device is two magnetic atoms placed on the surface of a two-dimensional electron gas.

The electron gas has Rashba spin-orbit coupling, which ties electron spin to motion. Each atom's spin couples locally to the electrons passing beneath it. That coupling creates indirect interactions between the two atoms, including twisted and dissipative ones. The authors work out the microscopic theory of how the pair behaves. An atomic spin diode could become a building block for tiny magnetic electronics.
arxiv-2601-19804:
Amiya Prakash Das and colleagues simulate how irregular mineral chunks move in water. Their subject is polymetallic nodules, potato-sized lumps rich in metals that litter deep ocean floors. Mining plans would lift them through pipes in vertical flows. Predicting that transport needs to know how non-spherical shapes behave.

The team uses resolved simulations that couple fluid flow with discrete particle motion. Particles are built from merged spheres to mimic real nodule shapes. Shape raises drag well above that of a round ball of the same volume, and the chunks settle far more slowly. Wake asymmetry drives much of the difference. The results help engineers judge whether nodule collection by hydraulic lift is feasible.
arxiv-2601-19904:
Ziyu Hu and colleagues benchmark a new class of AI hardware. Large language models have outgrown traditional processors as Moore's law slows. Dataflow accelerators, which stream data through fixed computation patterns, are a promising alternative. Yet there is no standard, in-depth way to measure them on language model training.

Their benchmark, DABench-LLM, fills that gap for post-Moore dataflow accelerators. It standardises how performance is tested and reported. Fair benchmarks let buyers compare hardware honestly and guide designers to real bottlenecks. Training workloads stress memory and interconnects differently from inference. The work gives the field a shared yardstick at a moment of rapid hardware change.
arxiv-2601-20104:
Nima Torbati and colleagues build a shared resource for segmenting cell nuclei in pathology images. Separating individual nuclei in stained tissue images is a basic step in automated histology. It feeds downstream tasks like cancer grading. Many algorithms exist, but they are trained and tested on scattered datasets, making comparison unfair.

Their work, NucFuseRank, fuses datasets and ranks methods' performance across them. A common benchmark shows which approaches truly generalise between labs and scanners. Most prior work proposed yet another algorithm instead of fixing evaluation. A fused dataset with honest rankings accelerates the whole subfield. The resource serves digital pathology teams building clinical tools.
arxiv-2601-20204:
Jiguang Yu, Louis Shuo Wang, Zonghao Liu, and Jingfeng Liu study how mass moves inside a tumor and its surrounding microenvironment. Their model has two moving cell densities plus two states that switch in place rather than move. The moving populations diffuse and also drift along chemical signals, a behavior called chemotaxis.

The authors derive spectral criteria, mode by mode, for the coupled system of equations. The switching states follow ordinary differential equations at each point. Such criteria help predict when a tumor pattern stays stable and when it breaks into growth. They inform both theory and the design of models used in cancer research.
arxiv-2601-20504:
Meiqi Wu and seven colleagues work on a weak spot of text-to-video models: motion. These models have made clear progress on still-looking scenes. But when a scene changes fast and hard, the quality of the motion drops. Noise breaks the flow of time in the clip, and the parts that move most are the hardest to learn.

The authors use latent temporal discrepancy, the gap between frames inside the model's latent space, as a motion prior. It guides a loss-weighting strategy that makes training pay more heed to moving regions. Video tools are judged on motion above all, so teaching a model where motion lives could lift the whole field.
arxiv-2601-21104:
Aidan Gleich and Scott Schmidler sharpen how diffusion models are steered without retraining. Their 2026 paper addresses training-free guidance for conditional generation. A trained diffusion model can be guided toward outputs that satisfy conditions. Existing methods approximate the posterior score with point estimates. Those estimates introduce bias. They also fail to capture the multimodality of the reverse process. Several good answers may exist, and a point estimate picks one blindly.

The authors bring multilevel and sequential Monte Carlo to the task. Monte Carlo methods track a cloud of candidates instead of one guess. That cloud can represent multiple modes honestly. Guidance then steers the whole cloud toward the condition. The result should be more accurate conditional samples. The work serves image and data generation where retraining is too costly.
arxiv-2601-21204:
Hong Liu and four co-authors argue that a neglected dimension beats the fashionable one for scaling language models. Their 2026 paper compares embedding scaling with expert scaling. Mixture-of-Experts designs are the standard for sparsity scaling. They route each token to a few specialist subnetworks. Such designs face shrinking returns and system bottlenecks. The authors explore embedding scaling as a strong, orthogonal dimension.

Through analysis and tests, they find regimes where embedding scaling wins. It reaches a superior Pareto frontier there. A Pareto edge means better quality for the same cost. Widening embeddings enriches each token's picture at once. The result challenges where labs should spend their next budget. It is an architecture argument with direct cost stakes.
arxiv-2601-21304:
Haoming Wang introduces a real-valued version of a classic statistical law on bundles over flag varieties. Flag varieties are spaces built from nested sets of subspaces, common in geometry. The paper sets up four matrix normal laws that extend a split covariance structure.

The laws allow links at the level of single variables, single samples, or both. From them, the author derives the joint law of sample variances and covariances. Such tools matter for data arranged as matrices, where rows and columns both carry structure. The work widens the set of models statisticians can fit to that kind of data.
arxiv-2601-21404:
A study of ergodic flows asks how fast long-run averages settle down. For a flow that mixes a space thoroughly, time averages of a quantity should approach its overall mean. The speed of that approach is called the rate of convergence of Birkhoff averages.

The work shows that every speed, from the fastest possible down to slower than any named rate, can occur. The trick is the choice of the quantity being averaged. For flows that wind around a torus, the averaging functions can still be kept continuous. The result maps the full range of calm and wild behavior these averages can show.
arxiv-2601-21604:
Kazuki Doi, Liang Li, Ung Nguyen, and Tadashi Takayanagi study how energy and entanglement cross between two linked quantum theories. The two theories are identical and entangled at one local spot. A local kick in one theory lets them watch what travels to the other.

When the theories have holographic duals, the crossing runs through a wormhole in the dual space. Signals can pass even beyond the horizon from one side to the other. The authors confirm the picture with direct calculations in the field theory. The result is a concrete case where geometry and entanglement tell the same story.
arxiv-2601-22004:
Agnieszka Bodzenta and Alexey Bondal give a test for when an abelian category is a highest weight category. Such categories organize representation theory: their objects are built from standard pieces with a controlled order, and they appear across geometry and algebra. Recognizing one in the wild is not always easy.

The authors present criteria stated through pairs of dual exceptional sequences, ordered collections of special objects that generate the category. Their 2026 preprint applies the criteria in three cases of geometric origin. It gives new proofs for one known fact. Perverse sheaf categories on complex-analytic manifolds are highest weight, with middle perversity. Clean criteria like this turn scattered examples into a theory others can use.
arxiv-2601-22104:
Paolo Andrich and co-authors map populations from social media, carefully. Disaster response and humanitarian planning need accurate, timely population data. Censuses are slow and often miss rapid change, while social media offer a fast, dynamic alternative signal of where people are.

Two problems block that promise. Social media users do not represent the whole population, and privacy rules limit how the data can be used. The team's 2026 preprint takes a Bayesian approach to both representativeness and privacy concerns. Sound population maps could direct aid after earthquakes and floods. Aid would go to where people actually are. It would not rely on where the last census found them years earlier.
arxiv-2601-22304:
A. Guskov, for the SPD team, lays out a new detector for spin physics at a collider in Dubna, Russia. The Spin Physics Detector will sit at one of two clash points of the NICA collider, now being built. Their 2026 report calls it a general-purpose setup.

The detector will probe the spin makeup of the proton and the deuteron. It will use beams of both, each with aligned spins, at energies no other lab offers in this form. Spin maps test how quarks and gluons build matter. The report sets out what the tool will do.
arxiv-2601-22404:
Kolagani Paramahamsa studies a seller who bundles a wanted good with an unwanted extra, such as ads. The extra earns the seller pay from a third party. His 2026 preprint notes that the buyer's private facts are two-fold: what the good is worth, and what they would pay to skip the bad.

The seller must set a deal that earns the most while still luring the buyer. That two-fold spread makes the design a subtle puzzle. The work speaks to ad-backed sales, from apps to media. It shows how ad pay bends prices and terms. Buyers may gain or lose by the shift.
arxiv-2601-22804:
Rourab Paul, Krishnendu Guha, and Amlan Chakrabarti work on protecting a core math step in post-quantum security. The step, the Number Theoretic Transform, speeds up the polynomial math behind schemes like Kyber and Dilithium. Fault attacks and hidden hardware flaws can flip control signals or add delays to break it.

The authors design a transform that resists both control-flow and timing faults on flexible hardware chips. As quantum-safe systems move into real products, their hardware must survive tampering as well as math attacks. Fault-tough designs help keep that promise.
arxiv-2601-23004:
Krystof Novotny, Laureano Moro-Velázquez, and Jiri Mekyska use speech to judge cognitive status. Speech carries both sound patterns and word patterns that reflect decline in thinking. Models that use only one of those sides miss part of the picture.

Their study fuses sound and transcript features early, and checks which encoder layers help most. Layer-aware fusion improved classification of cognitive status in their tests of the approach. A speech-based check is cheap and non-invasive, which suits early screening in clinics. Attention to encoder layer depth is the study's twist, because early and late layers carry different kinds of speech information.
arxiv-2601-23204:
Baoyu Jing and a large team release TSAQA, a benchmark for question answering over time series. Time series drive decisions in finance, health, transport, and environmental science. Earlier benchmarks for time series questions covered mainly forecasting and anomaly detection.

TSAQA widens the task range for judging models on temporal data. A model has to follow patterns over time, not just spot a single value. Broader tests should push models toward real analytical skill on the data types industries actually store. Forecasting and anomaly detection were the old benchmark limits, and the new one is built to move beyond them.
arxiv-2603-01704:
Changjiang Du defines and proves a convergence trait for modules used in p-adic Hodge theory in this 2026 work. The setting involves number fields built over the p-adic numbers, with several variables tracked at once. Such modules encode Galois representations, the symmetry data that number theorists study most.

Du works over a multivariable ring and defines what overconvergence means for this class of modules. Basic traits of the new notion are then explored step by step. The main proof shows overconvergence holds at the perfectoid level, a very large and rigid limit setting. The proof leans on the geometry of the relative Fargues-Fontaine curve, a central object in modern p-adic geometry. Results of this kind extend the bridge between Galois data and explicit analytic objects.
arxiv-2603-01904:
Tao Feng, Henk Hollmann, Weicong Li, and Qing Xiang classify the symmetry groups of a special family of error-correcting codes. Their 2026 work concerns irreducible cyclic codes, whose check polynomial cannot be factored over its field. A code counts as standard when its permutation symmetries are just the cyclic shift and the Frobenius map.

The team gives a complete classification of all non-standard cases among non-degenerate codes. Their proof leans on the classification of finite simple groups, a landmark of modern algebra. Apart from a few explicit exceptional families and their descendants, every such code proves standard. Degenerate codes flip the pattern, with all but four exceptions proving non-standard. Consequences include a description of related sequence subgroups and a settled conjecture for the non-standard cases.
arxiv-2603-02004:
Gershom Seneviratne, Jianyu An, Vaibhav Shende, and colleagues teach navigation robots to avoid obstacles the way humans prefer. Their 2026 work starts from a gap: vision-driven policies move well, yet they cut close to hazards in messy real spaces. Human intuition about safe clearance is hard to encode as a simple reward.

Their method, CHOP, shows annotators the executed path beside counterfactual paths the robot could have taken. People label pairwise preferences by expected collision risk and path efficiency. Those aggregated labels then fine-tune the navigation policy toward human safety taste. On a public navigation data set, near-collisions and path deviation fall sharply across several top models. Gains transfer to a real quadruped robot, with better goal success and clearance in live runs.
arxiv-2603-02204:
Amir Asiaee, Kaveh Aryan, and James Long improve forecast ranges under experiments in this 2026 paper. Conformal prediction gives ranges that cover the true value at a set rate. Ranges shrink when test cases are matched with like calibration cases. In gene experiments, likeness means a treatment left the target untouched, but that fact is often unknown.

The team proves how wrong matches weaken coverage, with an exact formula for the loss. They then learn only the needed fact: whether each gene sits downstream of a treatment. One method reads overlap patterns across treatments to find those links. Tests on fake gene models confirm the corrected ranges hold their rate. Even with heavy mismatch, coverage stayed at the target level.
arxiv-2603-02504:
Pratibha Zunjare and Michael Hsiao make language models prove their math in this 2026 paper. Models often produce fluent but logically broken solutions to math problems. Their framework, NeuroProlog, compiles word problems into executable Prolog programs. Formal checks then guarantee the reasoning, not just the final answer.

Training mixes three tasks in one symbolic space, a strategy they call the Cocktail effect. Tasks cover formula translation, problem-to-program synthesis, and program-answer alignment. Joint training lets symbolic grounding in one task lift the others. At run time, an error-aware decoder repairs programs step by step. Gains over single-task training were significant across four model scales. Their best setup beat larger program synthesis systems with far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2603-03204:
Ana Achúcarro, Perseas Christodoulidis, Jinn-Ouk Gong, and Oksana Iarygina rescue a class of early-universe models from a feared instability. In multi-field inflation, a negative mass for sideways perturbations usually signals disaster. Several known models seemed to break that rule, and their 2026 paper explains why they survive.

In what they call ultra slow-turn models, the trajectory's turn rate shrinks exponentially fast, switching off the would-be instability before it grows. The total entropy perturbation, they argue, is the reliable judge of stability, not the sideways mass alone. Popular string- and supergravity-inspired scenarios, including fibre inflation and modular inflation, fall into this safe class. The criterion should help model builders sort viable universes from unstable ones.
arxiv-2603-03404:
Tetiana Obikhod and Ievgenii Petrenko analyze one of the rarest Higgs boson production modes at the Large Hadron Collider: a Higgs made together with a single top quark. Because the top quark is the heaviest known particle, this channel probes its coupling to the Higgs, the top Yukawa coupling, with unusual directness. Their 2026 paper builds on the ATLAS experiment's search strategy at current collider energies.

Improved modeling aims to sharpen sensitivity to new physics and tighten Standard Model limits. Simulations map the expected rates for the channel's sub-modes, and a flipped-sign coupling scenario shows clear rate enhancements from constructive interference, matching expectations. Key motion and angle distributions agree with ATLAS projections. The work also optimizes event selection and error estimates, and projects what the future high-luminosity collider run could achieve.
arxiv-2603-03704:
Yoonwoo Kim and five colleagues let a language model whisper common sense into a robot's map of the unseen. A robot planning in a cluttered room cannot see every object, and naive planners ignore the stray objects they stumble on. Their 2026 framework, CoCo-TAMP, builds two commonsense rules into state estimation: objects have likely homes, and similar objects cluster together while dissimilar ones separate.

Writing those rules by hand would be endless, so a large language model supplies them on the fly. Its guidance shapes a hierarchical estimate of where task-relevant objects probably are, focusing the search. In simulation, planning and execution time fell by nearly two thirds against a commonsense-free baseline. In real-world robot demonstrations, the saving grew to nearly three quarters. Long-horizon chores become tractable when the robot guesses like a person.

Baha'u'llah, founder of the Baha'i faith, wrote the Kitab-i-Iqan, The Book of Certitude, in Baghdad in the early 1860s. Ali Kuli Khan made this first English translation, published in 1904. The work stands as the faith's foundational treatise on its central doctrine.

Valentine, a supposed fifteenth-century monk, lent his name to a shelf of Paracelsian writings. Antimony, a brittle metal-like substance, was the wonder drug of that school.

Its title pictures the metal riding in triumph over the diseases that resist common medicines. Bernard of Clairvaux ruled half of Europe from his abbey by letter, and Samuel J. Eales chose and translated a set of those letters in 1904. Bernard wrote to popes, kings, bishops, monks, and his own kin, in a voice that could scold, soothe, and blaze on one page. Readers meet the abbot rebuking luxury, defending his friend Abelard's enemies and attacking Abelard himself, and mourning the crusade's failure. His style is a river of scripture turned to daily business. The selection shows the man behind the saint: tender to novices, iron to princes. Eales adds notes to place each letter in its fight.

cia-0000015304: A letter to Samuel Goudsmit from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated January 5, 1958. It takes up points by Hynek and Lloyd, per the clipped title. Hynek was the Air Force's own astronomer on saucers. The mail shows agency men trading views with the few experts who knew the case files.
cia-0000022604: A dead American pilot was sighted in Hanoi, North Vietnam, in a CIA record dated in 1973. Hanoi was the capital, seat of the government that held American prisoners. A sighting there of a dead pilot carried weight for the final accounting of the war. Staff logged it in the year the living prisoners came home at last.
cia-0000028304: Stability of the present regime in Iran is weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1958. The present regime meant the Shah's government, five years after the coup that secured it. Stability papers asked how deep a ruler's support ran and where the cracks might open. For Iran the question would return with far greater force twenty years later.
cia-0000037104: Disbursements for travel and other expenses fill a CIA record dated November 5, 1942, naming Cook, Phenix, Osborne, Tyler, Rado, and others. The page comes from the OSS, the wartime office that stood behind the later CIA. It sets out payments name by name in the plain hand of a ledger keeper. Wartime secret work still ran on vouchers and receipts, and pages like this one kept the young office's spending in order.
cia-0000042704:
President Cristiani issued a statement on the murder investigation, in a CIA record dated October 1, 1989 in the catalog. Alfredo Cristiani was El Salvador's president during the war's last years. His government stood accused by critics of shielding the killers.

Inside, the president's own words on the investigation are set down. A head of state under fire chooses each such word with great care. The file preserves the official promise of an inquiry. Readers can weigh that promise against the slow course the case then took, as soldiers were named, held, and tried over the years that followed.
cia-0000049004: Many Salvadoran military officers were pleased by the assassination of leaders of the revolutionary movement, and a CIA item dated November 1, 1980, records their reaction. The item is a cold one: satisfaction at murder, noted in plain bureaucratic words. It survives among the Truth Commission files as evidence of the climate inside the armed forces.
cia-0000049104: Victor Manuel Santos Marinez is the named subject of a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. The series is full of such single-name files, each a person caught in the war's paperwork. What the system knew about him sits in the document, behind a title that gives nothing else away.
cia-0000049404: The Election Outlook in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049404, dated May 5, 1982. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper looks ahead to a Salvadoran election. It is a brief declassified forecast whose title states its aim, companion in spirit to the agency's other Salvadoran election outlook from two years later.
cia-0000098304: Chinese Communist short-range military intentions, with intentions misspelled in the heading, are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098304, dated June 4, 1962. The title limits its scope to the short range. Readers find a brief declassified intentions paper from China reporting, its spelling flaw preserved in the catalog beside its more polished neighbors.
cia-0000104904: Security Guidance and Procedures is the heading, ending with a semicolon, on declassified CIA document 0000104904, dated June 5, 1994. The sample shows the file is Director of Central Intelligence Directive 1/21, on physical security standards for SCI facilities. Its sample pages give an effective date of July 29, 1994. The directive states that such standards are established under the National Security Act and an executive order.
cia-0000119204:
From about November 1987, this CIA document reports a sighting of a possible burial site for missing Americans in Xieng Khouang Province, Laos. The province, home to the Plain of Jars, saw heavy fighting and bombing during the war. Reports of graves were among the grimmest leads the agency followed.

Each reported site had to be checked against records of lost aircraft and missing crews. Most leads led nowhere, but each one mattered to a family waiting for news. The document preserves the sighting as it was reported, a single entry in the huge file of the missing that stayed open long after the war ended.
cia-0000119704: A January 1953 CIA paper surveys conditions and trends in the Middle East that bear on American security. Oil, the new state of Israel, and rising Arab national feeling were combining into a lasting problem for Washington. The paper maps those pressures at the start of a stormy decade. Papers of this breadth set the frame for smaller country studies, giving leaders one map of a region that would occupy them for years.
cia-0000124304: An October 1972 CIA document covers air raid shelters at Luta, Shenyang, and Shih-chia-chuang, plus the Peking subway and suspected sites, the heading breaking off. China's civil defense building was read in Washington as a sign of fear of war. The paper maps the shelters as plotted. Shelter digging on that scale suggested a state preparing its people for attack, and analysts weighed it as evidence in judging how real China's war fears were.
cia-0000132504: Cuban reaction to anti-Castro invasions fills a CIA document dated February 3, 1961. The word invasions sits in quotation marks in the headline, showing the agency's care with the term. The great invasion was still two months off, but smaller raids had already begun. The short document gauges how Havana answered those early attacks and prepared its people for larger ones to come.
cia-0000132604:
A blunt verdict stands as the headline of a CIA paper dated August 6, 1960: the Cuban situation worsens. By that summer Washington had stopped hoping that a moderate Cuba would emerge from the revolution. Seizures of property, the Soviet embrace, and the coming break all pointed the same way.

The paper gives the worsening picture behind its own headline, fact by fact. For readers, it marks the month the agency's tone changed for good. Earlier reports had still weighed chances and options with some hope. This one records a slide that analysts no longer thought could be turned back. It dates that bleak judgment with care.
cia-0000135604: A Spanish-language document dated 2 September 1960 survives among the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force the CIA was training for an invasion of Cuba. September 1960 fell in the brigade's early buildup, well before the April 1961 landing. The catalog record gives no subject or author for this item. Readers who know Spanish can judge its contents directly; the title alone supports no more than its date, its language, and the file it belongs to.
cia-0000135804: Orders from Lincoln fill a CIA cable dated May 3, 1954. Lincoln was the code name for the base running the Guatemala operation. The cable carries both working orders and general guidance for the field. Its own headline grammar stumbles, a flaw kept from the original. Orders from Lincoln were the marching orders of the campaign. The short cable keeps them as sent.
cia-0000135904: The CIA document from 1 April 1954 deals with acts of force planned for the days before D-day, in a file now declassified. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136104: The cable dated 5 March 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with MT/4, a two-part code standing alone as the whole subject of a Lincoln cable. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136204: With a date of 5 May 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a meeting between Calligeris and Estrada. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136304: LINCOLN asked for authority to strike in this June 1954 PBSUCCESS cable, reporting that a setback at Chiquimula that morning made action by the army in the capital more likely. The station proposed a strike the next day by three fighter aircraft, calling it an impressive show against a military, isolated, and easy-to-identify target ringed by a moat. Timing mattered, the cable argues, so the cause and effect would be read the right way.
cia-0000136404: Names of people who know about communist infiltration fill this January 1954 cable. It went to the senior representative at LINCOLN. The names were offered as possible help. One man is an agent living abroad. He made recent trips to Guatemala. Another is a former White Russian. He keeps contact with refugee groups arriving in Cuba. He picked up word on penetrations there. Contact runs through still other named persons. The names themselves stay withheld as IDENs.
cia-0000136704: A Spanish document dated 4 August 1960, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the CIA's Cuban exile force. August 1960 fell in the brigade's first training season; the unit had been formed only that year. The catalog record names no subject for this item. It survives in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, an early dated piece of the brigade's paperwork from the operation's first summer.
cia-0000136904: Fuzz up the question of official backing, headquarters instructs LINCOLN in this May 1954 cable on deception and confusion activities. Reports keep arriving of a figure boasting of official United States backing, and those boasts are cutting into knowledge the operation wants blurred. With future Guatemalan charges in mind, it is particularly desirable to confuse them as to the sources of financial and other backing. The cable orders deliberate muddiness about who was paying for the rebellion.
cia-0000140404: Experiment in the field, not the laboratory. This April 1955 paper on hypnotism and covert operations argues that course. Academic experts are often too pessimistic, the writer says. Their caution rests on very few cases. Agency experimenters contradict much of it. He has personally witnessed responses that respected experts called impossible. Book knowledge feels cramped and closed-in to him. Evidence does not yet prove hypnotism a workable covert weapon. Only field tests can show what works, he argues.
cia-03019104: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1955/12/08, a CIA publication. Another December briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. The historical record keeps it. The paper lived through the years.
cia-03181204: May 3, 1955: the bulletin delivered the day's intelligence. The global summary reached Washington's leaders. The Cold War's spring brief. Time has kept the file intact. This declassified paper is maintained. The file remains. The document lasts.
cia-06007804: THE PRESIDENT'S DAILY BRIEF 29 AUGUST 1974, a CIA publication. The presidential briefing. This file preserves that declassified brief. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. The historical record keeps it. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
cia-06586904: DPRK PARTY DAILY BLAMES US FOR OPENING UP 'PRELUDE' TO 'CYBER WAR', a CIA document. The North Korean charge. This file preserves that declassified paper. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time.
coniston-volume-04: The fourth volume of Churchill's Coniston moves toward its close. Small-town politics reach their decisive hour in New Hampshire. The honest hero faces his greatest trial. A satisfying end to a fine American novel.
conrad-nostromo-1904:
Joseph Conrad published Nostromo in 1904, a large novel set in Costaguana, a made-up country in South America. A silver mine drives the plot and draws in foreign money and local politics. Nostromo is an Italian sailor trusted by all sides. Revolutions rise and fall around the mine and the port town of Sulaco.

Conrad follows many figures, from mine owners to rebels and their families. Silver brings wealth, but it also brings betrayal and death. Nostromo himself is changed by the trust placed in him. Readers prize the book as a vast and clear-eyed account of empire, greed, and power.
constitution-afghanistan-2004: Afghanistan's 2004 Constitution built an Islamic republic after Taliban rule. It set rights and a presidency. The Tower library holds the full text. It guided a fragile state. Words promised. Reality strained. Law stood. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.

More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-panama-2004: Panama's 1972 Constitution, amended through 2004, frames its republic. It took the canal. The Tower library holds the full text. It seized the ditch. Americans left. Ships paid. Nation profited. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-uruguay-2004: Uruguay's 1967 Constitution, amended through 2004, frames its republic. It guards calm democracy. The Tower library holds the full text. It ended army rule. Soldiers left. Voters came. Peace held. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-04:
The fourth number of The Equinox came out in September 1910, fat with the work of half a year. Crowley's journal had become a fixture of the London occult world by then. Each number aimed to be a small library of the order's mind.

Rites and holy books appear in these pages in their first print form. Around them stand poems, tales, and sharp reviews of rival works. The mix was the point: magic as a whole life of the mind. This number keeps the founding record of Thelema thick and rich throughout. It rewards any reader who opens it at random.
crowley-mathers-goetia-of-solomon-1904:
The Goetia, in the 1904 edition translated by Mathers and introduced by Crowley, is the first printed edition of the first book of the Lemegeton. The Lemegeton, or Lesser Key of Solomon, is a grimoire, a handbook of ceremonial magic ascribed to King Solomon. Mathers worked from manuscripts in the British Museum.

The text lists seventy-two spirits, with their seals, ranks, offices, and the hours and tools for calling them. Crowley's introduction frames the spirits as forces of the human brain rather than as literal demons. The edition defined modern ceremonial magic's demonology and set the pattern for later occult publishing.
davies-celtic-researches-1804:
Edward Davies, a Welsh cleric, wrote this study of the old Britons in 1804, five years before his book on druid rites. It was the first full try in the Romantic age to build a Celtic past in one scheme. He worked from Welsh verse, old tales, and stone works.

Davies traced the first Britons to the east and tied their faith to the druids. He read names, myths, and rites as clues to one lost world of belief. Later scholars set much of it aside, but the book set the form for Celtic studies.
defoe-the-storm-1704:
Daniel Defoe published The Storm in 1704, an eyewitness collection on the Great Storm of 1703. The book is often called the first work of modern journalism in English prose writing. Defoe advertised for accounts and wove his own survey into a national record of loss.

The storm of November 1703 sank ships, unroofed churches, and killed thousands across southern England in one night. Defoe prints letters from ports and parishes, lists of wrecked men-of-war, and chimneys down in London. He weighs natural causes against providence, and scolds both scoffers and panicked preachers of the day in print. Eddystone Lighthouse fell with its builder inside, a loss the book records in stark detail for readers. Its method, gather testimony fast and print it plain, set a pattern for news.
duckworth-morphology-anthropology-1904:
W. L. H. Duckworth, a Cambridge scholar of the body, wrote this text book on form and the study of man in 1904. It joins two themes: the shapes of ape and man, and the rise of man from ape kin. Cambridge men used it to teach the new field.

Duckworth sets out skulls, brains, and bones of apes and men side by side. He then turns to the fossil finds known in his day and fits them in the line of growth. The book forms a bridge from the living body to the claims for fossil man.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-04: Volume four of the Essays turns to friendship and loss. Montaigne writes of his beloved friend La Boetie with aching tenderness. These are among the most loved pages ever written. Grief made noble by a great mind.
europmc-pmc10017004:
Parasher reviews the state of knowledge on COVID-19 in a 2021 paper, with a focus on how the disease harms the body. The virus behind it, SARS-CoV-2, belongs to the coronavirus family. It first caused a wave of severe lung infections in Wuhan, China, and then spread worldwide.

The review explains the illness step by step, from infection to symptoms in the lungs and beyond. It covers how doctors recognize the disease and the treatments in use at the time. Readers get a clear summary of a fast-moving field at an early stage.
europmc-pmc10030804:
Chen and colleagues review how ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron, interacts with inflammatory signals, in a 2023 paper. In ferroptosis, iron fuels damage to cell membranes until the cell dies. Inflammation is the body's alarm and repair response, but when it runs out of control it harms tissue.

The review maps the shared signals between the two processes. It shows how each can trigger or restrain the other in disease. The authors discuss what this crosstalk means for treatment of cancer, organ injury, and other conditions where both processes run.
europmc-pmc10284704:
Nardou and colleagues report that psychedelic drugs reopen a critical period for social reward learning, in a 2023 study. Critical periods are windows early in life when the brain learns certain skills with ease, after which the window closes. Social reward learning, the pull of social approval, has such a window in mice and likely in humans.

The team found that several psychedelics reopen that window in adult mice. The reopening lasted from days to weeks depending on the drug. The result may explain why these drugs help in therapy that involves relearning social patterns.
europmc-pmc10903104:
Klemmensen and colleagues review the role of faulty energy hubs in brain diseases in this 2024 paper. Mitochondria are the parts of cells that make most of their energy. When they fail, nerve cells suffer, since the brain needs much energy. The review links such failure to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and two other nerve diseases.

The authors trace the history of this research and explain how healthy mitochondria work. They detail how harmful oxygen molecules from faulty hubs can damage DNA caps and gene controls. Current trials of drugs that target these hubs are surveyed. Current human trials of drugs that target these hubs are listed and weighed. The authors frame such drugs as a route to ease symptoms and slow the course of these diseases.
europmc-pmc11031404:
Brown and a large team report a phase 1 trial of engineered T cells for hard-to-treat brain tumours in this 2024 paper. High-grade glioma is an aggressive brain cancer, and cases that return after treatment respond poorly to current care. CAR-T therapy arms a patient's own T cells with a sensor for a tumour target. Here the target was a surface protein called IL-13Ralpha2, and cells were delivered near the tumour rather than into the blood.

Sixty-five patients took part, most with recurrent glioblastoma, the authors report. The trial tested three delivery routes: into the tumour, into the brain's fluid spaces, or both. No dose-limiting harms appeared in any arm, so no maximum tolerated dose was set. Two severe events were judged probably tied to treatment. The final arm paired dual delivery with an improved cell-making process and reached 200 million cells per dose cycle.
europmc-pmc11045904:
Adamu, Li, Gao, and Xue review brain inflammation as a driver of nerve cell loss in this 2024 paper. Neuroinflammation is the brain's immune reaction to injury, infection, or disease. Support cells called glia switch on, release alarm chemicals, and make harmful oxygen and nitrogen species. Short bursts protect the brain, but a reaction that runs too long turns harmful.

The review maps the major signal paths that link this reaction to Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease, and multiple sclerosis. Each disease shows its own spread pattern across brain regions. Three therapy routes get close attention: stem cell therapy, gene-based intervention, and nanoparticles, meaning specks engineered to carry drugs. All three aim to calm the reaction and slow nerve loss. The authors stress that grasping this link is pivotal for future treatments.
europmc-pmc11120204:
GBD 2021 Risk Factors Collaborators quantify how 88 risk factors drive disease worldwide in this 2024 study. Knowing what exposures cost in health terms is required to set sound public health policy. The study spans 204 countries and territories plus 811 subnational locations from 1990 to 2021. It is part of the Global Burden of Disease program.

The team drew on 54,561 distinct data sources, they report. They built estimates for 631 risk and outcome pairs, such as smoking paired with lung cancer. Each pair passed a data-driven check for a real association. Exposure levels, relative risks, and the share of disease blamed on each factor were estimated by age, sex, place, and year. The method follows a comparative risk framework that layers risks in a causal web. Results are given at global, regional, and national levels.
europmc-pmc11270804:
Liu and a large team review the protein tagging system that controls protein lifespan, and its role in cancer, in this 2024 paper. Ubiquitination attaches a small tag that marks proteins for destruction or changes their behaviour. Enzymes that add the tag and enzymes that remove it are both dysregulated in many cancers. The system as a whole is called the ubiquitin-proteasome system.

The review covers the system's part in all hallmarks of cancer, the classic traits that define malignancy. It also covers metabolic rewiring, tumour immune responses, and cell flexibility. Drug discovery progress gets a full survey. Two new strategies stand out: PROTACs, which drag a chosen protein to the destruction machinery, and molecular glues, which stick proteins together to force the same fate. The authors present both as a new generation of anticancer design.
europmc-pmc11271404:
Ekanem and a very large team assess the safety of pulsed field ablation for atrial fibrillation in this 2024 study. Atrial fibrillation is a chaotic heart rhythm that raises stroke risk. Pulsed field ablation uses electric pulses to scar the tissue that triggers the rhythm. Early data suggested it spares nearby structures, unlike heat-based methods.

The MANIFEST-17K study gathered post-approval data from 106 of 116 centres, covering 17,642 patients. No oesophageal damage, vein narrowing, or lasting nerve palsy was reported, the team found. Major complications hit about 1 percent of patients. Heart sac bleeding, called tamponade, led at 0.36 percent, then vascular events at 0.30 percent of patients. Stroke was rare at 0.12 percent and death rarer still, at 0.03 percent of patients. Unexpected events included coronary spasm in 0.14 percent of cases.
europmc-pmc1241104:
Olsson and co-authors studied cadmium levels in Swedish farm families in 2002. Cadmium is a toxic metal that builds up in kidneys. Food is a main source for nonsmokers. The team measured cadmium in blood and urine of farm residents.

Median blood cadmium was 1.8 nanomoles per liter across the group. Women had 1.8 times the blood cadmium of men in never-smoking couples. That gap held despite women eating less cadmium per body weight. Low iron likely raised absorption in women. Levels also rose with age and past smoking. Local farm food formed a small, varied share of intake.
europmc-pmc1409804:
Finding genes in a string of DNA is hard when the clues are patchy. Stanke and co-authors took on that task in 2006. Their method blends hints from outside sources, such as matches to known proteins, with clues inside the DNA itself. It weighs both kinds of proof in one math model.

The team built the method into the gene finder AUGUSTUS, making a tool called AUGUSTUS+. On human chromosome 22, hints from known genes helped it call 89 percent of exons right. An exon is a part of a gene that codes for protein. Stanke shows that even the lack of a match can guide a sound call.
europmc-pmc1463904:
A chikungunya virus outbreak swept the Indian Ocean islands in 2005 and 2006. Schuffenecker and co-authors read the virus genome to trace its spread. The virus, spread by mosquitoes, causes fever and severe joint pain. On Réunion Island it infected about a third of the people.

The team sequenced six full virus samples and parts from 127 patients. The outbreak strain came from East African stock. Its changes over time could be traced step by step. One sample from spinal fluid held unique shifts found in no blood sample. Two changes sat in a surface protein that fuses the virus with cells. Schuffenecker maps how a local strain grew into a regional wave.
europmc-pmc1564004:
Parents asked to rate a child's quality of life often disagree with the child. Cremeens, Eiser, and Blades measured that gap in 2006. They gave a standard survey to 149 healthy children aged five to eight, and to 103 of their parents.

Agreement was low, with correlation scores from 0.02 to 0.23. Parents and children differed on every subscale. The oldest children matched parents best on total and social scores. The youngest matched best on physical health. Parents' own quality of life colored their ratings of the child. Cremeens warns proxy reports are a weak stand-in for a child's own view.
europmc-pmc1790904:
Edgar presented PILER-CR in 2007, a program built to find CRISPR repeats in bacterial genomes. CRISPR elements are short, near-identical DNA repeats split by unique spacer sequences of similar length. General repeat-finding tools can spot them, but their output often needs heavy manual cleanup before study.

PILER-CR was designed for this one pattern, so it runs fast and reports the repeats in a usable form. It scanned a five-million-letter genome in about five seconds on a desktop computer of the time. Checks against hand-curated results and published surveys showed both high sensitivity and high specificity, meaning it missed few real repeats and flagged few false ones. Edgar also released a catalog of candidate repeats found across 346 prokaryotic genomes.
europmc-pmc1852404:
Kingsford, Ayanbule and Salzberg built in 2007 a fast method to find the stop signals that end gene transcription in bacteria. These Rho-independent terminators are short DNA motifs, usually a GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of thymine letters. Finding them maps operons, the gene groups read as one unit.

Few terminators had been verified outside two model bacteria, so computing was the only practical route at scale. Their method produced an extensive predicted collection across 343 prokaryotes. The survey let them probe a second puzzle: why some bacteria carry special DNA uptake sequences near these sites. Such sequences help cells pull in outside DNA. The terminator catalog and the uptake link together give a genome-wide view of how bacterial transcription ends.
europmc-pmc1896004:
Miller, Bosch and co-authors inventoried in 2007 the innate immune toolkit of cnidarians, the phylum of jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones. Innate immunity is the inborn first defense line, and in these early animals it was assumed to be simple. The team mined genomic resources from two cnidarian classes.

Sea anemones and their kin, the basal Anthozoa, turned out to hold several key parts of the vertebrate innate repertoire. Those parts include receptor and signaling pieces long thought to be later inventions. Hydra, a member of the other class, Hydrozoa, lacks many of them. The pattern suggests the common ancestor was already complex, and Hydra's line later lost genes by chance. Immune origins thus run deeper, and simpler toolkits can be the derived state, not the starting point.
europmc-pmc1964804:
Lombardo, Baron-Cohen and co-authors tested in 2007 whether autism involves thinking about oneself, not just about others. People on the autism spectrum show deep social difficulties, and empathy problems are well documented. Whether self-referential thought, the intrapersonal mirror of empathy, is also affected was unclear.

Thirty adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism, aged 19 to 45, were matched with 30 controls by age, sex, and IQ. In the self-reference task they judged adjectives about themselves, a close other, a distant other, or the words alone, then took a surprise memory test. The battery also measured alexithymia, private self-consciousness, self-focused attention, four empathy measures including the Eyes test, and autistic traits. The study design lets the authors ask whether self and empathy deficits travel together.
