europmc-pmc2244704:
Spurgeon, Jones and Ramakrishnan described a microfluidic gene expression platform in 2008 built around real-time PCR. Real-time PCR is the gold standard for measuring gene activity, but it is slow and low-throughput. Their chip uses tiny fluid channels to run many reactions in parallel. A single chip performs 2,304 simultaneous measurements, yet needs less pipetting than setting up a standard 96-well plate.

On one chip they measured 45 different genes across 18 tissues, with replicates included. Results agreed excellently with conventional real-time PCR on the same samples. Reproducibility beat commercial DNA microarrays, the usual high-throughput alternative. The platform targets the common workflow where a genome-wide study narrows interest to twenty to one hundred key genes. Those genes can then be measured across far larger sample sets than microarrays allow.
europmc-pmc2265304:
Selman, Pardo and Kaminski argued in 2008 that idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis may arise from embryonic programmes wrongly switched back on. This lung disease is chronic, progressive and usually lethal, with unknown cause. Injured alveolar epithelial cells are thought to activate mesenchymal cells, forming scar foci that destroy lung tissue with excess matrix. Such reawakening of developmental pathways is common in cancer but rare in non-malignant disease.

The authors review gene expression studies and animal models pointing to developmental signalling in the disease. Candidate pathways include Wnt, which guides embryonic patterning, and the TGF-beta family. TGF-beta promotes fibrosis and can convert epithelial cells toward a mesenchymal state. Related BMP signals often oppose those effects. Understanding which embryonic circuits reactivate could explain why the fibrosis persists rather than healing.
europmc-pmc2268004:
Caws and a large team tested in 2008 whether bacterial strain and host genes together shape tuberculosis disease form. Some Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains may spread beyond the lungs more readily, causing meningitis. The team compared 187 Vietnamese adults with tuberculous meningitis against 237 with uncomplicated lung tuberculosis, plus 392 cord blood controls. Bacterial isolates were typed by large sequence changes, and hosts by variants in two innate immunity genes.

The Euro-American bacterial lineage was underrepresented in meningitis, with an odds ratio of 0.395 for that outcome. Those strains may disseminate less. Hosts carrying one variant of the TLR-2 gene were more likely to carry the East-Asian Beijing strain. Its odds ratio was 1.57, and its confidence interval excluded no effect. The study population was Vietnamese.
europmc-pmc2292704:
Hundertmark and Hincha published this 2008 genome-wide survey of LEA proteins in Arabidopsis thaliana, a small flowering plant used widely in research. LEA stands for late embryogenesis abundant, meaning these proteins build up late in seed growth. They are thought to help cells survive drying out, cold, and other stress.

The authors found 51 genes that code for LEA proteins, and they sorted them into nine groups. Using a lab method that counts gene activity, they showed all 51 genes were switched on somewhere in the plant. Levels were higher in seeds than in leaves or stems. About a third of the genes sat in tandem repeats, side by side on the chromosome. Many were switched on by cold, drought, or a stress hormone.
europmc-pmc2346504:
Rosas and a large team searched for a blood test for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in 2008. In this disease the lungs scar and stiffen over time, and doctors lack a simple blood marker for it. A biomarker is a measurable sign of a disease.

They measured 49 proteins in blood from 74 patients and 53 healthy controls. A set of five proteins separated patients from controls with about 98% accuracy on both sensitivity and specificity. Two proteins, MMP1 and MMP7, stood out and were also raised in lung tissue and lung wash fluid. Both stayed normal in two other lung diseases, which helps tell them apart. Raised MMP7 also appeared in people with early, symptom-free lung disease and tracked falling lung power.
europmc-pmc2394204:
Clifford, Smith, Aguado, and Franceschi compared HPV types in precancerous cervical lesions and in cancer in 2003. Only some lesions progress to cancer, and the team asked whether the virus type predicts that step. They pooled published data on high-grade lesions, called HSIL, and on squamous cell carcinoma, the main cervical cancer form.

The combined data covered 8,594 cancer cases and 4,338 high-grade lesion cases. Three types, HPV16, 18, and 45, were each more common in cancers than in lesions. The reverse held for types 31, 33, 52, and 58, which sat more often in lesions that stayed put. The authors read this as evidence that lesions carrying 16, 18, or 45 preferentially move on to cancer. That matters for screening follow-up and for vaccine trials that use lesion prevention as their yardstick.
europmc-pmc2459204:
Jeon and Murray reviewed whether diabetes raises the risk of active tuberculosis in 2008. Tuberculosis is a bacterial lung infection still common in poorer countries, where diabetes is now rising fast. If diabetes truly feeds tuberculosis, the overlap threatens disease control on both fronts.

They gathered 13 observational studies covering 1,786,212 people and 17,698 tuberculosis cases. Combining the cohort studies, which follow people forward in time, diabetes came with a relative risk of 3.11 for developing active tuberculosis. Case-control studies varied widely, with odds ratios from 1.16 to 7.83 depending on the population studied. Effects ran stronger outside North America. The authors concluded the link holds across designs, making people with diabetes a priority group for tuberculosis screening and preventive treatment in high-burden regions.
europmc-pmc2568804:
Tyler and colleagues showed in 2008 that gentle ultrasound can switch on brain circuits without wires or implants. Stimulating the brain usually means electrodes or light-emitting devices placed invasively. Ultrasound instead passes through bone and tissue and can be focused from outside, so the team tested low-intensity, low-frequency pulses on mouse hippocampal slices and whole brains taken from mice.

The pulses remotely excited neurons and set network activity going. They worked by opening voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, the gates that launch nerve signals. The activation was strong enough to trigger the release machinery at synapses, so signals passed between neurons in the circuit. The authors conclude ultrasound offers a powerful noninvasive tool for probing and potentially treating brain circuits.
europmc-pmc2713404:
Towner and co-authors reported in 2009 that Egyptian fruit bats in a Ugandan cave carry diverse Marburg viruses and likely seeded infections in miners. Marburg causes a severe bleeding fever with high death rates in Africa. In 2007 two miners who worked in Kitaka Cave fell ill, and the cave held a huge colony of these bats.

Testing found virus RNA in about five percent of sampled bats, antibodies in bat blood, and live virus in bat tissues. Virus was taken nine months apart, which shows long-term circulation in the colony of over one hundred thousand bats. Bat and miner virus genomes matched closely, which supports bats as a major natural reservoir.
europmc-pmc2784904:
Corthay reviewed in 2009 how regulatory T cells work, the CD4 T cells charged with suppressing other T helper cells that might harm the body. Their proposed jobs include holding self-tolerance to prevent autoimmune disease, calming allergy and asthma, and protecting the fetus during pregnancy. Yet basic questions about these cells remain open, and the review defines them plainly.

Identifying regulatory cells is itself a problem. Every marker in current use, from CD25 to Foxp3, also appears on ordinary activated T cells, so none is truly specific. Their suppression switches on only for specific antigens, and their receptor patterns suggest they are usually not self-reactive. Even their status as a separate lineage is disputed, since ordinary helper subsets can also suppress. Some regulatory cells can even convert into effector cells in the body.
europmc-pmc2845804:
Hampshire, Chamberlain, Monti, Duncan, and Owen used brain scans in 2010 to settle what the right inferior frontal gyrus, a patch of frontal brain, actually does during self-control. Scans during stop-signal tasks, where people must cancel a started movement, light up this region. Yet those tasks mix stopping with simply spotting an important cue.

The team held the stimuli identical while varying what the cue demanded: stop, make a different movement, or do nothing at all. The region switched on whenever an important cue was detected, whether or not any movement was actually stopped. The finding reframes the area as a salience watcher for the brain, not a dedicated brake pedal for behavior.
europmc-pmc2860504:
Lohmann and colleagues introduced in 2010 a fast way to find hub regions in brain scans taken while people rest. The scans, called resting-state fMRI, record slow waves of activity across the whole brain with no task to perform. Their method scores each tiny volume unit by how strongly it links to other well-linked units, a math idea borrowed from how search engines rank web pages.

Unlike older hub measures, the new score needs no preset cutoff and runs fast enough for the whole cerebrum at once. It can work from simple correlations or from more robust links between regions. Tests on real scan data picked out known hub areas and showed the score stays stable, giving brain mappers a practical tool for whole-brain network studies.
europmc-pmc2896904:
Costa, Angelini, De Feis, and Ciccodicola surveyed in 2010 RNA-Seq, the method that reads all RNA in a sample by deep sequencing, and the hurdles it brings. New machines read hundreds of thousands of DNA fragments at once, so RNA can be counted directly instead of being probed indirectly. The approach measures gene activity, alternative splicing, where one gene yields several messages, and which parental copy of a gene is used.

That richness comes with cost: files are massive and riddled with biases that older analysis habits cannot handle. The survey walks through the workflow, from aligning reads to counting and comparing, and names the open problems in each step. Bioinformatics must mature alongside the sequencers, the authors stress, or data will pile up faster than insight.
europmc-pmc2904704:
Cattuto and colleagues demonstrated in 2010 a wearable sensor system that records face-to-face human contact with second-level detail. Knowing who meets whom, and for how long, is central to modeling how infections spread, yet diaries and surveys capture it crudely. Their active RFID badges exchange low-power radio packets only when wearers stand close and face each other, logging each encounter in real time.

Three deployments at very different community sizes produced contact networks with shared statistical fingerprints. Encounter lengths spanned from twenty seconds to hours with no typical duration, a heavy-tailed pattern. People with more contacts also held longer ones, a super-linear link the team highlights. Such data let modelers replace guessed contact patterns with measured ones.
europmc-pmc2921404:
Wu and colleagues set out in 2010 to standardize how gut bacteria are surveyed in human feces by DNA tag sequencing. Studies of the gut microbiome were exploding, but each lab stored, extracted, and sequenced samples differently. They took stool from ten people and varied each step: immediate deep freezing against one or two days on ice, three commercial extraction kits against hot phenol bead beating.

Samples taken one centimeter apart in the same stool matched closely, setting the natural noise floor. Against person-to-person differences, which were vast, the method choices moved results only modestly, especially when counting which bacteria were present rather than their exact shares. Storage on ice for a day or two was tolerable. The study gives the young field a validated, practical sampling recipe.
europmc-pmc2962904:
Salem and Thiemermann reviewed mesenchymal stromal cells, versatile adult cells that can become several tissue types, in a 2010 article on their biology and medical status. Reports credited these cells with aiding repair across many organs.

After growing in culture and delivery into the body, the cells home to injured tissue and calm inflammation, lowering harmful signals while raising protective ones. They also suppress immune attackers including T cells and natural killer cells. Lab progress, including use of donor cells from others, pushed trials forward, with heart and kidney uses highlighted in the review.
europmc-pmc2970904:
Lindorff-Larsen and colleagues refined part of a widely used protein simulation toolkit in a 2010 study, improving how amino acid side chains twist in computer models. Longer simulations had exposed small accuracy faults in existing force fields.

They singled out four residue types whose simulated twist patterns strayed most from database expectations, then refitted their settings against high-level quantum calculations. Microsecond-long test simulations in water matched laboratory NMR measurements far better than the old settings. The updated package, named ff99SB-ILDN after the improved residues, gives modellers a more faithful view of protein motion.
europmc-pmc2978704:
Suhre and colleagues ran a multi-platform scan of small molecules in blood from a German population study in 2010, hunting the metabolic footprint of diabetes. No single instrument can read the whole set of body chemicals, so they combined three.

Fasting blood from forty people reporting diabetes and sixty controls yielded measurements of several hundred distinct molecules by magnetic resonance and mass methods. Known diabetes signs reappeared, including a sugar marker, a ketone body, and certain amino acids, and traces of diabetes drugs were detectable. The exercise shows combined platforms can sketch disease chemistry in everyday population samples.
europmc-pmc3002804:
Omar reviewed oleuropein, the bitter phenolic compound that gives extra-virgin olive oil much of its bite, in a 2010 article. Olive products anchor the Mediterranean diet and carry a long folk reputation for health.

Recent studies tie oleuropein, found across the olive plant, to a wide portfolio of effects. It fights oxidation and inflammation and slows artery clogging. In lab work it also acts against microbes, viruses, and cancer cells. Reports also credit it with lowering blood fats and blood sugar in animal studies. The review gathers that pharmacology and weighs how a food chemical might inspire future medicines.
europmc-pmc3017804:
Hu and co-authors catalogued the NAC family of plant control genes in the poplar tree in a 2010 study. These plant-only switches steer development from seed formation to wood growth, and families exceed a hundred members in several species.

They found a hundred and sixty-three full NAC genes in poplar, sorted into eighteen subfamilies with conserved structures and motifs. Most sit in duplicated genome blocks, leftovers of an ancient genome doubling, and duplicates often share expression patterns with partial overlap. Expression data from tags and arrays showed most members active only at certain times or places.
europmc-pmc3052304:
Schmieder and Edwards built in 2011 a tool that finds and strips foreign DNA out of sequencing datasets. Samples are rarely pure, so reads from handlers, lab reagents, or host tissue can sneak in and corrupt genome assemblies and conclusions. Their program, DeconSeq, compares long reads against reference genomes and flags matches that do not belong, showing the results in clear graphics.

To show why it matters, they screened more than two hundred published microbe and virus community datasets. Possible contamination turned up in nearly three quarters of them, and in the worst case most reads were foreign. Human DNA was a frequent stowaway even in samples with no human link. The tool runs as a website or as local software that fits existing pipelines. The authors recommend screening as a standard step for every sequencing project.
europmc-pmc3101904:
Yip and coauthors reported in 2011 that disulfiram, a decades old drug used to deter drinking, kills breast cancer cells and their hardiest stem like cells when paired with copper. Drug resistance, blamed largely on cancer stem cells, is the main reason breast chemotherapy fails. In dishes, the drug plus copper killed standard breast cancer lines at low doses and sharply boosted a common chemotherapy drug's power, with a true synergistic pattern.

The combination generated corrosive oxygen molecules and switched on stress death pathways inside the cells. At the same time it shut down a survival factor that resistant cancers keep permanently active and that chemotherapy itself can provoke. Sphere forming growth and stem cell marker populations, the stand ins for cancer stem cells, both fell after a day of exposure. The authors propose repurposing this cheap, known drug as a resistance breaker, pending animal and clinical tests.
europmc-pmc3153204:
Olivier Puel, Pierre Galtier, and Isabelle Oswald reviewed a mould toxin common in apples in a 2010 paper in Toxins. The toxin, made by several mould genera, is the mould poison found most often in apples and in juice, cider, and baby foods made from them. Many countries cap its level in food because of the risks.

Exposure has been linked to immune, nerve, and gut effects in studies. The chemical path moulds use to build the toxin runs about ten steps. A cluster of fifteen genes behind it was recently reported, including the enzymes, a regulator, and exporters. The review sums up how the toxin is made and what it does, noting its genetics still lag behind better-studied mould poisons.
europmc-pmc3159904:
Paul Marik, Xavier Monnet, and Jean-Louis Teboul reviewed how to judge which patients need more fluid in a 2011 paper in Annals of Intensive Care. Giving fluid is the first rescue step for unstable patients, yet only about half actually respond with better circulation, and excess fluid raises harm. Older guides based on heart filling pressures have repeatedly failed to predict response.

Newer dynamic tests watch how the heart's output per beat shifts with breathing or with a brief leg raise, which temporarily moves blood toward the heart. Those swings, read continuously by Doppler, pulse-shape, or other bedside tools, separate responders from non-responders far better. The review explains the physiology and the devices, pushing intensive care away from static pressure numbers toward live functional tests.
europmc-pmc3213104:
Benjamin Howden and colleagues traced how Staphylococcus aureus becomes resistant to last-line drugs during infection, in this 2011 study in PLoS Pathogens. They sequenced five pairs of clinical strains, each collected from a patient before and after vancomycin treatment failed. Comparing each pair showed what changed as resistance evolved inside the patient.

The resistant strains repeatedly carried mutations in walKR, a two-gene regulatory system controlling cell wall metabolism. Swapping single altered letters in either gene into the original strains reproduced resistance to both vancomycin and daptomycin, plus the thickened cell walls typical of resistant isolates. The same changes weakened virulence and biofilm formation and shifted central metabolism. The study shows how one small mutation can reshape a dangerous pathogen.
europmc-pmc3223004:
Ruthann Rudel and colleagues tested how much food packaging contributes to exposure to two plastic chemicals, in this 2011 study in Environmental Health Perspectives. Bisphenol A and the phthalate DEHP are used in cans and plastic packaging and can disrupt hormones. Twenty volunteers from five families switched for three days to fresh foods with little packaging, bracketed by their usual diets.

Urine samples collected across eight days showed sharp drops during the fresh-food days. Levels of bisphenol A fell by about two-thirds, and breakdown products of DEHP fell by roughly half, with the highest individual readings falling even more steeply. The results show diet, and packaging in particular, is a major and changeable route of exposure, and that simple menu changes can cut it substantially.
europmc-pmc3241704:
Ioannis Mitroulis and colleagues linked a striking neutrophil behavior to the inflammation of gout, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Gout is a common inflammatory arthritis in which urate crystals trigger immune attack and release of the inflammatory signal IL-1 beta. Neutrophils are central players, and the team asked whether they cast out web-like traps of their own DNA during attacks.

Neutrophils from the joints and blood of patients in a gout flare were indeed forming these extracellular traps, which carried a pro-inflammatory alarm protein. Urate crystals, joint fluid, or serum from patients made healthy neutrophils do the same. Blocking cell-recycling machinery, known as autophagy, prevented trap formation, and IL-1 beta drove it in part, since its blocker anakinra reduced it. The authors suggest the recycling machinery as a new drug target in crystal arthritis.
europmc-pmc3319604:
Vestberg, Gustafson, Maurex, Ingvar, and Petrovic tested whether general thinking skills predict soccer success, reporting in 2012. Top players obviously need fitness and ball skills, but matches also demand fast decisions under pressure. The team gave standard brain function tests, covering creativity, stopping impulsive responses, and switching approaches, to players from Swedish divisions and compared them with typical scores.

Both high and lower division players beat the general population on these executive skills. Players in the top division scored higher still than those below them. When the researchers checked scoring records two seasons later, test results lined up with the goals and assists players had produced. The authors argue that raw thinking power, not just soccer specific instincts, helps separate elite players from the rest.
europmc-pmc3330104:
Stranger and colleagues compared how DNA variants tune gene activity across eight human populations, in a 2012 study. Genes are not simply on or off; nearby variants raise or lower their output, and those dial settings may differ by ancestry. The team measured gene output in blood derived cells from more than seven hundred people in the HapMap project and matched it against nearby variants.

Ancestry did shift overall gene activity patterns in measurable ways. The team cataloged nearly fifty seven hundred dial variants after careful corrections. About half of them showed up in more than one population, and where they did, the size and direction of the effect matched closely. Variants sitting near a gene's start tended to travel best across populations. The results form a resource for judging how disease findings in one population apply to others.
europmc-pmc3386304:
Arand and colleagues mapped in 2012 how living cells place and keep DNA methylation marks, both at standard CG sites and elsewhere. The enzymes responsible, called Dnmts, split into builders and maintainers, but their exact shares were murky. The team sequenced chosen genes and repeat elements at single-molecule detail in mouse stem cells.

Many CG sites turned out to be only half-marked, with the shortfall varying by cell type. Marks at non-CG sites appeared only in stem cells and came solely from two builder enzymes working with a helper. Modeling of more than a hundred thousand site pairs let the team weigh each enzyme's role. Even the supposed maintainer adds fresh marks at some repeats.
europmc-pmc3394104:
Elgendi surveyed in 2012 the analysis of fingertip pulse signals gathered by shining infrared light through the skin. The method, called photoplethysmography, is cheap, gentle, and handy, drawing researchers from many fields. Clinicians already use it for oxygen levels, blood pressure, heart output, and early warning of artery disease.

Much of the signal's diagnostic promise sits in the shape of its wave, beyond simple pulse counting. The overview catalogs the wave's features, the artifacts that corrupt it, and the indexes used to score it. A full grasp of what each feature means is still missing, Elgendi notes. The paper maps the groundwork needed before routine screening can rely on it.

Two Paris copy clerks inherit money, quit their desks, and set out to master all knowledge in Bouvard and Pécuchet. Flaubert left the novel unfinished at his death, and the Dunne translation of 1904 gives it complete in both parts. Farming, chemistry, medicine, and love each defeat the pair in turn.

Their failures pile up into a black comedy of human folly, aimed at every sure system of the age. Flaubert, who read hundreds of books to write it, mocks the very learning he gathered. The pair end where they began, copying, which may be the bleakest joke in French fiction.
flaubert-sentimental-education-dunne-190:

Walter Dunne translation of 1904 presents the novel complete in both volumes. Revolution breaks out in 1848 around Frédéric, yet even history cannot stir him to act.

Flaubert builds the great anti-Bildungsroman, a tale of education that teaches its hero nothing he can use. Friends rise, scheme, and fall while Frédéric watches, always a step behind his own life. Critics rank the book among the finest French novels, a cold, exact portrait of a wasted generation.

Fries worked in Kant's shadow and reshaped Kant's teaching for his own school. His followers became known as the Friesian school.

Fries sought the roots of knowledge in the structure of the mind itself. He held that careful inner study could show why our basic beliefs must hold. The system covers knowing, acting, and faith in one frame. German readers kept his name alive through the century. The original text shows Kant's legacy taking a new path.

frus-1862-d204:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 13 January 1862, in a note printed as Document 204 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, handled the American war from the legation there.

Mid-January found both governments glad to leave the Trent quarrel behind, yet watchful. The Union blockade of Southern ports and British trade losses from it promised fresh disputes. Short formal notes like this one were the everyday tools for managing those disputes before they hardened, and the file holds many from this winter. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d304:
Dated 18 August 1862, Document 304 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

The letter went out eleven days before the second battle of Bull Run, in the last stretch of the summer's buildup. Seward's tone in this period stayed formal and assured, whatever the news. That practiced calm was policy: envoys abroad took their cue from the Secretary's voice, and foreign governments read it as a measure of Union confidence. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d404:
One day after his previous order, on 24 June 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote once more to Horace J. Perry in Madrid. The note is Document 404 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress with the annual message.

Back-to-back instructions usually meant fast-moving news or a point Seward wanted stressed without delay. In June 1862 the fighting in Virginia and the allied quarrel in Mexico both pressed on Spanish policy. Small as it is, the dispatch shows how closely Washington managed its Madrid post. Much of Civil War diplomacy was done this way, in brief, frequent letters rather than grand notes.
frus-1862-d504:
On 4 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. It is Document 504 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

June opened with the armies facing each other before Richmond and the war's outcome once again in doubt. Seward's orders that month mixed resolve with careful answers to specific Dutch questions about ports and shipping. The Netherlands file in the volume is long because both sides wrote often and on small matters as well as large. An instruction of this kind is best read as maintenance: keeping a friendly neutrality in good repair while the great battles were decided elsewhere.
frus-1862-d604:
Admiral Jurien de la Gravière, the French naval commander in the Mexican expedition, wrote this letter to Spain's General Prim on 20 March 1862. It is Document 604 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, annexed to Prim's own despatch.

An annex travels with the document that encloses it. So a French admiral's letter survives here inside a Spanish general's report. The report is printed in an American volume. The layering is the point: the allied commanders in Mexico were already at odds that March, and their private exchanges show it. For the reader, the letter is a small, sharp piece of the coalition's breakup, preserved through three governments' paperwork.
frus-1862-d704:
Charles N. Riotte sent this dispatch from Costa Rica to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 September 1862. Riotte was the American minister there. The letter is document 704 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

By the fall of 1862 Riotte had a year's worth of Central American ground to report on. His mail dealt with the republics' affairs, the transit trade, and the claims of Americans in the region. Letters like this one formed Washington's best source on a part of the world it cared about chiefly for the road between the seas. The record still shows that care, one dispatch at a time.
frus-1863p1-d104:
On 2 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the eighth of twelve to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 104 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Late in a long batch, a writer turns to the smaller heads of a brief: the points that need a word but not a speech. Seward's eighth sheet of the day is of that kind, by its place in the row. Together the twelve gave Adams a full kit for the spring's talks in London. This letter is one tool in that kit, plain and to its point.
frus-1863p1-d204:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 19 May 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 204 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d304:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 5 October 1863. The letter is document 304 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. By then the British government had moved to hold the Confederate rams, and the sharpest crisis of the year was cooling. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d404: On 28 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 404 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d504:
Secretary William H. Seward directed a letter to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 11 May 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d604:
Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons took up his pen on 7 August 1863 and wrote to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late summer of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d104: Ambassador Winant wrote to Roosevelt from London on November 8, 1943, and the letter is Document 104 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Winant's reports in the final pre-summit weeks carried the mood of Churchill's government as the British party readied its own journey. The record supplies the date and the two men and nothing narrower. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' November run.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d204:
President Roosevelt sent Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek a personal, secret message on 10 November 1943 about the new long-range bombers America hoped to base in China. With them, he writes, heavy attacks on vital targets in Japan itself could begin much sooner than once seemed possible.

The plan needs five airfields for the big new planes in the Chengtu area, with basic housing, ready by the end of March 1944. America would supply the engineering skill, but Chiang must provide the labor and materials so the air supply line is not drained. Roosevelt offers Lend-Lease funds to speed the work, and promises a sudden, crippling blow against Japan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d304:
James Byrnes, director of war mobilization, answered President Roosevelt's urgent landing craft telegram on 24 November 1943. Working from Bureau of Shipping predictions, his message is mostly tables, listing how far one building program, program C, could be raised in each month from January to May.

The pattern is the same across the craft types named, from the larger infantry landing craft down to small mechanized boats. No increase at all is possible in January. Then come small gains in February and March, growing through April and May. One type, the LCT-7, shows no increase in any of the five months. The figures gave Roosevelt the hard limits within which the Cairo and Tehran planners had to fit Overlord and every rival landing plan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d404:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt telegraphed the Secretary of State from Ankara on 1 December 1943, repeating a most-secret message he had sent to Cairo for the President. It concerns the hoped-for meeting between President Roosevelt and President Inönü of Turkey.

Foreign Minister Numan, in a conversation that morning, referred again to Roosevelt's presence in Cairo and renewed his hope that a meeting with Inönü could be arranged. Given sufficient notice, Numan hinted, Inönü could meet the President at Aleppo. Aleppo lies just across the Turkish frontier, about twenty-six hours by special train from Ankara. It would be satisfactory, Steinhardt adds, from a security point of view. He asks that any reply be transmitted by the security officers as quickly as possible, since the invitation traffic with Tehran had gone missing the same day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d504:
Roosevelt and Churchill spoke together in this joint message to Marshal Stalin on December 6, 1943, as the Second Cairo Conference ended. A message signed by both Western leaders carried more weight than either could send alone. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

The two leaders used joint messages to show Stalin a united front and to report what the Western allies had settled in his absence. Coming at the close of Cairo, this one belongs to the careful effort to keep the three-way partnership in step after Tehran. Readers see the alliance's odd shape plainly: two partners conferring together, and writing to the third.
frus-1944-quebec-d104:
September 2, 1944 brought a Hull letter to President Roosevelt. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. It dates from ten days before the Quebec Conference opened. German forces were then retreating across France and Belgium.

Hull's early September letters kept the President briefed for Canada. The department tracked allied politics as armies advanced. At Quebec, Roosevelt would face questions on Germany's treatment. He would also face British requests for continued aid. For readers, the letter shows steady staff work behind the summit. Advice flowed upward while the conference machinery assembled.
frus-1944-quebec-d204:
An editors' note prints Morgenthau's diary of his long evening conversation with Roosevelt on September 15, 1944. The president was completely relaxed, and the talk ranged over the week's work. Roosevelt explained he had deliberately held back the zones question until Churchill was in good humor and everything else was settled. Leahy, he added, had been favorable to Morgenthau's plan for Germany.

The United Nations meeting also came up: Roosevelt wanted it in late October, having learned from the League of Nations delay after the last war. Morgenthau called it good window dressing for the campaign, and the president agreed. Morgenthau then volunteered to go to Moscow and sell the Ruhr and Saar program to Stalin himself, and Roosevelt seemed to like the idea.
frus-1944-quebec-d304: The White House issued this press release on 26 September 1944, and the Foreign Relations editors reprinted it as document 304. Press releases were the public face of diplomacy, saying openly what could be said while talks stayed secret. Placed at the end of the Quebec volume, it shows how the Roosevelt administration presented the conference to newspapers and the American public.
frus-1945-50-intel-d104:
Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 1, dated 19 February 1946, is the new body's first numbered order. The CIG had been created by the president's directive four weeks earlier. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

First directives set a body's working habits: who may task it, what it may collect, and how its products reach the departments. Directive No. 1 turned the January compromise into daily practice. Readers should read it as the CIG's birth certificate in operational form. Everything the group later became, a true central agency in embryo, starts from the authorities and limits written here, under its first director, Sidney Souers.
frus-1945-50-intel-d204:
A memorandum dated 23 January 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division of the Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). Readers meet it as document 204 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d304:
A letter from Secretary of Defense Forrestal reached Acting Secretary of State Lovett on 13 October 1948. It is document 304 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

A letter fixed a position in a way a phone call never could: dated, signed, and filed for both sides to cite later. Its worth now is the voice: a chief stating his case as he wished it to be read. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d404:
James Lay, acting executive secretary of the National Security Council, sent a memo to the Council itself on 14 December 1949. The paper is document 404 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Council joined the President with his top foreign and defense aides. Its executive secretary handled the flow of papers that set up each meeting and recorded each choice. A memo from that office to the Council shows the staff machine behind Cold War choices at the highest level. Lay later held the secretary's post in full, a sign of the trust this staff work earned.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d104:
“American Policy Toward Spheres of Influence” is a briefing book paper with a blunt summary. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It lays out the facts, as Washington knew them, of the British and Soviet arrangement over southeastern Europe.

The deal covered Rumania, Bulgaria, Greece, and Yugoslavia and took effect in the early summer of 1944. After American objections it was limited to three months, though in some respects it seemed still at work. The paper states the American stand: such arrangements may serve the war, but Washington cannot approve them beyond the military field. An annex from the Joint Chiefs warns against a British and Soviet contest for power.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d204:
Admiral Leahy sent the President a ready-made answer to Stalin on 6 December 1944. His note, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, forwards the draft reply the State Department had approved. Leahy adds that it should be quoted to Churchill for his information.

The draft thanks Stalin for his two messages on the de Gaulle talks. On the proposed Franco-Soviet pact, Washington would have no objection in principle, if both parties judge it good for their countries and for European security. On France's postwar frontier, the President states complete agreement with Stalin's replies to de Gaulle. No gain for the common war effort would come from settling the question now; after Germany's collapse is the better time.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d304:
Concrete American proposals on Poland open this United States delegation memorandum, dated February 1, 1945, as the Malta talks began. On borders, it urges the Curzon Line in the north and center, with the Lwow area kept Polish in the south. It also seeks to limit the German land handed to Poland as payment for ground lost in the east.

Readers see the exact line the American team planned to defend before meeting Stalin at Yalta. The paper ties Poland's eastern border to its gains in East Prussia and along the Baltic coast. Papers like this one show how the delegation fixed its aims before the hard bargaining started.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d404:
Wrapping up the military talks fills this Combined Chiefs session of February 9, 1945. The chiefs took up the paragraphs added to their draft final report to the President and Prime Minister. Sir Alan Brooke drew attention to the directive for the Supreme Allied Commander in the Mediterranean, in an appendix. One clause covered which ground formations would be withdrawn.

It also covered the arrangements for their transfer, a live question as troops shifted between Italy and northwest Europe. The minutes show the Argonaut military conference closing its books. Two days later the chiefs' report would go to the leaders for approval.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d504:
Care and repatriation of liberated prisoners and civilians form this agreement between the United States and the Soviet Union, signed February 11, 1945. The two governments wished to arrange care for Americans freed by forces under Soviet command. Soviet citizens freed by forces under American command would receive the same treatment.

Article 1 sets the rule: all such persons, without delay after liberation, fall under the agreement's terms. The text grew out of the draft the Combined Chiefs had approved three days earlier. It governed the fate of millions of displaced people in 1945, and its forced returns became one of Yalta's darkest legacies.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d104:
General Deane relayed a request from Marshal Zhukov in a paraphrased telegram to Air Chief Marshal Tedder on June 27, 1945. The message is document 104 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Word had just arrived that Zhukov would meet Field Marshal Montgomery, General Clay, and their party in Berlin on Friday, June 29.

Zhukov asks urgently to be told at once, through the Allied representatives already in Berlin, what subjects Montgomery, Clay, and their party want to discuss with him. The cable went widely: to SHAEF, to Montgomery's army group, to the Air Ministry in London, and to the Combined Chiefs of Staff. The request marked the shift from quarreling over access to planning the first direct meeting between the Western commanders and the Soviet commander in Berlin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d204:
Admiral Leahy relayed the President's orders from the cruiser Augusta on July 9, 1945. The short instruction to the White House Map Room is document 204 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Truman and Byrnes were at sea, sailing to Europe for the meeting with Stalin and Churchill.

Leahy directs that two of Ambassador Harriman's messages be sent to Acting Secretary Grew, with word that Secretary Byrnes wishes him to prepare the studies recommended in them. One of those messages urged a study of the American reading of the Yalta Far East agreement and of the planned trusteeship for Korea. The note shows the shipboard headquarters working the agenda even while crossing the Atlantic.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d304:
Schoenfeld wrote from Budapest on July 6, 1945, directly to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow. His point was about signals. Hungarian Communists and local Soviet officials, he said, would soon learn whether Washington meant to take an active interest in Hungary. The test was equal American part in the Allied Control Commission.

Marshal Voroshilov had already said at a June 5 commission meeting that revised procedure was in view. Meanwhile, Schoenfeld reported, Communist efforts to build local power went on steadily, though with care. The message shows how closely men on the ground watched small procedural fights for signs of larger intent.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d404:
Partition of Germany is the eighth topic in Dunn's extracts of his July 14, 1945 conversation with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam. The two men had spent two hours ranging over the conference agenda. On this point, Dunn reports, the British Foreign Office chief took a notably cautious line for a government often linked with dividing Germany.

Cadogan agreed that partition would be desirable if the Germans themselves promoted it. It should not, he said, be forced on Germany. He also professed ignorance of French projects for internationalizing the Ruhr. The short extract shows Britain's top foreign official keeping his government's options open on the conference's largest question.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d504:
Britain's recognition mechanics are set out in a note from Ambassador Halifax to the Secretary of State, dated at Washington on July 5, 1945. On instructions from Foreign Secretary Eden, he informs the Department of the Foreign Office's telegram to the British ambassador in Moscow. Sir Archibald Clark Kerr is to concert with the American ambassador there.

Some five hours in advance of the agreed release time, 7 p.m. Eastern War Time on July 5, Clark Kerr will address the Polish ambassador a communication formally recognizing the new Polish government. It will take the form of a message from Prime Minister Churchill to Premier Osóbka-Morawski. A like note, Halifax adds, goes to the Soviet government.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d604:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff sent a top secret paper on command in the Japan war, July 9, 1945. It is document 604 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The paper was prepared for debate at the next Allied conference.

The attached British memo reviews command and control as a whole. It takes up Southeast Asia Command and the Southwest Pacific Area in turn. For each, it weighs boundaries, the chain of command, and the date of any transfer. It then turns to higher strategic control of the war against Japan. The British agree that the Southwest Pacific command should soon change hands in some way. Views from the Australian and New Zealand governments had been sought but had not yet come in.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d704:
The British Embassy in Washington set out London's planned protest on Turkey in a secret memo of July 7, 1945. It is document 704 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It follows the State Department's cooler memo of June 23 on the same dispute.

London has instructed its Moscow ambassador to approach the Soviet government in general terms. The decision, it stresses, came only after most careful weighing of all factors. The second Molotov-Sarper talk of June 18 counted among them. London thinks it better that Moscow learn its views before the conference, called Terminal here. Springing them at the conference itself might look like indifference followed by ambush. Clark Kerr is to say that Turkey has consulted London about the talks. Britain, he is to add, was very much surprised by the Soviet land claims and the demand for bases in the Straits.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1004:
Seymour Rubin cabled Covey Oliver from Babelsberg on August 2, 1945. His subject is the decree vesting German foreign assets. President Truman has sent General Clay a memorandum on the subject. It states the Big Three agreement to issue such a decree.

The memorandum also directs that the Control Council be urged to adopt the decree. Truman regards it as urgent that control and power of disposal over German external assets be obtained. Rubin adds one change to the draft already sent to Washington. The part setting up a special board, with American and British members, to direct the vesting body has been struck out.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1104:
Five days before the Potsdam Conference closed, on 30 July 1945, the Soviet team tabled another formal proposal. By then the shape of the final deal was nearly set. Late papers were often last bids, put forward when each side was pushing for final gains.

Moscow's word carried great weight at the table. The Soviet Union had borne the worst losses of the war, and its team used that fact in the bargaining. A late proposal like this one shows where the Soviet side still hoped to move the terms. It survives word for word in the American record of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1204:
Shantz wrote from Yugoslavia again on 29 July 1945, two days after his last dispatch. A quick follow-up means events in Belgrade were moving fast enough to need fresh word. Each cable added to Washington's file on Tito's state.

Yugoslavia sat on the seam between the Western and Soviet worlds. Its moves raised fears and hopes in both camps during the summit's last week. The envoy's steady reporting kept the home office from guessing. This dispatch keeps his close watch going. It is the second of three Shantz cables in this part of the record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1304:
Harrison wrote to Stimson again on 17 July 1945, the day Potsdam opened. The acting chairman of the Interim Committee kept the war secretary supplied as the atomic news ripened. Their exchange ran beside the public talks like a second, hidden summit.

Stimson, at Potsdam, was the one man there who carried the whole atomic secret for the American side. Harrison's notes fed him the home end of that file: test word, committee views, and pending choices. This message is one link in that channel. It shows the bomb's policy being handled in quiet notes while the conference made its noise.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1404:
Caffery cabled the acting secretary of state again on 7 August 1945, the day after his cluster of Paris reports. The Potsdam Conference had closed five days earlier. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

The week after a summit is when its choices land on the desks of ambassadors, who must explain them to the governments they live among. Caffery's steady cables show that landing in France. Readers can watch the post-conference work unfold: questions from Paris, answers from the embassy, reports to Washington. It is less grand than the summit itself, and closer to how the settlement was actually carried into the world.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-104:
Thompson's minutes cover a Potsdam session held on July 25, 1945. By that date the conference was a week old and its hardest topics were still open. Thompson kept one of the running American records of the talks. His minutes were printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, alongside other note-takers' sets.

The record follows the exchange as it unfolded. Readers can watch a point raised, pressed, and then deferred or settled. Comparing Thompson with the day's other minutes shows how staff heard the same words. Together the sets give the conference a depth no single summary could match.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d804:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 20, 1945, as document 804. It joins the run of Soviet texts in the volume's first week. Moscow's drafts stated its claims in firm, spare lines. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Another Soviet text from the same week lets readers sort themes. Some drafts pressed land; others pressed money or rights. The pattern of claims is itself evidence. The document helps map what the Soviet side valued most. Set against the final protocol, it shows where persistence paid and where it met a wall.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d904:
Soviet delegates submitted this draft definition of war trophies at Potsdam on July 21, 1945. It was offered to the Economic Sub-Committee during talks on reparations terms. The draft covers two classes of goods.

First come all German military supplies and equipment. That class includes gear used by enemy military and paramilitary units, or by their members. Second come supplies the enemy used for military needs. The Allies must have captured them before the war ended, on land where fighting took place. A note by Murphy records a sharper claim behind the text. Soviet negotiator Maisky insisted his country had the right to take and remove anything from its zone.
gao-gaoreports-b-297804: LLH & Associates took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298804: Exploration Partners took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299504: IBM took its June 2007 contract fight to GAO — two case numbers, one tech prize — and the combined ruling settles both. Big Blue said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the claims. When the industry's giant cries foul, the referee's answer carries extra weight.
gao-gaoreports-b-299804: TELESIS Corporation took its August 2007 contract dispute to GAO, and this ruling ends it. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call weighs the protest and decides. One more verdict in the public ledger of how federal tech deals must be contested.
gao-gaoreports-b-299904: Synergetics cried foul on a 2007 award, and GAO's ruling is the last word. The firm said the bid contest was mishandled; the call tests the charges against procurement law. Each published verdict sharpens the shared rulebook — what agencies must do, and what bidders can demand.
gao-gaoreports-b-309604: A 2007 GAO money-law ruling with a modern twist: could the border agency spend its budget on credit watch for staff after a data breach? GAO said yes — guarding workers' good names fit the agency's purse rules. The call sets a small but telling marker on what counts as fair spending in the age of hacks.
gao-gaoreports-b-309704: Tense games with budget language — GAO's 2007 ruling parses 'words of futurity' in the ATF's 2006 spending law. The call decides what Congress's forward-looking phrases legally unlocked for the firearms bureau. Fiscal-law rulings like this are where grammar meets the public purse.
gao-gaoreports-b-310004: This 2007 GAO ruling is about cost of Living Payments at United States Capitol Police. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-310904: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by FlowSense, LLC. The March 10, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-311004: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. The March 28, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-304: The F/A-22's numbers needed justification in 2005, and GAO's report says the Air Force still needed a business case for the quantities and upgrades. The review demands the math. The stealth jets deserved the honest count. The case had to be made.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-404: Trusted-shipper cargo breaks were too trusting in 2005, and GAO's report says the easy lane lacked real proof of safety. The review calls out the soft deal. The shipping containers deserved the real screening. The proof was missing. The deal was soft.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-804: The Klamath Basin restoration funding needed assurance in 2005, and GAO's report says limited assurance existed on the federal funding requirements. The findings demand the proof. The report warns that the river's restoration deserved honest money. The assurance had to be limited no more.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-104: COPS grants modestly cut 1990s crime in 2005, and GAO's report says the community policing grants were a modest contributor to declines. The findings do the math. The report warns that the safer streets deserved honest credit. The contribution had to be measured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-204: Money sent home abroad got a GAO look in 2005, and the report covers products, costs, and disclosures for remittances. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the senders deserved honest fees. The costs had to be disclosed. The senders deserved honest fees.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-304: Federal PSA campaigns got a GAO accounting in 2006, and the report tracks activities and financial obligations across seven departments. The findings do the counting. The report shows the public-service spots' costs were tallied. The campaigns had to be transparent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-404: The visitor-tracking system's contracts needed strengthening in 2006, and GAO's report says management and oversight had to improve. The findings demand the controls. The report warns that the immigrant-status program's buying needed discipline. The oversight had to be strengthened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-704: Medicare doctor visits were rising in 2006, and GAO's report says service use was increasing nationwide, with few beneficiaries reporting access problems. The findings balance the trend and the access. The report shows the seniors were getting seen. The access had to hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-804: Social Security's indexing choices mattered in 2006, and GAO's report lays out the implications of the different options. The findings do the math. The report warns that the formula tweaks would shape retirements for decades. The choices had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1004: NASA's people planning earned a guarded nod in 2007 — GAO's report says the space agency's workforce strategy had improved, but moon-shot staffing puzzles loomed. The findings balance credit for progress against the hard math of hiring rocket scientists. Big dreams need bench depth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-104: The Indian trust reforms were taking hold in 2007, and GAO's report says the Special Trustee had implemented several key changes required by the 1994 law. The findings credit the progress. The report warns that the trust had to be earned, not just promised. The reforms had to reach the people.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-304: The promised base-closing savings were inflated in 2007 — GAO's report says the fleet readiness center math did not hold. The findings deflate the rosy projections and demand fixes. The report is a reminder that shutdown savings are easy to promise and hard to bank.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-404: Russia's loose nukes were getting safer in 2007, and GAO's report says security at the nuclear sites had improved, though the long-term future was shaky. The findings credit the gains. The report warns that the guarded atoms needed guarding forever.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-604: The next pandemic was a when-not-if in 2007 — GAO's report says efforts to delay the flu's arrival were underway, but spotting the riskiest nations stayed tricky. The findings blend epidemiology with geopolitics. The report reads now as a dress rehearsal for the real thing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-904: America's story abroad needed better research in 2007 — GAO's report says public diplomacy had to get smarter about studying its audience. The findings press for strategic, joined-up polling and analysis. Winning hearts and minds, the report argues, starts with knowing whose hearts and whose minds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-104: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at military Health Care: Cost Data Indicate That TRICARE Reserve Select Premiums Exceeded the Costs of Providing Program Benefits. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1104: The Government Accountability Office dug into federal Pensions: Judicial Survivors' Annuities System Costs in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-304: The Government Accountability Office dug into environmental Protection: EPA Needs to Ensure That Best Practices and Procedures Are Followed When Making Further Changes to Its Library Network in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gospel-of-thomas-oxyrhynchus-fragments-1:
Egyptian sand kept three scraps of a lost gospel for some fifteen centuries. The Oxyrhynchus Sayings of Jesus, edited by Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt in 1904, prints those Greek fragments with English renderings. In 1945 the full Gospel of Thomas came to light, and these scraps proved to be parts of it.

The sayings are short, sharp words of Jesus, with no birth tale, cross, or empty tomb around them. Scholars of 1904 knew only these pieces and argued hard over their age and worth. The pamphlet is the sole public-domain edition of the Thomas pieces. It shows a famous gospel at the hour of its first return.
griffith-thompson-demotic-magical-papyru:
F. Ll. Griffith and Herbert Thompson published their edition of the great Demotic magical papyrus in 1904. The papyrus, split between London and Leiden collections, comes from Roman-era Egypt. Demotic script had kept its contents closed to most scholars.

Volume one gives full transliteration and English translation of the handbook. Spells address healing, protection, love, and speaking directly with gods. The editors' notes untangle the strange mixture of Egyptian, Greek, and Jewish elements. Their work remains the foundation for studying Egyptian magic of this period. Any serious reader of ancient spells still starts here.
hammurabi-code-harper-1904:
Robert Francis Harper published his translation of The Code of Hammurabi, King of Babylon in 1904. Hammurabi ruled Babylon in the 1700s BCE, and his laws were carved on a stone pillar found in Persia in 1901. Harper, a scholar at the University of Chicago, gave English readers the full text.

Some 282 laws cover trade, wages, marriage, injury, and slavery, often with the famous measure of an eye for an eye. Penalties differ by the rank of the persons involved, a window into Babylonian society. The code is the oldest complete legal code known. Harper's translation made it a standard source for law schools and historians alike.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol5-extra-190:
Hastings issued an extra fifth volume for his Dictionary of the Bible in 1904, two years after the main set closed. It gathers articles that arrived too late, plus fuller indexes and a map of Palestine. James Hastings meant the set to stay current.

The extra volume adds fresh work on topics like the Dead Sea region and new finds from excavation. Indexes of texts, names, and subjects bind all five volumes into one tool. Many sets in libraries lack this volume, which makes a complete run prized. It rounds out the greatest one-generation Bible dictionary in English.
hesse-peter-camenzind-1904:
Peter Camenzind, Hermann Hesse's first successful novel, appeared in German in 1904. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. Peter grows up in a Swiss mountain village, loses his mother young, and leaves to seek the life of a writer.

Cities, love affairs, and friendships fail to give Peter the belonging he craves. He drinks, drifts, and returns at last toward home and a simpler duty. Hesse fills the tale with Alpine weather, lakes, and long walks. The novel made his name in Germany at age twenty-seven. Its themes of seeking and homecoming run through all his later work.
hinton-fourth-dimension-1904:
Charles Howard Hinton set out his full case for a fourth dimension in 1904. The book builds on his past work on cubes and higher space. Its 1912 print kept the work in wide use. Hinton was a math man with a deep bent for big thought.

He shows how a cube gains a new form, the tesseract, in four reaches of space. Tales, drills, and clear cuts help the mind grasp the leap. Hinton also asks what higher space means for faith and the self. The book stays his full plea for a world past our three reaches.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume four of Thomas Carlyle's monumental history of Frederick the Great, the labor of thirteen years. Thunderous, worshipful, and endlessly detailed, it follows the Prussian king through the wars and courts of the 18th century. History written as hero-worship, and the longest biography in the language. Not quick reading, but an unforgettable immersion.
history-of-the-revolt-of-the-netherlands: Schiller brings his history of the Dutch revolt to its close, as the young republic secures the freedom so dearly won against Spain. His admiration for a small people who defied a mighty empire shines through every page. A noble finale to one of the great stories of liberty, told by Germany's poet of freedom.
howitt-the-native-tribes-of-south-east-a:
Alfred William Howitt devoted his life to the peoples of the southeast, and The Native Tribes of South-East Australia of 1904 is his magnum opus. The Kurnai, Wiradjuri, and neighboring nations fill its pages. Kinship systems, initiation ceremonies, and magic stand at the center of his lifelong record.

Howitt learned from Aboriginal elders over decades, in an age when few settlers listened at all. His marriage classes and clan rules became building blocks of kinship theory worldwide. The book stands as the fullest early account of the southeast tribes, gathered by a patient friend of their old men.
hus-letters-workman-pope-1904:
Jan Hus, the Bohemian reformer, was burned at Constance in 1415 after a trial for heresy. The Letters of John Hus, in the 1904 English rendering by Herbert Workman and Martin Pope, gathers his full correspondence. His letters from prison at Constance form the heart of the book.

Hus writes to friends, backers, and the faithful at Prague, holding firm as the court closes in. The captivity letters show a man who knows the fire waits and will not bend. They are the key record of his trial told from inside the cell. Few martyrs of the age speak so plainly for themselves.
james-ghost-stories-antiquary-1904:
Cambridge don M. R. James reshaped the ghost tale in Ghost Stories of an Antiquary, his first set, from 1904. His ghosts rise from old books, coins, prints, and church lore. A look or a touch wakes them. Then calm turns to dread.

Tales such as the curse on a count's line set his mold. Learn the lore, touch the old thing, pay the price. James wrote in a dry, sly voice that makes fear bite more. Later ghost tales still walk the path he cut. James read his tales aloud to friends at Yule by fire light. That warm start makes the cold dread in them feel all the more sharp.
james-golden-bowl-1904:
Henry James published The Golden Bowl in 1904, the last great novel he completed. James wrote it in his densest late style, where a raised eyebrow can carry a chapter's weight. He took the title image from Ecclesiastes: a golden bowl, beautiful and ready to crack.

American millionaire Adam Verver buys his daughter Maggie a husband, the Italian Prince Amerigo, and then marries the prince's former lover, Charlotte. Father and daughter are so close that the two outsiders drift back together. Maggie slowly perceives the affair and, without a single scene of accusation, maneuvers to win her husband back. The novel is James's most architectonic work, built like the bowl itself: flawless, and full of strain.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-04:
With Volume 4, from 1897, the scene shifts from Acadia toward Quebec. Thwaites follows the mission as it moves to the great St. Lawrence River. Champlain's world and the first posts on the river come into clear view.

Jesuit eyes record the founding years of New France in fine detail. They describe trade, travel by canoe, and talks with Native nations. Hopes run high, yet money and men stay scarce each year. The tone shifts from mere survival toward bold plans for growth. Readers watch a colony and a mission find their stride at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lwow-aaron-mose:
Aaron Moses ben Zebi Hirsch Lwow, a grammarian of Lemberg, is the subject of a short 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He served his city as a scribe and as a dayyan, or religious judge, in the eighteenth century. His fame rests on his Hebrew grammar work. He wrote in both verse and prose.

The article lists his books in order. Shirah Hadashah, printed at Zolkiev in 1764, is a Hebrew grammar in verse, built as six poems with prose explanations. It follows the model of Elijah Levita's Pereq Shirah. Ohel Mosheh, a full grammar in four parts, appeared the next year. It follows Kimhi's system and criticizes the grammarian Zalman Hanau. Two further works, on Talmud and on the Hebrew language, stayed unpublished. The brief entry preserves a teacher who put grammar into poetry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-margarita-anton:
Antonius Margarita, a sixteenth-century convert whose book attacked Judaism, is treated in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. Born about 1500 at Ratisbon, he was the son of its rabbi, Jacob Margolioth. Baptized in 1522, he taught Hebrew at several universities. From 1537 until his death he held a post at Vienna.

The article deals plainly with his book of 1530, The Whole Jewish Faith. In it Margarita mocked Jewish ceremonies and accused Jews of usury and hostility to Christians. He denounced the Alenu prayer and charged Jewish physicians with ignorance and greed. The writers call the book a libel outright. Its influence was real: Luther drew on it for his own attack on the Jews. Josel of Rosheim complained to Emperor Charles V when it appeared. A committee examined the charges, and Margarita was jailed and expelled from Augsburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maxims-legal-10:
Legal maxims, the short sayings in which wide principles of law are packed, are collected for Jewish law in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Lewis N. Dembitz. Every legal system has them, the article notes: Roman law has "Ignorance of the law harms," and English equity demands that a suitor come with clean hands. The Talmud's own maxims cover both the substance of the law and evidence and procedure in court.

The article then works through examples, translating each Hebrew saying and explaining its reach. "A man's agent is, in effect, the man himself" matches a Roman rule almost word for word. "Who pays is not flogged" bars a second punishment once compensation is made. "Damage by seeing is called damage" protects a householder's privacy. Each maxim carries its Talmudic citation, so the piece doubles as a small index to rabbinic legal thought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melihah-salting:
Melihah is the salting of meat to make it ritually fit for cooking. Solomon Schechter and Julius H. Greenstone explain it step by step. They do so in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The rabbis stretched the Bible ban on blood to flesh that still holds it. But only the blood of mammals and birds counts. It must be blood in the veins, clotted on the surface, or flowing. A washed piece of raw meat may be eaten as it is. Meat meant for the pot, which will discharge blood as it cooks, must first be salted dry.

The article gives the working rules from the codes. The meat soaks about half an hour to open the pores. It lies on a wicker tray or slanting board. It is thickly salted on every side. It rests about an hour, twenty minutes in haste. Poultry is opened and emptied first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merwan-ha-levi-:
Merwan ha-Levi was a French philanthropist of the second half of the eleventh century. Richard Gottheil and A. Peiginsky notice him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was one of the most prominent Jews of Narbonne. He gave his time and his fortune to that community. He seems to have stood in favor with the government. That favor put him in a position to check unfavorable measures. The measures were aimed at the Jews.

The notice is four sentences long. It is drawn from Gross's "Gallia Judaica." Its second half is genealogy. Merwan headed a family that produced several famous scholars. Among them were his son R. Isaac of Narbonne. Among them was his grandson, the nasi Moses ben Joseph. In the encyclopedia's alphabet, his entry stands a few pages from that grandson's brother Meir. So the family's Narbonne century can be read across the two notices.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-midian-and-midi:
Midian, son of Abraham by Keturah, gave his name to the Midianites, a people who move through the Bible as herders, traders, and enemies of Israel. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on them in 1906. His five sons, from Ephah to Eldaah, stand in Genesis as the nation's founding fathers.

Much of the article is detective work on where Midian lay. Abraham sent Keturah's sons eastward, yet Moses herds Jethro's flocks by Mount Horeb, placing Midianites in the Sinai peninsula. Other passages set them between Edom and Paran on the Egypt road, or beside Moab, whose elders joined Midian's to hire Balaam against Israel. The writers weigh each clue in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-model-marx-1090:
Marx Model was court Jew to Margrave William Frederick of Brandenburg-Ansbach, in a career the Jewish Encyclopedia reconstructs through Gotthard Deutsch and Alfred Feilchenfeld in 1906. From 1691 his family paid no duties on imported goods and held the privilege of printing the Talmud. The margrave shielded him by decree and ordered his debts collected, so that Model could go on helping the court.

Power at home cut both ways: as elder of the Fürth community Model protected his coreligionists and also ruled them with threats of prison and fines. His enemy Elhanan Fränkel tried in 1711 to have him jailed for dishonesty and was himself ruined instead. About 1716 a charge of defrauding the public revenues finally reached him — the standard fate hanging over every court Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-na:
Mordecai ben Naphtali Hirsch Kremsir was a Polish commentator who died at Cracow in 1670. He was a disciple of Shabbethai Sheftel. Wilhelm Bacher and S. J. Levinson note him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His most important work explains the Aramaic Targums. It is Ḳeṭoret ha-Sammim, a commentary on Targum Jonathan and Targum Yerushalmi, printed at Amsterdam in 1671.

His most moving work is smaller. It is a Ḳinah, an elegy for the Polish martyrs of 1648. The entry gives their number as a hundred and twenty thousand. It was published at Lublin in 1650, while the catastrophe was still fresh. He also commented on the legends of tractate Berakot. Grief and grammar were the twin occupations of his generation of Polish scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-joseph-ha:
Joseph Hayyim Elijah Moses was a cabalist and Talmudist who led the Jewish community of Bagdad. Joseph Jacobs and N. E. B. Ezra wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry while he was still living. He was the grandson of a chief rabbi of Bagdad. His books appeared at Jerusalem and Bagdad between 1870 and 1900.

The best known of them is the Ben Ish Hai, one of the titles in the entry's list of his works. Jews in India and the Far East sent him their questions on ritual.
