His other titles include Rab Pe'alim, Ben Yehoyadah, and Adderet Eliyahu. The short entry catches the Bagdad sage at the height of his authority.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muhsam-samuel-1:
Samuel Mühsam was an Austrian rabbi born at Landsberg in Prussian Silesia on May 22, 1837. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied at Breslau and Vienna and took his doctorate at Leipsic in 1864. His pulpits ran from Postelberg in Bohemia to Graz, where he settled in 1877.

Mühsam wrote a string of scholarly booklets in German. They treat the Jews in the writings of ancient Rome, food and drink among the old Hebrews, and magic in the ancient world. A fourth studies fire in the Bible and the Talmud. At Znaim he also taught French in the Realschule, a rabbi at home in two worlds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-names-personal-:
Personal Names, Joseph Jacobs's Jewish Encyclopedia article, studies how the Bible's people got their names. In early times a name usually marked some circumstance of the birth, as with Jacob's sons. The mother commonly chose it, sometimes the father or another person. Before the Exile no child was named after a relative, not even a king after David.

Most of the twenty-eight hundred names in the Bible carry a plain meaning. Some come from birth order, some from looks: Laban means white, Gideon maimed. Others come from animals, Rachel the ewe and Deborah the bee among them. The compound names speak of God: He gives, helps, heals, remembers, hears, and judges. A whole theology, Jacobs says, hides in the name list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nebich-nebbich-:
Nebich is a Judæo-German word of regret and pity. Cyrus Adler and Gotthard Deutsch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. People use it as a noun, an adverb, and a cry. Most often it comes out as an interjection. Nebich, the poor man, is the entry's own example.

A great nebich is a person who draws pity. The word's origin, though, is in real doubt. Zunz thought it came from a Polish source. Gruenbaum traced it to German words, nie bei euch. That means, may it never come upon you. He tied it to a line in Lamentations. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read that line the same way. Polish Jews say the Hebrew words, lo 'alekem, as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-newark-11504:
Newark was New Jersey's largest city in 1904. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Leucht wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its first congregation, B'nai Jeshurun, began in 1848. Services wandered until a synagogue rose in 1858. A new temple followed in 1867.

Rabbi Joseph Leucht entered that pulpit at its dedication. The congregation now follows the Reform ritual. Oheb Scholom began in 1860, B'nai Abraham in 1857. Russian immigrants lately formed Anshe Russia together. Nine smaller congregations dot the city besides these. The Plaut Memorial School teaches 800 pupils, mostly Russians' children. An orphans' home opened in 1865 on Clinton avenue. Newark's Jews numbered about 20,000 in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-omri-11704:
Omri was a king of the north realm of Israel. Ira Maurice Price, Emil G. Hirsch, and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was first a captain in the host of King Elah. That host lay at Gibbethon, a Philistine town. Then word came that Zimri had slain the king.

The host at once made Omri their king in Elah's place. They marched on Tirzah and took the town fast. Zimri burnt his own palace over his head there. A rival named Tibni still fought Omri for the crown. At the end of four years Omri ruled alone. He bought a new site for his chief town. He paid Shemer two talents of silver for the hill. He built Samaria there, a strong fort town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottensooser-dav:
David Ottensooser was a German author from Fürth. Isidore Singer and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in the year 1784. He died at Fürth on May 22, 1858. As a child he was a prodigy of great gifts.

David read all books in reach from his youth on. He was a full scholar, though self taught in all fields. His style of words is oft dark, for want of school. His work in books took a host of forms and themes. He put Job, Isaiah, and Jeremiah into new tongues. He gave notes on works by Maimonides and others. He wrote a Jewish past based on Josephus, the old writer. He put out tales from the Talmud for all to read.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parashah-plural:
A parashah is a part of the five books of Moses. Cyrus Adler and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Sephardic Jews use the word for each week's lesson. The Torah is split into fifty-four such lessons in a year. They use the word for small parts of the text too.

The Ashkenazic Jews call the week's lesson a sidra instead. They give the name parashah to the parts read at feasts. They use it for the seven parts of the week's read too. Those seven parts are read on Sabbath days in turn. In old Palestine the Torah was split in a new way. It was read through in a span of three full years. Those parts, 153 in all, are called sedarim there. Genesis holds twelve parashiyyot and forty-three sedarim in that count.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philippopolis-t:
Philippopolis, now Plovdiv, was the capital of eastern Rumelia. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there when Turks took the city in 1360. A Jewish queen of Bulgaria came from nearby Tirnova.

In 1492 exiles from Aragon built a synagogue there. They named it K. K. Aragon for their lost home. Under late Turkish rule Jews held city offices. When Russians neared in 1876, most Jews fled the city. Their general promised shelter to those who stayed. The town later supported five Jewish journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-platon-platyon-: Platon of Rome was a scholar of the second century. The Executive Committee and S. Mendelsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He taught under persecution in Rome. He urged his fellow Jews to hold fast in faith. Others, he said, had suffered before and been delivered. He cited the three youths who faced Nebuchadnezzar's fire. He also read Sinai as literally lifted from earth. Israel, he taught, stood beneath the floating mountain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posnanski-adolf:
Adolf Posnanski was an Austrian rabbi born at Lubraniec near Warsaw in 1854. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Breslau in school, university, and seminary. Heinrich Graetz and Manuel Joël were among his teachers. At Paris he read for the scholar Joseph Derenbourg.

While still a student, Posnanski taught religion at Breslau schools. He served as rabbi at Reichenberg from 1888 to 1891. He was then called to Pilsen in Bohemia. He sat on the board of a Berlin society for Jewish learning. That society worked to spread the science of Judaism. His own books and essays are listed in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-provins-12404:
Provins is a French town in the department of Seine-et-Marne. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews had settled there by the twelfth century. In 1230 Count Thibaut of Champagne made a pact with the town. In it he kept all rights over its Jews for himself.

In 1298 a Jew of Provins named Hagin held a crown trust. He was charged with handing tax money to royal officers. The taxes came from his fellow Jews of Troyes. In 1301 two sons of a Jew named Simon made a sale. They sold land to a widow named Perronelle. The entry keeps such small records of a lost community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabin-b-adda-12: Rabin bar Adda was a Babylonian teacher of the third set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a brother of Rabbah bar Adda. He was a pupil of Judah ben Ezekiel of Pumbedita. He passed on teachings in the name of Isaac. He passed on one ruling in the name of Rabbi too. None of his own teachings has been kept.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rayner-william-:
William Solomon Rayner was a merchant and financier born on September 23, 1822. Cyrus Adler and C. A. Rubenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Oberelzbach, Bavaria. He died in Baltimore on March 1, 1899.

The article says he moved to the United States in 1840. He turned down a teaching post and chose business in Baltimore. After the Civil War he helped shape the city's finance. He sat on bank and railroad boards for years. Rayner also helped found the Har Sinai congregation. He pushed for Reform and brought Rabbi David Einhorn there. He gave the first building for a Hebrew orphan asylum. The entry joins business success with wide public giving.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roest-meyer-mar:
Meyer Roest was a Dutch bibliographer born at Amsterdam in 1821. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Amsterdam in 1890. Work with a bookselling firm sparked his taste for bibliography.

The article says he published a catalogue of Oriental books in 1857. His best known work catalogues the Rosenthal library. That catalogue of Hebraica and Judaica fills two volumes. It appeared at Amsterdam in 1875. After Baron Rosenthal gave his collection to Amsterdam's library, Roest became its custodian. He wrote for Dutch and Jewish periodicals for years. He also edited the Israelitische Letterbode for several years. The Jewish Chronicle is the entry's cited source. The record honors the keeper of a great collection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roth-philipp-12:
Philipp Roth was a German violoncellist born at Tarnowitz, Upper Silesia, on October 25, 1853. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied in Berlin at the Königliche Hochschule für Musik in the 1870s.

Roth published a method for the violoncello, teaching its technique step by step. He also wrote a guide through the whole cello literature, Führer Durch die Violoncell-Litteratur. In 1890 he founded Berlin's Freie Musikalische Vereinigung, a free musical society. He directed its publication, the Berliner Signale, as well. He died at Berlin on June 9, 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saint-louis-130:
Saint Louis is the largest city in the state of Missouri. Cyrus Adler and Bernhard Greenfelder wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its pioneer Jew was Wolf Bloch, from Schwihau in Bohemia, settled there in 1816.

The first Jewish services there came at the New Year of 1836. Ten men rented a small room over a grocery store for worship. In 1837 they organized the United Hebrew Congregation, still existing then. Its own temple on Sixth Street was consecrated on June 17, 1859. Other congregations followed, B'nai El in 1840 and Shaare Emeth in 1866. Henry J. Messing held the United Hebrew pulpit there for twenty-six years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-b-hiyya-:
Samuel ben Hiyya was a Palestinian amora of the second half of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. None of his own legal or homiletic sayings has been preserved at all.

He is known only through the statements of others that he hands on. Twice the Babylonian Talmud names him: once passing on an apothegm of Rabbi Mani, once citing Rabbi Eleazar. He seems identical with Samuel ben Hiyya ben Judah of the Palestinian Talmud. There he is named often, quoting the maxims of Rabbi Hanina ben Hama. Genesis Rabbah gives the same Hanina statement under both name forms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sargon-michael-:
Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Michael Sargon. He was an Indian convert to Christianity. Sargon was born at Cochin in 1795. He died about 1855. T. Jarrett of Madras converted him in 1818. Sargon became the first missionary in India of the London Society for Promoting Christianity Among the Jews.

At Cochin, Sargon's own parents received him kindly. By 1822 he had 116 Jewish children under his charge. In 1824 he moved to Bombay and opened a school for Jews. It drew forty pupils. The Cochin work yielded only three baptisms by 1828. The London society then quit India. Sargon and his brother Abraham taught on in Bombay for nearly thirty years. They taught Jewish children their own faith, with no push to convert them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schor-moses-eph:
Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Ephraim Solomon Schor. He was a Polish rabbi who died at Lublin in 1633. People call him the elder Tebu'ot Shor. He descended from the tosafist Joseph Bekor Schor. He married Hannele, daughter of Saul Wahl of Brest-Litovsk. He later became rabbi of that city.

Schor succeeded Samuel Edels, the MaHaRSHA, as rabbi of Lublin. He held that post until his death. His book Tebu'ot Shor shortens Joseph Caro's Bet Yosef. A later kinsman wrote a work with the same title. The elder label keeps the two men apart. His son Jacob wrote Bet Ya'aḳob on Sanhedrin. Jacob served as rabbi of Brest-Litovsk from 1652 to 1655.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seligmann-franz:
Frederick T. Haneman worked with Isidore Singer on this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Franz Romeo Seligmann. He was an Austrian physician and Persian scholar. Seligmann was born at Nikolsburg on June 30, 1808. He died at Vienna on September 15, 1892. He studied at Vienna's gymnasium and university. He took his medical degree in 1830.

Seligmann became a privat-docent at Vienna in 1833. He assisted at the general hospital until 1838. In 1869 he won the chair of the history of medicine. He resigned that post in 1878. His De Re Medica Persarum renders the oldest Neo-Persian medical manuscript. Another work edits Abu Mansur on the foundations of drug lore. He also wrote on Persian manuscripts of great rarity. His later books treat healing systems and burial customs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shapira-isaiah-:
Isaiah Meir Kahana Shapira was a Polish-German rabbi and author born at Memel in 1828. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. By age thirteen he reportedly knew both Talmuds well. As a young man he added philosophy, mathematics, and astronomy.

Shapira first worked as a merchant, until fire destroyed all he owned. He then prepared for the rabbinate with nine months of secular study at Lemberg. Installed at Czortkow in 1860, he soon faced a feud between Hasidic groups. His peace effort turned anger on him for a time. Peace returned, and he served until his death in 1887. The entry shows learning and conflict in one rabbi's life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slonimski-hayyi:
Hayyim Selig Slonimski was a Russian author, scientist, and inventor. Isidore Singer and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Byelostok in 1810 and died in Warsaw in 1904. He first taught eastern European Jews popular science in Hebrew. He coined many Hebrew technical terms for that purpose.

His strict religious conservatism won readers' full trust. In 1842 he perfected a calculating machine of his own. It won the Demidoff prize of 2,500 rubles at St Petersburg. He later devised a way to send four telegrams at once. In 1862 he founded Ha-Zefirah, a Hebrew weekly for science. He also led the rabbinical seminary at Jitomir for twelve years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomons-adolph:
Adolphus Simeon Solomons was an American communal worker born in 1826. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in New York city on October 26. He was educated at the University of the City of New York. He rose fast in a firm of wholesale importers.

In 1851 Daniel Webster sent him to Berlin with despatches. At Frankfort he first saw a Jewish hospital ward. He resolved to found such a hospital in New York. A charity ball he helped arrange raised the first funds. That money helped start the present Mt Sinai Hospital. He later held government printing contracts in Washington.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stein-philip-14:
Philip Stein was an American jurist born at Steele, Prussia, in 1844. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on March 12 of that year. He emigrated to the United States in 1854 as a boy. He was educated at Milwaukee and the University of Wisconsin.

He took his master's degree and joined the bar in 1868. After study at Heidelberg, Bonn, and Berlin, he settled in Chicago. In 1870 he began practice in that city of Illinois. In 1892 and 1898 he won election to the Superior Court. In 1903 he became judge of the appellate court. By 1905 he was presiding justice of that court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sulamith-14104:
Sulamith was the first Jewish monthly magazine in the German language. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Its first volume appeared at Leipsic in July 1806. David Frankel and Joseph Wolf edited it at first. Frankel later edited it alone from Dessau.

The magazine aimed to spread culture and humanity among Jews. It followed the reform path of Mendelssohn's German followers. Pages held biographies, history sketches, sermons, and poems. Education news and Hebrew pieces appeared as well. Contributors included David Friedländer and Ignatz Jeiteles. Volumes ran in loose years until 1840, then revived in 1846. Much content is now dated, the entry notes. The rest still feeds research on modern Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-of-herod:
Herod's rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem is described in this article. George A. Barton wrote it with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Herod began the work in 20 or 19 B.C. He wanted a shrine as grand as his other buildings.

Jews feared the old Temple would fall and never rise again. Herod stored all materials first to prove his good faith. Priests worked as masons, since only priests could enter the holy place. The main building rose in eighteen months. Courts and outer works took eighty years. The article gives sizes, veils, and the golden candlestick. It also notes the Greek warning sign that barred Gentiles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tirzah-14404:
Tirzah names both an ancient royal city and a daughter of Zelophehad. Immanuel Benzinger wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jeroboam made Tirzah a royal city of Israel. It housed Israel's kings until Omri's reign. The Song of Songs praises its beauty.

Where the city stood remains uncertain today. Robinson placed it at modern Talluza, near Nablus. Conder instead chose Tayasir, with its caves and tombs. Neither Josephus nor Eusebius gives firm details. The district lay in Manasseh, in Zelophehad's portion. The second Tirzah was his youngest daughter. Numbers names her among his five daughters. Those sisters famously claimed an inheritance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trevoux-hebrew-:
Trévoux, a French town in Ain, barred Jews by its charter of 1300. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Some Jews settled there anyway for a yearly tax. Refugees from Lyons arrived in 1420 after expulsion. They worked at making gold and silver wire.

In 1425 the town forced a large loan contribution from them. Neighbors grew jealous of Jewish commercial success. In 1429 they accused Hebrew books of blasphemy. Investigators seized and burned the books at once. Fines and expulsion followed for the whole community. Some Jews returned within three years. Fresh expulsions came in 1467 and 1488.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uri-ori-ben-sim:
Uri ben Simeon was a sixteenth-century scholar of Safed who cataloged holy tombs. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born at Biel and settled at Safed. He abstracted a manuscript of 1537 for his work. That list named tombs of patriarchs, prophets, and sages.

His own travels added descriptions and grave illustrations. The book, Yihus ha-Abot, appeared at Venice in 1659. Hottinger translated it into Latin at Heidelberg. Carmoly later rendered it into French with twenty-seven pictures. A Judaeo-German version appeared at Wilna in 1853. Uri also compiled a forty-year calendar, printed in 1575. Jacob Christmann translated that calendar into Latin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wayikra-rabbah-:
Wayikra Rabbah is a homiletic midrash on Leviticus. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Nathan's Aruk first names the work in later sources. Rashi quotes it often in his commentaries. Zunz dated its origin to the mid seventh century. It arose in Palestine from older materials.

The book is not a running commentary on Leviticus. It holds thirty seven separate sermons, each a chapter. Their themes come from texts across the book. Its editor drew on Genesis Rabbah and the Jerusalem Talmud. Babylonian Talmud phrases appear in it as well. The entry maps its sources, shape, and sermon topics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolper-michael-:
Michael Wolper (born 1852) was a Russian teacher and maker of school books. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Wilna, he trained at the rabbinical school there. He left that school in 1872 with his degree. From then on he taught in Jewish grade schools.

By 1905 he also checked the Jewish school at Wilna. He served as censor of Hebrew books as well. His own books teach faith and tongue to the young. One book gives first lessons in the Jewish faith. A second book gives a new way to learn Hebrew. He wrote that book in 1888. With a co-worker he made a short creed book for class use. More Russian-Jewish school books came from his pen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-nappaha-:
Yizhak Nappaha was a scholar of Palestine in the 300s and 400s. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His name means the smith in the tongue of his day. That name stands in the Babylon books, not the Palestine ones.

As a teller of tales he ranks with the first of his age. The Babylon books mix him with more than one like name. That mix came from the free hand of a late sage. So the true name of his sire can not be known now. An older smith of his name was a rich man of old. That man held five courts in the town of Usha. No proof ties the two men as kin to this day. He was a pupil of Johanan, the great sage of the north.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-mende:
Zechariah Mendel ben Aryeh Lob was a Galician preacher and scholar. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Podhaice early in the 1700s. He died at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in the year 1791.

He came of the house of Solomon Luria and Moses Isserles. That house traced its line back to Rashi of France. His chief teacher was Jacob Joshua of Pene Yehoshua fame. He preached in the Talmud Torah of Frankfort in his prime. He left a great store of works at his death in that town. Just three of them reached print in his life time. One holds notes on the tract Shabbat and feast sermons. One is a mate to that work with more Talmud notes. One is a guide to faith thought and true Cabala lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zurishaddai-153: Zurishaddai was the father of Shelumiel, a chief of the tribe of Simeon. Emil G. Hirsch and Bernhard Pick wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When Moses counted the people of Israel, Shelumiel was chosen to help him. The book of Numbers names Zurishaddai each time it names his son in that duty. The entry gives the verses in Numbers chapters one, two, seven, and ten.
journal-of-discourses-vol-04:
Volume Four, from 1857, was preached while a federal army marched on Utah. Johnston's troops drew near, and war talk filled the Salt Lake valley. The Saints readied to burn their homes and flee south.

Young's discourses breathe defiance and faith in the same breath here. Speakers vow to leave a scorched desert rather than yield their faith. Plans for flight, food stores, and guard duty share the pulpit's time. A people under siege hears its prophet plan and pray at once. The sermons catch a kingdom braced for its hardest test yet by arms. Trust in God and trust in Young stand as one here.
kelvin-baltimore-lectures-1904:
Lord Kelvin gave twenty lectures at Johns Hopkins in 1884, and they appeared in print in 1904. The Baltimore Lectures treat molecular dynamics and the wave theory of light. Kelvin built mechanical models to picture how the ether might carry light waves. Twelve appendices extend the lectures with later work and corrections.

Kelvin thinks aloud here, testing models, noting doubts, and pushing analogies hard. His pages show a great physicist before quantum and relativity changed the field. The ether models failed in the end, yet the effort taught much. Historians value the lectures as a record of classical physics at its height. The style stays vivid throughout.
kenelm-chillingly-volume-04:
Volume four of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Kenelm Chillingly opens Book Four in London, a year and a half later. The season has not yet begun before Easter. Fashionable London gathers at an evening reception at Lord Beaumanoir's house. The chapter works through presence chambers and saloons, amassing talk and faces.

Gerard Danvers, a member of Parliament, gets a full portrait here. Danvers mixes energy, ability, and self-reliance with a tolerant indulgence toward others. Townsfolk say he might one day be prime minister. Against this worldly company, Lytton sets Kenelm's sharper questions about success and sincerity. This volume moves the novel from country roads into politics and society.
kent-lectures-homoeopathic-materia-medic:
James Tyler Kent published his Lectures on Homoeopathic Materia Medica in 1904, from lectures given at the Post-Graduate School of Homoeopathics. The first edition staged here is the Calcutta printing of Roy Publishing House. Kent, an American physician, became the defining voice of classical homeopathy in the United States.

Remedy by remedy, from Abies to Zincum, he pictures the patient type each medicine fits: symptoms, temperament, and all. His vivid drug pictures taught generations of homeopaths how to prescribe. The remedy lectures are complete in this scan, though its printed index breaks off at Carbo veg. in the final leaves. Kent's book remains a working manual for practitioners of his school. Few medical lectures have been so often reprinted.
letter-of-aristeas-thackeray-1904:
H. St. J. Thackeray translated the Letter of Aristeas into English in 1904. The Letter is a Hellenistic Jewish work about the making of the Septuagint. It purports to be a courtier's report to his brother.

The tale claims seventy-two scholars translated the Torah in seventy-two days. King Ptolemy's library in Alexandria supposedly commissioned the Greek Bible. Banquets, sage answers, and a tour of Jerusalem fill out the story. Scholars treat the account as charming legend rather than plain history. Its influence on later tradition was enormous regardless. Thackeray's translation presents the founding story of the Greek Bible gracefully.
london-sea-wolf-1904:
Jack London published The Sea-Wolf in 1904, his novel of a shipwrecked intellectual brutalized into manhood at sea. A seal-hunting schooner ruled by the terrifying Captain Wolf Larsen carries the tale. London, who had sailed those waters, loaded the book with sea craft and his creed.

Humphrey van Weyden, a critic and gentleman, is picked up from a ferry wreck and made a cabin boy by Larsen. Larsen, a superman of body and nihilist brain, crushes mutiny, reads Milton, and argues that life is yeast and appetite. Maud Brewster, a poet cast away in turn, joins Humphrey in escape to an island and a slow, tender stand against despair. Larsen, blinded by headaches, dies unbowed, and the pair are rescued from Endeavor Island at the close. The debates between captain and critic still give the sea tale its voltage.
lucretia-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Lucretia opens the novel's second part with a wide retrospect. Years have passed, and Napoleon has fallen from his thrones. The plough has crossed Waterloo, and harvests glitter on that grave. On the terrace at Laughton, one figure now paces alone.

The bride no longer clings to the bridegroom's arm. She is pale and worn, yet still commanding. Lytton pauses to muse on how memory lights only our own track. The story resumes in a changed world and a changed house. Old deeds begin to bear their harvest here. This volume turns the tragedy toward its reckoning.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume four of Margery rides through deep snow to a forest lodge. December wind leaves the riders with red faces and frozen hands. Yet Margery finds joy in the glittering winter woods. Snow crowns every stock and stone like tiny white hats.

Her heart stays heavy with care for her friend Ann. Ann seems doomed to share the sorry life of the Magister. Under God's open heavens, that fate feels impossible to Margery. Friendship, pity, and young love fill these winter chapters. Ebers sets bright nature against a girl's anxious thoughts. The volume carries Gred's story deeper into sorrow.
marlowe-doctor-faustus-1604:
Christopher Marlowe wrote The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus near the end of his short life. He drew on German tales of a scholar who bargained with the devil. The play reached print in 1604, eleven years after Marlowe's death. It became the defining English tragedy of the overreaching mind.

Faustus, bored with law, medicine, and theology, sells his soul for twenty-four years of magic and pleasure. A good angel and a bad angel fight for him while devils stage shows and tricks. The years slip away in pranks until the final hour arrives. Faustus's last speech, begging time to stop, remains one of the most powerful scenes in English drama.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-04:
Volume four of Bourrienne's memoirs holds chapters twenty seven to thirty five. The years in view are 1799 and 1800, by the contents. A new government rises on the ruins of the old in this part.

Bonaparte, now First Consul, writes to all foreign powers at once. He seeks peace, or at least the show of seeking it, Bourrienne says. Talks with England and Austria fail in those first months. Kleber's letter and the Egyptian reports fill the later heads of the volume. Italy was lost, and war with near all Europe ran on. Order, not revolt, was the face the new rule wished to show.
monro-digest-justinian-vol1-1904:
Charles Henry Monro, a Cambridge lawyer, published the first volume of his English translation of Justinian's Digest in 1904. The Digest is the great anthology of Roman law, compiled for the Emperor Justinian in the sixth century from the writings of classical jurists. For centuries, English readers had needed Latin to use it.

Volume 1 opens the work: the nature of law and justice, the courts, and the standing of persons before the law. Monro translates with a lawyer's precision, keeping the jurists' terse style readable. The Digest became the foundation of legal systems across Europe, so an English version served scholars and barristers alike. Monro's volume began the task of making the Corpus Juris of Rome accessible in the language of the common-law world.
my-novel-volume-04:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's fourth book opens with talk of marriage. Mr. Caxton praises how Pisistratus showed a lover's growing love. Signor Riccabocca left off his spectacles to look his best. Uncle Roland doubts this, citing Shakespeare's slovenly lover instead.

Caxton answers that love has many phases and degrees. A scorned lover may pine, while a hopeful one may primp. Blanche tosses her head at Miss Jemima's forward ways. Mrs. Caxton tries to keep the family's dignity intact. The chapter turns courtship into a learned, funny debate, as the tale's own love plot warms beside it.
nassau-fetichism-in-west-africa-1904:
Robert Hamill Nassau summed up forty years on the Gabon coast in Fetichism in West Africa, published in 1904. Nassau, an American Presbyterian missionary and physician, observed native customs across the Ogowe region for decades. Fetishism, in his term, witchcraft, and secret societies form the heart of his account.

He writes as a convinced missionary, yet also as a careful witness who learned languages and sat in village councils. Tales, trials, and charms fill pages drawn from life rather than books. The volume stands as a major period record of religion on the Gabon coast, to be read with its era in mind.
nernst-theoretical-chemistry-palmer-1904:
Walther Nernst systematized physical chemistry in his Theoretical Chemistry, Englished by L. M. Palmer in 1904. The English text was the second edition, drawn from the fourth German edition. The subtitle names his twin guides: Avogadro's rule and thermodynamics. Together they frame his account of matter and its changes.

Nernst applies heat theory to solutions and to electrochemistry in depth. Readers learn how energy rules reactions, cells, and the balance between states. His path here leads toward his later heat theorem, the third law of thermodynamics. The book served as the field's great textbook for years. Its order and scope set a standard.
new-york-at-the-louisiana-purchase-expos:
DeLancey M. Ellis prepared and compiled this report for the New York State Commission to the Louisiana Purchase Exposition. That fair was held at St. Louis in 1904. The report is dated 1907, and the commission sent it to Governor Charles E. Hughes at Albany on March 25 that year.

The letter up front calls it the final report required by statute. Twelve commissioners signed it, among them Edward H. Harriman and Lewis Nixon. Their charge was to account for New York's part in the fair. State reports like this one preserve what a state showed, spent, and claimed at a great national fair.
newton-opticks-1704:
Isaac Newton published Opticks in 1704, a treatise on the reflections, refractions, inflections, and colours of light. Unlike the Principia, Newton wrote Opticks in English and built it from experiments readers could picture. Prisms, slits, and dark rooms are its stage.

Newton showed that white light splits into colors and joins again, proving color lies in light itself, not in the glass. He measured the bending of rays and studied the rings now named for him. Closing queries speculated on gravity, matter, and God's role in nature. The book founded physical optics and set a model for experimental science: ask nature plain questions and record exact answers.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume four of The Ocean of Story, from Penzer's ten-volume edition begun in 1924, continues Tawney's rendering of Somadeva. The Kathasaritsagara now braids its hero's fortunes with tale cycles told by sages, wives, and wandering ascetics. Every narrator opens a new door, and behind it waits another narrator with a stranger tale.

Somadeva wrote to divert a queen, and diversion remains the law of the book. Penzer's notes in this volume chase the tale of the grateful beasts and other wanderers across three continents. The translation's calm surface over such abundance is Tawney's quiet triumph. Readers may dip anywhere and surface with a complete story. The ocean, by design, has no dull stretches for long.
openalex-w1267646904:
Gillinder Bedi, Cheryl Corcoran, and eight co-authors wrote this study. It came out in a journal on schizophrenia in 2015. Doctors lack firm tests for mental illness, they note. The team asked if a computer could read speech for risk. They worked with youths at high risk for psychosis.

The team taped talks with thirty-four youths and tracked them for years. Five of them later fell ill in that time. A computer scored how clear and rich their speech was. Those scores flagged each youth who later fell ill. They beat the calls made from clinic talks alone. The team says speech tests could give doctors a firm tool.
openalex-w1969726504:
Hazel McLellan, Paul Birch, and co-authors studied potato blight. Their paper appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2013. The blight pathogen secretes effector proteins into host plants. Those proteins disarm defenses and aid colonization, they note. Little was known about their host targets before.

One effector, of the RxLR class, drew their focus. It blocks two plant control proteins, called NAC factors. Those factors should move from a cell membrane to the nucleus. The effector stops that move, trapping them outside. Trapped factors cannot switch on defense genes properly. The work exposes a precise act of molecular sabotage.
openalex-w1994728704:
Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration published a methods paper in Physical Review C in 2013. It explains how the team measured centrality in lead-lead collisions. Centrality tells how head-on a crash was. The work used collisions at very high energy at the Large Hadron Collider.

The team linked the signals seen in the detector to the overlap of the two lead nuclei. They used a Glauber model, a simple geometric picture of the crash. From it they estimated how many nucleons took part and how many pairs collided. The model values matched values drawn from the data. The method lets ALICE results be compared with other experiments and with theory.
openalex-w1997328904:
Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration measured two short-lived particles in lead-lead collisions. Their paper appeared in Physical Review C in 2015. The particles are named K star and phi. The team asked how much of each particle the collisions made.

The team used the ALICE detector and studied particle decays. They measured yields across central and less central collisions. K star yields were lower in central collisions than expected. The authors link that drop to decay products scattering in the hot matter. Phi yields were not reduced in the same way. Flow models matched the phi pattern fairly well. The results showed that mass and outward flow shape the particle patterns.
openalex-w2068012504:
Alejandro Schijman, Margarita Bisio, Liliana Orellana and colleagues compared PCR tests for Chagas disease across many labs. Their study appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2011. Chagas disease is still a major neglected threat. Doctors need tests that find the parasite well. They also need markers of how treatment works.

Labs in many countries joined the test comparison. Each lab checked the same blood sample panels. Methods differed in how they pulled out and copied DNA. Test strength varied between methods and labs. The study picked out the approaches that found more cases. Shared test rules would help trials compare results. The work set the next steps for better Chagas tests.
openalex-w2102356204:
Kerrie Wilson, Emma Underwood, Scott Morrison and colleagues built a framework for spending conservation money wisely. Their paper appeared in PLoS Biology in 2007. Conservation funds are scarce worldwide. Priority lists often name places but not actions. Decision makers need to know what to fund, where and when.

Their framework links places with specific actions. It also weighs the threats each action addresses. Costs and likely benefits enter the calculation. They applied it to Mediterranean-type regions worldwide. Seventeen of the world's hotspots were included. Different actions won funding in different places. Timing mattered as much as location. Smart allocation can save more species per dollar.
openalex-w2462225304:
Matthew Aliota, Stephen Peinado, Iván Vélez, and Jorge Osorio published this study in Scientific Reports in 2016. With no vaccine or drug against the exploding Zika outbreak, one hope was Wolbachia, a bacterium already being seeded into mosquitoes against dengue. Infected Aedes aegypti resist several viruses; whether they resist Zika was unknown.

The team tested mosquitoes carrying the wMel strain, the same stock being released in Medellín, Colombia. Crucially, the mosquitoes fed on a virus-carrying host, mimicking real transmission rather than spiked laboratory blood. The infected mosquitoes showed reduced ability to catch, carry, and pass on Zika. The authors back expanding Wolbachia releases as a multi-virus shield across the Americas.
openalex-w2588121804:
Ana María López-Colomé, Irene Lee-Rivera, and Regina Benavides-Hidalgo, with Edith López, reviewed the protein paxillin in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology in 2017. Paxillin works as a scaffold at focal adhesions, the spots where cells grip their surroundings. It recruits the structural and signaling molecules that let cells move. Its activity switches on when certain parts of the protein gain phosphate groups.

The review explains how paxillin coordinates signals controlling cell migration, including small switch proteins like Rac1 and RhoA. It plays different roles across tissues, development, and the immune response. When its control goes wrong, paxillin helps drive oxidative stress, inflammation, and barrier failure in blood vessels. It is also an essential player in cancer growth and spread, the authors note. Understanding this crossroads protein may suggest new ways to block harmful cell movement.
openalex-w2746235704:
Ubirajara Oliveira, Britaldo Silveira Soares-Filho, and Adriano Pereira Paglia lead a large team assessing Brazil's protected areas in Scientific Reports in 2017. Brazil is a megadiverse country and a top conservation priority. Yet nobody had measured how well its protected area network covers its species. Earlier studies leaned on single groups like birds as stand-ins for all life.

The network holds over seventeen hundred units covering about a quarter of Brazil's territory. It shelters nearly forty percent of the remaining native vegetation. The Amazon holds the largest protected extent, while biomes like the Cerrado hold far less. Worryingly, under one percent of protected areas are well sampled for species records. The team combined distribution data and family trees across vertebrates, arthropods, and flowering plants. Their map exposes both protection gaps and knowledge gaps, showing where new reserves and surveys matter most.
openalex-w3020838504:
Stephen Zhang, Jing Liu, Asghar Jahanshahi, and colleagues posted this preprint on medRxiv in May 2020, before peer review. It surveys the health and job satisfaction of health care staff in Iran at the peak of the country's COVID-19 epidemic. The sample held three hundred four doctors, nurses, radiologists, technicians, and others.

Sizable shares of staff crossed cutoff levels for anxiety, depression, and distress, at roughly three in ten for the first two. Age, gender, schooling, access to protective gear, workplace type, and infection status each predicted some outcomes but not others. Access to protective equipment varied greatly across staff. The authors show that who suffered most depended on a mix of personal and workplace factors.
openalex-w4283589104: Laura Coates, Enrique Soriano, Heidi Bertheussen, and colleagues present the GRAPPA group's updated treatment recommendations for psoriatic arthritis. The guidance, dated 2021, appeared in Nature Reviews Rheumatology in 2022. The preserved sample holds only the publisher's citation page and the article's opening author list. It has no readable abstract, so the guidance itself cannot be summarised from it here.
openalex-w4393120004:
Ben Kirk, Peggy Cawthon, Hidenori Arai, and colleagues present a global expert consensus on what sarcopenia is, in Age and Ageing in 2024. Sarcopenia means losing muscle mass and strength as the body ages. It matters clinically, yet no worldwide agreed definition existed. The Global Leadership Initiative in Sarcopenia gathered representatives of all major scientific societies to settle the concept.

The group used a two-phase Delphi study, in which experts rate statements until they converge. One hundred seven participants from twenty-nine countries took part. Twenty statements won strong agreement. Muscle mass, muscle strength, and muscle-specific strength all belong in the definition, the panel agreed. A shared concept is the base for shared diagnosis and treatment research.
openalex-w7127983704:
Hitomi Kato, Juliana Yumi Ishisaki, Yoshiki Kuwatsuru, and colleagues test magnetic resonance angiography for mapping uterine arteries. Their study appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. The patients had symptomatic uterine fibroids. Many are treated by blocking the uterine artery, a procedure called embolization.

The artery's branching pattern varies between women, in four known forms. Knowing the pattern beforehand makes catheter work safer. Invasive angiography had mapped these variants in hundreds of arteries. The team checks whether non-contrast scans classify the anatomy just as well. They confirm the scans' accuracy against standard angiography. A reliable non-invasive map could spare patients a needle-based step before treatment.
openalex-w7204197604: Brazilian law requires schools to teach Afro-Brazilian and Indigenous history, but mandates do not teach themselves. This article studies how art-based teaching, grounded in Vygotsky's cultural theory, can turn those laws into real learning. The authors show mediation making policy live in the classroom. A hopeful study of culture as pedagogy.

osler-aequanimitas-1904:
Osler's Aequanimitas gathers his addresses to medical students, nurses, and doctors, first printed in 1904. The title essay praises calm steadiness, the quality its Latin name describes. Osler believed a doctor's temper shapes a patient's trust. His talks mix practical advice with wide reading and warm humor.

Other addresses in the volume treat study, books, and the conduct of a medical life. Generations of students received the book at graduation as a kind of charge. Its essays became the most quoted medical humanism in English. Osler writes as a mentor who expects much and scolds gently. The volume keeps his voice alive. Readers outside medicine enjoy it too.
osler-science-immortality-1904:
William Osler delivered Science and Immortality as the Ingersoll Lecture in 1904. The lecture series asked speakers to address human immortality from their own field. Osler, a leading doctor and teacher, brought a clinical eye to the old question. He asks what science can and cannot say about survival after death.

He sorts people into groups by their stance toward the question. Some hold faith, some doubt, and some rest in calm acceptance. Osler treats each stance with respect and dry wit. His own position stays modest and humane. The address became his most famous piece of philosophy. It shows medicine thinking about its limits.
pargiter-markandeya-purana-1904:
F. Eden Pargiter translated the Markandeya Purana for the Bibliotheca Indica series, completing the English text in 1904 after years of work. The Purana ranks among the oldest of its kind in India, and its crown is the Devi Mahatmya, the great hymn to the Goddess. Kings, sages, cosmic ages, and the deeds of gods fill the frame around that core.

In the Devi Mahatmya the Goddess rises to fight demons no god can master, and she wins in glory. That section shaped goddess worship across India and is still sung aloud at her festivals today. Pargiter's careful version remains the standard scholarly English rendering of the whole Purana for students.
paul-clifford-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Paul Clifford begins at chapter sixteen, in Bath. Clifford and his companions keep a splendid lodging in Milsom Street, over a hairdresser's shop, to please Ned. Yet they slip away to a mean alehouse in a remote suburb, where old Mr. Bags and the gang gather.

Clifford, here called Lovett, lounges silent while Ned jokes and Tomlinson reads a newspaper. The double life is the point: fine gentlemen by day, thieves in low rooms by night. Lytton uses Bath's polish and the alehouse's smoke to show how thin the line between the two worlds is.
pelham-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Pelham brings the hero back to London, and chapter forty-four finds him taking rooms at Mivart's. A year abroad has changed him: pleasure now serves ambition, and his foppery hides a close, keen, inquiring mind. His first visitor is Mr. N—, the tailor, come to renew his measure.

The tailor's advice is pure philosophy of the surface: padding here, an inch across the shoulders, for we must live for effect. Pelham gives exact measure and exact instructions instead. The volume follows his London campaign, where dress, dinners, and politics are all moves in one game.
petrie-methods-aims-archaeology-1904:
W. M. Flinders Petrie laid down the laws of the dig in Methods and Aims in Archaeology, his guide of 1904. Ere Petrie, most digs were hunts for gold and show pieces. He demands that each scrap be kept, drawn, and placed by its layer. A plain pot in place, he says, tells more than a loose gem.

Rules for camps, crews, notes, and print fill the guide. Young dig men learned their trade from it for years. It is the first true field guide of the craft. The laws in it still rule good work on site.
pirandello-late-mattia-pascal-1904:
Luigi Pirandello published The Late Mattia Pascal in 1904, an Italian novel about a man freed by a mistake. Mattia Pascal leaves his unhappy home and his debts behind. While away, he reads that a drowned man has been named as him. Everyone at home thinks he is dead.

Mattia takes a new name and tries to start a fresh life. He soon finds that a man with no past has no rights and no real place. Love and money both slip from his grasp. He returns home to find his wife remarried. The novel mixes comedy and sadness in its study of identity.

plos-pbio-0020004:
Tomoko Ishino, Kazuhiko Yano, Yasuo Chinzei, and their group traced a step in malaria infection for PLOS Biology in 2004. After a mosquito bite, malaria parasites travel to the liver. A sheet of cells lines the liver's blood vessels, and the parasites must cross it to reach liver cells.

The team found that the parasites need a cell-passage skill to make that crossing. They actively move through cells rather than slipping between them. Blocking that skill could, in theory, stop infection before the liver stage takes hold. The paper matters because the liver stage is a brief, quiet window. A drug or vaccine that works there could prevent illness outright.
plos-pbio-0020104:
Zhixin Xie, Lisa K. Johansen, Adam M. Gustafson, and a large team mapped small RNA pathways in plants for PLOS Biology in 2004. Plants use small RNAs to silence genes, fight viruses, and control growth. The team sorted the many small RNAs of the model plant Arabidopsis and traced how they are made.

They found that the pathways branch more than expected, with distinct sets of small RNAs doing distinct jobs. Some guard the genome against jumping genes, while others fine-tune growth genes. A full catalog of these RNAs gives plant science a working map. It also informs crop work, since the same pathways shape traits like yield and disease resistance.
plos-pbio-0020304:
Dennis R. Harris, Masashi Tanaka, Sergei V. Saveliev, and their team studied a radiation-proof bacterium in PLOS Biology in 2004. Deinococcus radiodurans survives doses of radiation that shatter its genome into hundreds of pieces, then rebuilds it. The authors focus on a protein called DdrA that appears after damage.

DdrA guards the broken ends of DNA, keeping them from being chewed away before repair starts. That protection buys time for the cell's rebuilding tools. The bacterium's tricks are of keen interest for cleaning up radioactive waste and for understanding DNA repair in general. Each named part, like DdrA, brings the full system closer to view.
plos-pone-0000004:
Douglas Strathdee, Helen Ibbotson, and Seth Grant asked a practical question about mouse genetics in work published by PLOS ONE in 2006. Gene engineers often park an added gene at the Gt(ROSA)26Sor locus, a safe harbor site in the mouse genome. The team tested whether the inserted gene works the same in either direction.

Their finding sits in the title: expression depends on orientation. A transgene facing one way at that locus behaved differently from the same gene facing the other way. For labs building mouse models of human disease, that is a warning worth knowing before the animals are bred. Design the insert carelessly, and the experiment can mislead from the start.
plos-pone-0000104:
Michael A. Pickart, Eric W. Klee, Aubrey L. Nielsen, and a large team built a genetics toolkit in PLOS ONE in 2006. The secretome is the set of proteins a cell secretes, its outward messages and tools. Many of their jobs were unknown. The team's framework knocks down these genes one by one in vertebrate embryos to reveal their roles.

Reverse genetics starts from the gene and asks what breaks without it. Applied at genome scale to secreted proteins, it promises a catalog of what our cells say to each other. Secreted proteins are prime drug targets, since they can be reached outside the cell. A map of their functions is thus both basic biology and a drug hunter's chart.
plos-pone-0000204:
Nikolas Nikolaidis, Dimitra Chalkia, D. Neil Watkins, and colleagues published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It argues for the ancient origin of a group of developmental genes the authors call DANGER, described as a new developmental superfamily. These genes are involved in how embryos build their bodies.

Tracing a gene family to an ancient origin changes when scientists think its roles began. The authors compare sequences across species to date the family. If the superfamily is as old as they argue, its genes were part of the toolkit of very early animals, not a later addition.
plos-pone-0000304:
Xavier Dramard, Thierry Heidmann, and Silke Jensen published this genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The I-factor is a LINE retrotransposon, a jumping gene in fruit flies that can cause sterility when it runs loose. The authors describe natural epigenetic protection against it: fragments left by ancestral invasions of the element silence the modern copies.

The genome, in effect, keeps souvenirs of old invasions that vaccinate it against new ones. The authors document that protection in Drosophila. The work is a neat case of an arms race written into DNA, where the host's defense is built from the invader's own remains.
plos-pone-0000404:
Remus Oşan and colleagues applied a mathematical technique to brain data in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Neural networks in the brain encode information in patterns spread across many cells, and those patterns are hard to read from raw recordings. The team used subspace projection methods to classify and display these network-level encoding patterns.

Subspace projection simplifies high-dimensional data by finding the directions that carry the real signal. Applied to neural activity, it can sort patterns by what they represent and show them in pictures a human can grasp. Better readouts of population activity serve research on memory, movement, and brain-computer interfaces, where decoding many cells at once is the whole problem.
plos-pone-0000504:
Cindy Voisine and colleagues used a millimeter-long worm to screen for Huntington's disease drugs, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Huntington's is a fatal inherited brain disease with no cure. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans can be engineered to carry the disease's defect, and the team used it for identification of potential therapeutic drugs.

Worms are cheap, fast, and easy to dose, so thousands of compounds can be tested in weeks. Hits from a worm screen still face a long road through mouse and human testing, but the screen widens the funnel's mouth. The study is an example of model-organism drug discovery aimed at a disease that human trials alone cannot explore quickly.
plos-pone-0000604:
Elena M. Boggio and colleagues watched a signaling enzyme light up in two cell compartments at once after visual input, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. ERK is an enzyme that relays activity signals inside neurons. The team showed that visual stimulation activates ERK in two parts of rat cortical neurons. ERK rose in the synaptic compartment and in the somatic compartment. Both responses ran on the same timetable.

Parallel timing suggests the synapse and the nucleus-bound machinery are coordinated when the visual system adapts to input. ERK activation is a step in plasticity, the process by which seeing reshapes the seeing brain. Rat visual cortex is a standard model for how experience tunes sensory systems early in life.
plos-pone-0000704:
Jeroen R. P. M. Strating, Gerrit Bouw, Theo G. M. Hafmans and colleagues compared two members of a protein transport family, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The p24 family is thought to help move proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, the cell's shipping and sorting stations. A subset of p24 proteins rises when frog pituitary cells are activated to produce more hormone.

The title previews a contrast: p24 alpha and p24 delta have disparate effects on secretory protein transport and processing. Two relatives pulling differently complicates any simple family story. For cell biologists, sorting out who does what in the early secretory pathway underpins everything cells export, from hormones to antibodies.
plos-pone-0000804:
Tsunglin Liu, Thales Papagiannakopoulos, Kathy Puskar and colleagues searched living tissue data for the fingerprint of microRNAs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs are short non-coding transcripts, about 21 nucleotides long, capable of regulating gene expression. The best-studied mechanism has a microRNA binding its target messenger RNA, after which translation is inhibited and the message may be destroyed.

If microRNAs act in vivo, sets of real mRNAs should carry a detectable signal of that action, in their sequences or levels. The team reports detecting such a signal in an in vivo expression set. Confirming lab mechanisms in whole organisms tells researchers microRNA rules learned in dishes still govern living systems.
plos-pone-0000904:
Eriikka Heikkinen, Teemu Kallonen, Lilli Saarinen and colleagues compared whooping cough germs across Finland, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough and has returned in many countries. Finland has used the whole cell vaccine for more than fifty years, yet cases rose again.

The team compared genomes of Finnish strains and report steady gene loss over time. A germ that sheds genes while a vaccine presses on it raises hard questions about adaptation. Their comparison helps health officials judge whether vaccines still match the germ in circulation. It also shows evolution at work inside a single country.
plos-pone-0001004:
Samantha Morris, Alexandra Almeida, Hideaki Tanaka and colleagues showed how a factor called Tsukushi tunes embryo signals, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In early frog development, the middle germ layer forms when lower cells signal to cells above them. Whole body layers arise from such local conversations.

Tsukushi modulates three signal families at once: Xnr2, FGF and BMP. Tuning several signals together can set the borders of the germ layers with precision. The work was done in Xenopus, the standard frog for embryo studies. A single factor touching three pathways is a reminder that embryo signals form a web, not separate wires.
plos-pone-0001104:
Jeffrey Petrella, Steven Prince, Lihong Wang and colleagues tested a brain signal's power to predict decline in mild cognitive impairment, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Healthy people deactivate a region called the posteromedial cortex during many tasks. Brain imaging had suggested that this deactivation during memory tasks is impaired in Alzheimer's disease.

Mild cognitive impairment sits between normal aging and Alzheimer's. The team assess the prognostic value of posteromedial deactivation in such patients: does a weaker signal foresee worse decline. A predictor at this stage would help families plan and trials recruit the right patients. Imaging markers are plentiful; prognostic proof is the rare part.
plos-pone-0001204:
When immune cells meet, they form a structured contact zone called the immunological synapse. Oded Rechavi and colleagues report a surprising event at that zone in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. An oncogenic protein, H-Ras, transfers from one cell to another there. The synapse is known for regions of membrane fusion and exchanges of membrane fragments between the cells.

The authors show that the cancer-associated form of H-Ras moves between cells at the synapse. A growth-promoting protein passing hand to hand could change how the receiving cell behaves. The finding adds a new route by which signals, healthy or harmful, spread through the immune system.
plos-pone-0001304:
Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep caused by prions, infectious proteins. Gillian McGovern and Martin Jeffrey describe the disease's specific pathology in sheep lymphoid tissues, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Prion diseases often cause accumulation of the disease-associated prion protein in the lymphoreticular system, the network of immune tissues.

The protein builds up in association with follicular dendritic cells and tingible body macrophages in secondary lymphoid organs. Mapping exactly where it accumulates helps diagnose scrapie from tissue samples, which matters for flock surveillance. The lymphoid pattern also hints at how prions spread through the body before reaching the brain.
plos-pone-0001404:
Sheena Lee and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on spinal muscular atrophy, a gene based ill that weakens muscle. In this disease, one gene is lost, but a near twin gene gives weak backup. The protein's full job was still not clear. The team read gene use across the genome in a model of the disease.

Their broad scan named sets of genes whose use shifts when the key protein is low. Those shifts point to paths that may drive the muscle loss. They also give a list of fresh drug targets to test. The work moves from one lost gene to the wider web it disturbs.
plos-pone-0001504:
Mehmet Somel and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on diet and gene use in humans and chimps. The human diet strays far from that of our close primate kin. What that stray means for gene gaps was unknown. The team fed lab mice diets in the style of human or chimp food.

Gene use in the mice shifted with diet. Some shifts copied the known gaps between human and chimp gene use. That hints diet alone can drive part of the species gap. It warns that gene comparisons must weigh food and lab life. It also gives a tool to test diet effects in a strict way.
plos-pone-0001604:
Dean Smith, Julie Rosenheimer, and Ronald Kalil published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on ion channels in young rat nerve stem cells. These channels help set how cells fire, and they matter for growth and cell division. No full account of them existed for nerve stem cells from the rat brain's growth zone. The team recorded the currents cell by cell.

They chart two main channel types and how each opens and shuts. The chart is a base map for how these stem cells talk in bursts. It helps labs tell stem cells from their mature kin by their currents. It may also hint at how channel faults skew brain growth.
plos-pone-0001704:
Geraldine A. Wright, Sonya M. Kottcamp, and Mitchell G. A. Thomson studied how honeybees judge odors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Animals use smells to tell mates, kin, and food apart, even though natural odor amounts vary a lot. Generalization, treating two different stimuli as alike, helps an animal decide that a changed smell still means the same thing.

The authors show that generalization is what lets bees stay sensitive to complex odor features despite that variation. The full text gives the training tests, the odor blends, and the bees' choices. The work explains a puzzle in animal senses. A nose can be both finely tuned and tolerant of noise, a balance that robot sensors still struggle to copy.
plos-pone-0001804:
Mustafa Raoof, Haq Nawaz, Rabeeya Nusrat, and their co-authors surveyed sedative use in Pakistan in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Benzodiazepines are prescribed too freely in Pakistan and are available over the counter without prescription, a major public health problem. Data on how much people knew about these drugs, and how much they used them, was limited.

Their one-time survey covered healthy volunteers and clinic patients visiting a large care hospital. The full text gives how much people knew, the usage rates, and where people got the drugs. Benzodiazepines are habit forming, so measuring casual use and low awareness gives health chiefs the baseline they need to tighten supply and warn the public.
plos-pone-0001904:
Wassim Chehab and co-authors split apart two plant defense signals in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When pests or germs attack, plants fire back with chemical defenses. Two groups of signals drive much of that response. One is the jasmonates, and the other is six-carbon aldehydes, both made from fats in the leaf by two rival branches of one pathway.

Because the branches compete, their roles are hard to untangle. The team used plants in which one branch or the other was changed, to see what each signal group does on its own. Clear roles for each signal help crop science breed or treat plants that resist pests with fewer sprays.
plos-pone-0002004:
Elizabeth Clement and co-authors recorded brain waves that cycle like sleep under anesthesia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Sleep and general anesthesia both bring unconsciousness and share some brain steps. But sleep is not flat: it cycles between active REM sleep and quiet sleep. Whether anesthesia shows like cycles was less clear.

Under urethane anesthesia, a standard lab drug, the team recorded spontaneous shifts of brain state. As the title states, the brain showed cyclic, sleep-like alternations. If an anesthetized brain still cycles, depth of anesthesia may rise and fall on its own. That fact matters for both brain science and surgery.
plos-pone-0002104:
Timur Akchurin and co-authors tracked the birth and death of bone-eating cells in long-term culture, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Osteoclasts are the cells that resorb bone. They contribute to degenerative, metabolic, and neoplastic bone diseases, which often show lasting changes in the bone's local setting. How a population of these cells rises and falls over time was not well charted.

The team aimed to investigate the dynamics of osteoclast formation and death in cultures kept for the long term. They report complex dynamics, not a simple rise and fade. Bone drugs act on these very dynamics.
plos-pone-0002204:
Kwasi Torpey, Mushota Kabaso, Liya Mutale, and co-authors described a staffing fix for HIV care in Zambia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Clinics offering antiretroviral therapy, the drugs that keep HIV in check, face severe staff shortages. Good adherence counseling helps patients take their drugs on schedule, but nurses and doctors have little time for it.

The Zambia Prevention, Care and Treatment Partnership trained community volunteers as adherence support workers at health facilities. These lay workers took on counseling and follow-up tasks. The program shows how care can be shared more widely, so scarce clinical staff can focus on the work only they can do.
plos-pone-0002304:
Heather Ishak, John Dumbacher, Nancy Anderson, and co-authors surveyed blood parasites in owls, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. All three subspecies of the Spotted Owl are threatened by habitat loss and by the spread of the Barred Owl into their range. One unexamined threat was whether Barred Owls carry blood parasites that could infect Spotted Owls.

The team screened owls for blood parasites and compared what each species carries. If the invading Barred Owl brings new parasites, contact between the two could add disease pressure to a bird already losing ground. Surveys like this one tell conservation teams whether disease belongs on the threat list.
plos-pone-0002404:
Led by Iwai, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Yoshiko Iwai, Hiroaki Hemmi, Olga Mizenina, and others. Its subject is an IFN-γ-IL-18 Signaling Loop Accelerates Memory CD8 + T Cell Proliferation. Rapid proliferation is one of the important features of memory CD8 + T cells, ensuring rapid clearance of reinfection.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002504:
Research by Hemminki and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Kari Hemminki, Asta Försti, Justo Lorenzo Bermejo, and others. Its subject is the ‘Common Disease-Common Variant’ Hypothesis and Familial Risks. The recent large genotyping studies have identified a new repertoire of disease susceptibility loci of unknown function.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002604:
Bunnell and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Tina M. Bunnell, Michele A. Jaeger, Daniel P. Fitzsimons, and others. Its subject is destabilization of the Dystrophin-Glycoprotein Complex without Functional Deficits in α-Dystrobrevin Null Muscle. α-Dystrobrevin is a component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC) and is thought to have both structural and signaling roles in skeletal muscle.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002704:
Research from Eva Madi Riising and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers the polycomb repressive complex 2 is a potential target of SUMO modifications. The catalog record names Eva Madi Riising first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) functions as a transcriptional repressor through a mechanism that involves methylation of Histone H3 at lysine 27. The authors add a further point. The PRC2 complex activity is essential for cellular proliferation, development, and cell fate decisions. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002804:
Work by Sigeng Chen and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with dopamine inhibits mitochondrial motility in hippocampal neurons. Authorship is credited in the record to Sigeng Chen and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The trafficking of mitochondria within neurons is a highly regulated process. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002904:
Jijun Hao, Marie Daleo, Clare Murphy and co-authors tested a small drug called dorsomorphin in stem cells in 2008. Embryonic stem cells can become any tissue type, which makes them a hopeful source for repair medicine. Guiding them into one chosen type, such as heart muscle, needs precise signals.

Dorsomorphin selectively blocks BMP signaling, one of those growth signals. In PLOS ONE the team reports that blocking BMP this way promotes cardiomyogenesis, the making of heart muscle cells, in embryonic stem cells. That gives labs a simple chemical tool for steering stem cells toward the heart.
plos-pone-0003004:
Sven Hoffmann and Michael Falkenstein compared two ways to clean eye blink artifacts from EEG in 2008. Blinks swamp the brain signals that electroencephalograms record. The study investigated what impact blinks leave behind after correction by a regression method and by independent component analysis.

The two prominent methods are named EMCP for the regression approach and ICA for the component approach. Published in PLOS ONE, a head-to-head check on residual impact helps labs pick a cleaning method with evidence. Clean EEG matters for any study reading thought or perception from scalp signals. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003104:
Adam de Smith, Robin Walters, Lachlan Coin and co-authors studied small deletion variants in human DNA in 2008. Copy number variants contribute greatly to human genomic variation, with over 5,000 loci reported covering more than 18 percent of the genome. Little was known about the origin and stability of variants of different sizes.

Small deletions have stable breakpoints commonly associated with Alu elements, repeated DNA sequences, the title reports. Stable break points suggest these variants arise and persist in orderly ways. Published in PLOS ONE, the work helps interpret the deletions found in patient genome scans.
plos-pone-0003204:
Monika Madan and Salomon Amar link an immune sensor to atherosclerosis in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Accumulating evidence implicates a fundamental link between the immune system and atherosclerosis, the artery disease behind most heart attacks. Toll-like receptors are principal sensors of the innate immune system. The team report an assessment of the role of the TLR2 pathway in atherosclerosis linked with a high-fat diet and pathogens.

They present proteomic findings, a broad survey of proteins, to support that role. Readers see diet, infection and immunity drawn into one artery story. The work suggests immune sensors could be targets in heart disease prevention.
plos-pone-0003304:
Bindu Chandrasekharan, Vanitha Bala, Vasantha L. Kolachala and colleagues delete a neuropeptide gene in a colitis model in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Neurogenic inflammation plays a major role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease. The team examined the role of neuropeptide Y and neuronal nitric oxide synthase in shaping colitis. Colitis was induced by giving dextran sodium sulphate.

The title reports that targeted deletion of neuropeptide Y modulates experimental colitis. Readers see gut nerves treated as active players in bowel inflammation, not bystanders. Nerve signals may offer drug angles apart from calming the immune system alone.
plos-pone-0003404:
Danhua Jiang, Yuqi Wang, and Yizhong Wang studied flowering control in a small plant in 2008. The plant, Arabidopsis, times its blooms with a set of switch genes. One gene machine, called Polycomb repressive complex 2, turns genes off. The team tested its grip on two flowering genes.

Parts of the machine, named CLF and EMF2, helped hold both genes down. The genes are FLOWERING LOCUS C and FLOWERING LOCUS T. Keeping them off delays flowering until the right season. The work explains one brake plants use before they commit to bloom.
plos-pone-0003504:
Jacob Shun-Jen Yang, Jia-Min Bai, and Tzumin Lee traced protein delivery in fly neurons in this 2008 paper. Neurons sort membrane proteins to dendrites or axons, their two branch types. How that sorting is set up and kept was little known. The team followed one protein, Dscam, with a TM1 segment.

A motor complex called dynein-dynactin proved essential for its dendrite restriction. The motor hauls cargo along the cell's inner tracks. Without it, Dscam lost its proper branch address. The work exposes the shipping system behind neuron branch identity. Fruit flies remain a fast, cheap stand-in for basic neuron questions.
plos-pone-0003604:
Tao Yang, Juliet K. Knowles, and Qun Lu tested small protective molecules in this 2008 paper. Alzheimer's disease involves a toxic protein fragment called amyloid-beta, or Aβ. That fragment drives nerve cell death and synapse damage. A receptor called p75 NTR can mediate part of that harm.

The team used small, non-peptide ligands that bind p75 NTR. Those ligands inhibited Aβ-induced neurodegeneration in their tests. They also reduced the synaptic impairment the fragment causes. Drug-like blockers of this receptor point toward new Alzheimer's treatments. Amyloid is the best known target in Alzheimer's, yet drugs against it keep failing.
plos-pone-0003704:
Mari Kumashiro, Osamu Yokoyama, and Hidetoshi Ishibashi published this primate study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Eye contact and pointing are classic ways to direct another's attention to a target. The authors had earlier asked whether such joint attention relates to copying actions in Japanese monkeys.

Here they report that imitation of body movements was eased when joint attention came first. Eye contact and pointing set up a shared focus between monkey and human model. The result ties social attention to learning by copying in our primate cousins, a link also claimed for human children.
plos-pone-0003804:
Rogerio Meneghini, Abel L. Packer, and Lilian Nassi-Calò published this bibliometric study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Journal impact factor is widely taken as a mark of an article's relevance and quality. Peer review inside one journal is supposed to be uniform. The authors tested whether authors' country still shapes later citations.

They found articles by Latin American authors in prestigious journals receive fewer citations. The gap appears despite the same journals and review process. The finding exposes a geographic bias in how science notices and rewards its producers, with costs for researchers outside rich countries.
plos-pone-0003904:
Patricia Resa-Infante, Núria Jorba, Noelia Zamarreño, and co-authors studied how flu virus copies itself in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article focuses on the virus polymerase, its copying machine. That machine has three parts, PB1, PB2, and PA. It works inside the nucleus of infected cells.

PB2 helps decide which hosts a flu strain can infect. The team placed a tagged PB2 in human cells and pulled out its partners. They found that host importin proteins must engage PB2 for copying to proceed. Blocking that contact could offer a new angle for flu drugs. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004004:
Andreas C. Fröbius, David Q. Matus, and Elaine C. Seaver studied pattern genes in a marine worm in 2008. Hox genes assign body region identities along the head-to-tail axis. In many animals, their order on the chromosome matches their body order. That neat match is called colinearity.

Their PLOS ONE article examines Hox genes in the worm Capitella sp. I. They report both the genomic layout and where genes switch on. The worm belongs to a major animal branch with few such studies. Its pattern tests how universal Hox colinearity really is. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004104:
Keiko Takahashi, Sawako Yoshina, Maekawa Masashi, and co-authors studied a mental retardation gene in worms in 2009. PQBP1 is a causative gene for X-linked mental retardation. Patients with its mutations often show lean bodies. The worm C. elegans carries a strictly conserved version of the gene.
