Their PLOS ONE article made glowing and mutant worms for that homologue. Analysis tied the gene to lipid metabolism in the animals. Fat handling may explain the lean build in patients. A simple worm thus models a human brain disorder's body signs. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004204:
Taeg Kim and Thomas Braciale published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dendritic cells sit at body surfaces such as the skin, airways, and gut. There they start adaptive immune responses against germs and harmless substances alike. The respiratory tract holds several distinct subsets of these cells.

The authors compared how well each lung dendritic cell subset supports the induction of virus-specific killer CD8 T cells. They report that the subsets differ in this capacity. Knowing which subset does the heavy lifting helps vaccine designers aim at the right cell.
plos-pone-0004304:
Haguy Wolfenson and colleagues published this cell adhesion study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Focal adhesions are multi-protein complexes that link a cell to the matrix around it and let the cell sense that matrix. Much is known about their molecular composition, yet the rules governing their dynamics were less clear.

The authors examined the juxtamembrane cytoplasm, the cell interior just beneath these adhesions, and its role in adhesion behaviour. They show that this thin layer helps govern how focal adhesions move and remodel. A cell's grip on its surroundings, it turns out, is managed from just under the surface.
plos-pone-0004404:
A protein called Tollip does more inside cells than once thought. Alessia Ciarrocchi, Romina D'Angelo, Chiara Cordiglieri, and co-authors report a new role in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. Tollip interacts with the interleukin-1 receptor and helps control its turnover in endosomes.

Together with Tom1, Tollip also has a general role in endosomal protein traffic. The authors show Tollip is a mediator of protein sumoylation, a tagging process that changes protein behavior. A second job for Tollip links immune signaling to a wider cell control system. Sumoylation tags alter many proteins, so a mediator role places Tollip in wider networks.
plos-pone-0004504:
Bone marrow cells can be coaxed toward the pancreas and turn into insulin makers in living animals, report LuGuang Luo, John Luo, Fang Xiong, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team proposed that certain marrow lineages, helped by cytokine treatment, would migrate into the pancreatic islets. Those islets are the clusters of cells that make insulin, the hormone missing in diabetes.

They focused on a marrow group marked as SCA positive, and on which cytokine signals draw them in. Once in the islets, the arriving cells converted into insulin-positive cells in the body, as the title reports. If the route can be made reliable, a patient's own marrow might one day help rebuild insulin production.
plos-pone-0004604:
Proteins wander oddly inside mitochondria because of the folded shape of the inner membrane, model Valerii Sukhorukov and Jurgen Bereiter-Hahn in PLOS ONE in 2009. Diffusion of inner membrane proteins is a prerequisite for mitochondria to function correctly. The inner membrane is folded into cristae: tubular, vesicular, or flat folds connected to the outer region by small junctions.

Those tight connections constrain how proteins move, making their diffusion anomalous: not the free random walk of simple physics. The authors model how cristae geometry produces that behavior. The geometry matters because energy production depends on proteins meeting each other in the membrane. A shape that traps proteins in compartments changes how the cell's power plants run.
plos-pone-0004704:
Olga Valverde and colleagues tested a brain receptor called GPR3 in mood like behavior, for PLOS ONE in 2009. GPR3 is a sensor with no known natural trigger, yet it stays active on its own. It occurs widely in the brain, with the most found in a small hub tied to mood and reward.

The team removed the gene in mice and ran a set of behavior tests. They asked how loss of the receptor changes stress, fear, and reward acts. The results tie this quiet receptor to emotional response. That makes it a lead for new mood drug research.
plos-pone-0004804:
Nora Lawo, Felix Wäckers, and Jörg Romeis reported that Indian Bt cotton varieties do not affect performance of cotton aphids, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cotton varieties expressing Cry proteins from Bacillus thuringiensis are grown worldwide for management of pest moths. To prevent non target pest outbreaks and retain biological control by predators and parasitoids. Effects on other insects must be checked carefully before and after commercial release.

Aphids are a key non target herbivore on cotton. The study found no effect of Bt varieties on aphid performance. That supports the specificity of the technology. Continued monitoring remains prudent in farming practice.
plos-pone-0004904:
Karla Passalacqua and colleagues compared gene use in Bacillus cereus group strains grown in two kinds of air in PLOS ONE in 2009. These spore forming bacteria are found all over in soil and food. Close kin in the group cause anthrax, while others cause food borne illness, so the group holds both high risk and low risk strains.

The team grew strains in air rich in carbon dioxide, like host tissue, and in plain air. Gene use shifted a great deal between the two settings. Those shifts show which genes may switch on when the bacteria enter a host. That helps explain how mild strains and deadly strains diverge.
plos-pone-0005004:
ALS is a paralyzing nerve disease. Some cases run in families through mutations in the protein SOD1. Zeynep Oztug Durer and colleagues studied what makes SOD1 clump. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They tested three kinds of damage. One was loss of the protein's metal ions. Another was breaking its stabilizing disulfide bond. The third was the ALS mutations themselves.

All three pushed SOD1 to form amyloid-like aggregates. Such clumps appear in the neurons of patients. The study unites several ALS triggers under one toxic process. If clumping poisons motor neurons, blocking it becomes a clear goal. The work gives that goal a firm experimental basis.
plos-pone-0005104:
Songbirds build nests from local materials. The broad design is typical of the species. Adèle Mennerat, Philippe Perret and Marcel Lambrechts asked about individual taste. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They studied a passerine bird's choices of nest materials. Learning shapes much animal behavior. Nest building might be one case.

Individual birds showed local preferences for particular materials. Two neighbors could favor different stuff for the same job. The choice goes beyond species habit. It suggests learning and experience shape building. The work reveals character in nest construction. Animal personality is a growing field. Even a nest can carry a signature of its builder.
plos-pone-0005204:
Before a young cortical cell can become a neuron, it must switch on fate genes such as Neurogenin1. That switch is brief but decisive for building the brain's outer layer. Cundiff and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that the kinase ERK5 helps control that switch.

ERK5 is an enzyme that passes signals inside the cell. The study found it regulates Neurogenin1 during the period when cortex neurons are born. Placing ERK5 upstream of the fate switch gives brain researchers a new point of control for studies of development and repair.
plos-pone-0005304:
Age-related macular degeneration is a leading cause of central vision loss in older people, and smoking is a primary risk factor. Wang and colleagues examined retinal pigment cells exposed to cigarette smoke in PLOS ONE in 2009 to find the cellular basis of that link.

The pigment layer supports the retina and suffers early in the disease. Smoke changed those cells in ways that fit the disease process. Pinning down the changes helps explain why smokers face higher risk and may reveal steps where the damage could be slowed. The skin of the eye is thin and light hits it all day. So smoke-borne harm there builds up fast, which fits why smokers lose their core sight more often than non-smokers.
plos-pone-0005404:
Polyphosphate is an ancient chain of phosphate units, tens to hundreds long, joined by high-energy bonds. It forms complexes with many proteins and modulates their activity. Zakharian and colleagues asked what it does to TRPM8, the cold-sensing channel, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Inorganic polyphosphate modulated TRPM8 channel function in their tests. A simple polymer tuning the body's cold sensor adds a control layer to temperature sensation. The result also hints at how energy-rich phosphate stores might adjust other ion channels. Cold sense guards us from frost and burn alike,. A plain chain of phosphates as its dial hints that the most old parts of the cell still run some of its most fine-tuned senses.
plos-pone-0005504:
Michael Miksa and co-authors studied sepsis in rats for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Sepsis is a whole-body inflammation that can follow infection and damage organs. Early in sepsis, the stress hormone noradrenaline rises and can make immune cells react too strongly.

The team found that one receptor for the hormone, on immune cells in the gut, plays a central role in driving organ harm. Blocking that path may calm the harmful response. The work names a target for future sepsis drugs, an area where new options are badly needed. Sepsis still kills many patients in intensive care, so any firm drug target in the pathway draws close attention.
plos-pone-0005604:
Rosa Molfetta and co-authors studied how allergy receptors are removed from cell surfaces in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Tagging surface receptors with ubiquitin often sends them to be destroyed, quieting their signals. The IgE receptor, central to allergy, sits on mast cells and is tagged quickly when it meets its trigger.

The team showed that the tagging happens in special fat-rich patches of the cell surface. Adapter proteins that read the tags then pull the receptor inside. Blocking that removal could be a new way to calm allergic responses. Mast cells drive hay fever and asthma attacks, so their receptor handling is watched closely by drug teams.
plos-pone-0005704:
Jaklien Leemans and co-authors examined in 2009 how a sensor protein drives damage in failing kidneys. Long-term kidney disease brings swelling and scar tissue, called fibrosis, until the organ stops working. The sensor, toll-like receptor 2, sits in kidney tissue and can be set off by the body's own alarm signals.

The team followed the sensor's role as injury deepened over time. Their work links TLR2 to both the swelling and the scarring that follow. Blocking that sensor could slow the slide toward kidney failure. The study gives that idea a firm base in animal evidence.
plos-pone-0005804:
Maria Marchetti and co-authors reported in 2009 that a common anti-inflammatory drug makes cancer cells easier to kill under oxidative stress. Sulindac, an approved NSAID, blocks enzymes that make prostaglandins. It has long drawn interest for preventing colon polyps and cancer.

Under stress from reactive oxygen, sulindac-treated cancer cells died more readily in the team's work. That pairing could matter for therapy: stress the cell, then remove its shield. The drug's long safety record makes such ideas quicker to test in people. The study adds a mechanism to an old drug's anticancer reputation.
plos-pone-0005904:
Elodie Magnanou and co-authors tested in 2009 whether steady melatonin keeps an aging shrew's daily rhythms young. In the lab, shielded from seasons, animals often live longer and show a drawn-out old age. Activity rhythms fray as senescence advances.

The greater white-toothed shrew was given continuous melatonin treatment. Treated animals kept youthful rhythmic activity patterns for much longer into old age. Melatonin is the hormone of darkness and a known rhythm keeper. The result suggests rhythm decay in aging is not fixed. It also models how light and hormone cues might support healthy aging.
plos-pone-0006004:
Histamine is best known for allergy, yet it also shapes how malaria attacks the brain. Walid Beghdadi, Adeline Porcherie, Bradley Schneider and colleagues studied one of its receptors in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper focuses on the H3 receptor and on cerebral malaria, the deadly brain form of the disease.

Blood histamine rises in malaria, in people and in mouse models alike. The title reports that signaling through the H3 receptor protects mice from cerebral malaria. A protective pathway turns an allergy chemical into a possible ally, and it names a receptor that drug teams could aim at in the search for new malaria treatments.
plos-pone-0006104:
Human regulatory T cells wear a control protein in more than one cut. Reiner Mailer, Kirsten Falk and Olaf Rötzschke compared two cuts of FOXP3 in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies a natural isoform missing two exons, including the part that forms its leucine zipper, the clasp by which such proteins pair up.

Losing the zipper did not stop the protein pairing, yet it wiped out its suppressive capacity, the title reports. Pairing and working are thus separate traits. The distinction matters for any therapy that aims to raise T cell regulation, since a present but toothless protein could fool a test that counts forms instead of function.
plos-pone-0006204:
Heavy metals pollute water and settle into the living mats that coat rocks and mud. Mireia Burnat and colleagues grew cyanobacteria, simple photosynthetic bacteria, in small test systems for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They measured how lead and copper changed the populations living in those microcosms.

Counting living mass alone can miss shifts in which species thrive or fade. The team therefore tracked the populations in place, inside the mats themselves. Their approach shows metal harm at the community level, not just in single lab strains. Such tests help predict how pollution reshapes the base of aquatic food webs.
plos-pone-0006304:
Glucokinase senses glucose and tags it with phosphate, keeping blood sugar steady. Jian Zhang and colleagues pinpoint a key residue, lysine at position 169, in human glucokinase in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme is a drug target for two disorders: a young-onset diabetes and a condition of excess insulin in infancy.

The lysine proves a determinant for the phosphorylation step, the authors report. Atomic-level detail explains how the enzyme performs its chemistry. Such detail guides drugs meant to raise or lower its activity. It also clarifies how patient mutations in the enzyme cause disease.
plos-pone-0006504:
Anne-France Petit-Bertron and colleagues studied a histamine receptor in blood formation for PLOS ONE in 2009. The H4 histamine receptor is the most recently characterized of its family. It is expressed preferentially in the bone marrow. That pattern raises the question of its role during hematopoiesis, the making of blood cells.

The authors show that H4 receptors mediate cell cycle arrest in hematopoietic progenitor cells. The effect appears in both murine and human progenitors grown with growth factors. A brake on progenitor division could help balance blood cell production. It also gives histamine, known for allergy, a role in the marrow.
plos-pone-0006604:
Mohammad Fallahi-Sichani and Jennifer Linderman modeled a large family of cell receptors in PLOS ONE in 2009. This family, the G-protein coupled receptors, is the largest set of receptors on cell surfaces. They switch on G-proteins when a signal molecule binds. Many of these receptors work in pairs, and many sit in lipid rafts, which are stiff patches of the cell membrane.

Their model shows how rafts shape receptor signals when the signal molecule changes pairing. Membrane layout can boost or damp a signal in a strong way. Many top drugs act on this receptor family. Knowing raft effects could help make those drugs work in a better and safer way.
plos-pone-0006704:
Brian E. Roe and colleagues linked a nicotine receptor gene to risk attitudes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuroscience had begun to explain why people differ in risk taking. Attention then turned to genetic contributions to those differences. The authors studied two single-letter variants in the CHRNA4 gene. That gene helps build a receptor that responds to nicotine.

Participants' risk attitudes were measured in financial and psychological terms. The team tested whether either variant tracked with those attitudes. A gene tied to both nicotine response and risk could help explain addiction patterns. It could also show how one pathway shapes everyday choices. The work joins behavior genetics with the economics of risk.
plos-pone-0006804:
Herbert Schulz and colleagues built a genomics database for mouse embryonic stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Embryonic stem cells renew themselves indefinitely. They can also become a wide variety of cell types. A consortium studied gene networks in these cells and their descendants. The project was called Functional Genomics in Embryonic Stem Cells.

Their resource is the FunGenES database. It gathers differentiation data for public research use. Users can trace how gene networks change as cells specialize. Shared data spares each laboratory from repeating the same profiling. The database supports the wider effort to direct stem cells toward useful cell types.
plos-pone-0006904:
Kinga Michno and her team gauged calcium in fly nerve cells that bear Alzheimer's-linked genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kin-born forms of brain loss teach much of what we know of such ills. Faults in the presenilin genes bring Alzheimer's on young. The fly cells bore sound or faulty presenilin. They were cells that speak with acetylcholine, a nerve signal.

Calcium sat too low in those cells. Bad calcium care is a theme that keeps surfacing in Alzheimer's work. A lack seen in so plain a model gives that theme more weight. The fly lets labs test fast what sets calcium right. Such a fix is one lead in the fight against the kin-born form of the disease.
plos-pone-0007004:
Lorenzo Masia, Maura Casadio, Giulio Sandini, and colleagues studied hand-eye adjustment in PLOS ONE in 2009. In tasks like tele-surgery, what the eyes see and what the hands do can be misaligned. Operators must compensate to keep the needed precision. The mental machinery behind that compensation was the team's focus.

Volunteers worked under rotating visual feedback that shifted over time. The researchers tracked how eye movements and hand movements adapted together. Dynamic rotations are harder than fixed ones, since the target keeps moving. The findings inform training and interface design for remote surgery and similar skilled tasks.
plos-pone-0007104:
Abhishek Jain and Lance Munn modelled white blood cell flow in tiny channels in PLOS ONE in 2009. New fabrication methods make PDMS devices that mimic real microvessels. In such vessels, leukocytes drift toward the walls, a behavior called margination. That drift is the first step in reaching injured or infected tissue.

Working with rectangular microchannels, the pair determined what controls margination. Channel shape and flow conditions both mattered. Knowing the rules helps design lab vessels that behave like real ones. It also informs devices meant to sort or capture blood cells.
plos-pone-0007204:
Anne-Claude Crémieux, Oana Dumitrescu, Gerard Lina, and colleagues studied a bacterial toxin in bone infection in 2009. Community-associated MRSA had spread widely in the United States by then. Severe infections, including bone infection called osteomyelitis, were rising even in healthy children.

The authors test Panton-Valentine leukocidin, a toxin made by some Staphylococcus aureus strains. They use a rabbit model of MRSA osteomyelitis. They report that the toxin makes the bone infection more severe. Their findings sharpen the ongoing debate about which bacterial factors drive the very worst community MRSA cases.
plos-pone-0007304:
Régine Audran, Floriana Lurati-Ruiz, Blaise Genton, and colleagues tested a synthetic malaria vaccine candidate in a phase I trial in 2009. Fully efficient vaccines against the early, pre-erythrocytic stage of malaria were still lacking. That stage occurs before the parasite reaches red blood cells and causes symptoms.

The candidate is a peptide from the parasite's circumsporozoite protein, called PfCS102. The authors ran a randomized controlled trial to find dose and adjuvant combinations. They evaluate safety, reactogenicity, and immune responses. Their PLOS ONE results guide whether this peptide approach deserves larger efficacy trials.
plos-pone-0007404:
Stephen J. Lycett used stone tools to trace ancient hominin dispersals in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Reconstructing dispersal patterns of extinct hominins is challenging but essential. Archaeological evidence in the form of stone tools can supplement the sparse fossil record, because tools survive far more often than bones in most ancient sites.

Acheulean handaxes spread widely across the Old World. Based on broad dating, their appearance marked major population movements. Lycett performs a phylogeographic analysis of handaxe data, treating tool variation like inherited traits. His approach tests whether handaxe patterns match proposed dispersal routes out of Africa.
plos-pone-0007504:
Isabelle-Anne Bisson, Kamran Safi, and Richard Holland published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how migration evolved in bats. More than thirty bat species migrate, some over long distances. Bird migration has been studied for decades, but bat migration drew little notice. The team looked at the largest bat family and traced migration on its family tree. They asked whether the habit arose once or many times.

The evidence points to repeated, separate origins of migration. Distinct branches of the family invented the traveling life on their own. Such repeat invention hints that the pressures favoring migration are strong and common. It also lets scientists compare branch by branch to find what triggers the habit. The study brings a neglected group into a classic question. Its answer favors many origins over a single one.
plos-pone-0007604:
Ikjin Kim and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the cell's protein quality control. Misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum are eliminated by a pathway called ER-associated degradation. Failure of that disposal underlies many diseases, including neurodegenerative ones. A protein called Usa1 helps the pathway tag targets with ubiquitin, the cell's disposal label. The team dissected how Usa1 does its helping.

Usa1 facilitates the tagging through two separate domains. Each domain contributes its own part to substrate ubiquitylation. A helper with two hands can hold the machinery and the target together. Understanding such helpers clarifies how the disposal system chooses its victims. That system protects every cell that makes secreted proteins. The study adds fine detail to a pathway whose breakdown is costly.
plos-pone-0007704:
Nadege Sarrazin and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns receptors for stress hormones in a brain area called the dentate gyrus. These glucocorticoid receptors switch genes on and off in brain cells. High hormone levels acting through them can shift behavior.

The team changed receptor activity in that one brain region in mice. The change altered which genes were switched on there. It also raised anxiety-related behavior in the animals. The results tie a single brain circuit to stress and anxiety, and point to a target for future treatments.
plos-pone-0007804:
George Han and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests tiny particles that release nitric oxide against a stubborn germ. Staphylococcus aureus is a leading cause of skin abscesses and other infections. Nitric oxide is part of the body's natural defense against it.

Using the gas as a drug had been limited by delivery problems. The team packed it into nanoparticles that let it out slowly. In a mouse model, the particles treated abscesses caused by the germ. A topical particle therapy could add a weapon against drug-resistant staph infections.
plos-pone-0007904:
Luisa Cironi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains why one cancer-causing fusion protein works in some cells but not others. Nearly all synovial sarcomas carry a fusion gene, SYT-SSX1, born from a chromosome swap. The tumor is thought to start in primitive stem cells.

The authors tested human mesenchymal stem cells, a candidate cell of origin. Their epigenetic features decided whether the cells were permissive. Only in the right epigenetic state did SYT-SSX1 switch on its target genes. The work shows a cancer gene needs a receptive cell to act.
plos-pone-0008004:
Takayuki Manabe and colleagues cataloged where a DNA-bending protein likes to land in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, HMGA1a, shapes DNA to help switch genes on and off. It favors stretches rich in the letters A and T.

The team gathered candidate landing spots across the human genome. Each spot is a place where this shaping hand may do its work, from growth to immune defense. The catalog turns a vague sense of the protein's reach into a map that other teams can test gene by gene. Each entry on the list can now be checked in focused lab tests.
plos-pone-0008104:
Iris Alchanati and colleagues found the crew that clears a poisoned DNA enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some cancer drugs work by trapping topoisomerase enzymes on DNA, where they block and break the strand. The cell must clear those traps for the drug to kill cleanly.

A tagging enzyme pair, Bmi1 and Ring1A, marks the trapped Top2 alpha for the cell's shredder. Without the marks, the traps linger. The clearing path is a fresh drug target: blocking it might make standard cancer drugs bite harder at lower doses. The pair now joins the short list of known clearing crews.
plos-pone-0008204:
Till Geib and Klemens J. Hertel reported a gene therapy approach in PLOS ONE in 2009 for spinal muscular atrophy. The disease is inherited and destroys motor neurons, the cells that drive muscle. It stems from loss or faults of the SMN1 gene. A backup copy, SMN2, remains but makes only low levels of the needed protein.

The team used adenoviral vectors to deliver antisense pieces built into U7 small RNAs. These pieces push SMN2 to make full-length SMN protein. Raising protein from the backup gene could ease the disease. The work tests one route toward treatment for affected children.
plos-pone-0008304:
Francisca Gushiken and her team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about how blood clots form in mice. A clot starts when a part on the platelet surface, called an integrin, is switched on. Platelets are the small blood cells that seal cuts. Kinase and phosphatase proteins inside the platelet run the switch. One phosphatase part, PP1c gamma, was their main focus.

They tested how this part shapes the platelet response to thrombin. Thrombin is a strong clot signal found in blood. The switch must be firm but not too firm, or clots may block a vein. Their work shows, step by step, how one small part helps set that balance.
plos-pone-0008404:
Bridget A. Quinn and colleagues created a mouse model of ovarian cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. About one in ten epithelial ovarian cancers is inherited. Most inherited cases result from mutations in the BRCA1 gene. Mutations in p53 are also often found in these cancers. The team conditionally inactivated both genes in mouse ovaries.

Turning off Brca1 and p53 induced ovarian leiomyosarcomas in the mice. These are cancers of smooth muscle tissue in the ovary. A model that produces tumors on demand helps test treatments. It also shows how two famous cancer genes cooperate.
plos-pone-0008504:
Edward Cachay and co-authors study hidden infections in HIV-positive men in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Health guidance recommends screening for sexually transmitted infections in such men. The guidance rests on self-report of unprotected anal sex. But some men deny risk behavior when asked. The team ask if denial rules out silent anorectal infection. Silent cases show no symptoms yet can harm health and spread.

They test men regardless of what they reported. They estimate how valid self-report is for screening decisions. Denial does not exclude asymptomatic infection in their data. Screening rules based only on self-report would miss real cases.
plos-pone-0008604:
Anatasha Crawford and co-authors study drug resistance in breast cancer in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. BCL2 family members affect cell fate decisions in breast cancer. The role of BCL-W, also called BCL2L2, was unknown. Both BCL-W and BCL2 block apoptosis, the cell death program. Antiestrogen drugs such as fulvestrant treat hormone-sensitive breast cancers. The team test how these blockers affect response to that drug, using cell and tumor models.

Co-inhibition of BCL-W and BCL2 restores antiestrogen sensitivity. It does so through BECN1, a gene that drives autophagy. The treated cells die by an autophagy-associated necrosis. Blocking both survival proteins may rescue failing hormone therapy.
plos-pone-0008704:
Mutsuki Amano, Yuta Tsumura, Kentaro Taki, and colleagues built a dragnet for kinase targets. Their methods study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Kinases are enzymes that tag other proteins with phosphate groups. Each tag can switch a protein on or off. Mapping which proteins a kinase tags reveals whole signaling routes. Such mapping is slow when done one protein at a time.

Their protein-chip approach screens many candidate proteins in parallel. They tested it on Rho-kinase, a kinase that shapes cell movement and tension. The screen caught known targets and flagged new ones. Other kinase studies can borrow the same broad net.
plos-pone-0008804:
Sharon Perry, Bouke de Jong, Jay Solnick, and colleagues reported a surprising shield against tuberculosis. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach for life, usually without symptoms. It reshapes stomach immunity in lasting ways. Such reshaping might spill over to other infections. Tuberculosis, a slow lung germ, was the test case.

People carrying H. pylori showed signs of protection against tuberculosis. The stomach germ may keep certain defenses on alert. A usually unwelcome resident could thus do quiet good. The finding complicates plans to wipe out H. pylori everywhere.
plos-pone-0008904:
Stuart Meier, Oziniel Ruzvidzo, Monique Morse, and colleagues gave a plant defense gene a second job as a signal maker. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plants link outside warnings to responses using messenger chemicals. One messenger, cGMP, serves in many plant processes. The Arabidopsis gene WAKL10 sits in the cell wall's sensing system. Its activity rose alongside known pathogen defense genes, hinting at an immune role.

Tests showed the WAKL10 protein truly makes cGMP, acting as a guanylyl cyclase. A wall sensor that also brews a messenger tightens the alarm chain. Plant immunity gains a new named link between attack and response.
plos-pone-0009004:
Michael Siegal and co-authors asked whether growing up with two languages sharpens children's social sense, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bilingual children are common worldwide, but their conversational skills were little studied. Understanding talk means catching irony, white lies, and what speakers really mean. The study involved children aged three to six.

The children were exposed to English, German, Italian, Japanese, or pairs of those languages. Bilingual children read the point of conversations better than one-language children. Juggling two tongues seems to train attention to a speaker's intent. The edge adds a social benefit to the known list for bilingual upbringing.
plos-pone-0009104:
Lina Shehadeh and co-authors proposed a blood marker that might expose Parkinson's disease early, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Roughly five million people around the world live with Parkinson's, a slow brain disease. Diagnosis still rests on a doctor reading symptoms and patterns of movement. No lab test could yet confirm the disease or catch it beforehand.

The team screened patients' blood for signs of heavy alternative splicing. One gene, SRRM2, stood out clearly in the blood samples from patients. SRRM2 itself helps run the cell's splicing machinery day to day. A blood flag like this could sharpen diagnosis and open detection before symptoms show.
plos-pone-0009204:
Loro Kujjo and colleagues published this fertility study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancer treatment often damages a woman's eggs, and current ways to save her fertility work poorly. The same loss happens with plain aging. The team looked for the switches that decide whether a damaged egg repairs itself or dies.

Working with mouse egg cells, they targeted two proteins, Bax and Rad51. Bax helps push damaged cells toward death, while Rad51 helps repair broken DNA. Adjusting those targets raised the survival of eggs after chemotherapy or aging. The result points toward treatments that could protect fertility instead of only trying to replace lost eggs.
plos-pone-0009304:
Hans-Christian Ingerslev and co-authors published this fish immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fibroblasts are the cells that build connective tissue and repair wounds. In mammals they also act as immune sentinels, sounding alarms when tissue is damaged. Almost nothing was known about that role in fish.

The team worked with a fibroblast cell line from rainbow trout skin. The cells responded to signals from germs and from damaged tissue alike. They switched on genes tied to immune defense. The result says fish fibroblasts are front-line watchers too, not just builders, which changes how fish immunity is pictured.
plos-pone-0009404:
Anna Torri and co-authors published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dendritic cells are the sentries that show invaders to the rest of the immune system. They can either raise the alarm or calm things down. What gene patterns mark each mood was the team's question.

They isolated RNA from dendritic cells treated with activating or inhibiting substances. Comparing the gene expression profiles revealed inflammatory signatures. Those signatures let researchers read a dendritic cell's state from its genes alone. Such readouts help vaccine and drug designers check whether a treatment wakes the sentries or quiets them.
plos-pone-0009504:
John Mengshol and co-authors studied hepatitis C and liver immune cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. About two hundred million people carry this virus. Most of them stay infected for life, and the liver is slowly harmed. The team focused on galectin-9, a protein that binds sugars. Liver immune cells called Kupffer cells release it.

Galectin-9 from those cells shaped how T cells acted during infection. It could calm some responses and, in context, help the virus persist. The study names this protein as a key lever in the immune fight in the liver. Adjusting it might help patients clear the virus at last.
plos-pone-0009604:
Lasse Ramsgaard and colleagues studied a damage sensing receptor in a mouse model of silicosis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Silicosis scars the lungs of workers who breathe silica dust. No cure exists for the scarring. The receptor, called RAGE, senses signs of tissue damage and can feed inflammation. The team asked what role it plays as the disease develops in mice.

Comparing mice with and without the receptor showed how much of the harm runs through it. If the receptor drives part of the scarring, blocking it could slow the disease. The study tests that logic in a controlled model. It gives a basis for judging RAGE as a treatment target.
plos-pone-0009704:
Natural scenes have patterns, like the way brightness fades across fine detail. Satohiro Tajima and Masato Okada asked how groups of brain cells encode those patterns. Their study of neuronal population codes appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

A population code spreads information across many neurons at once, not just one cell. The authors tested how well such codes can tell natural image statistics apart. Work like this links vision science with information theory. It helps explain how the visual system reads the scenes animals meet every day. Their approach treats vision as a coding problem.
plos-pone-0009904:
A damselfly's sperm quality can shift before and after mating, and many forces act on it. Kaori Tsuchiya and Fumio Hayashi measured those forces in calopterygid damselflies. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Calopterygids are the broad-winged damselflies often seen over streams.

Sperm quality decides how well males fertilize eggs after mating. The authors tested which factors move quality up or down around the mating event. Damselflies are a favorite for studying mating behavior and sperm competition. The results add detail to how insects manage reproduction. Mating itself can change what a male passes on.
plos-pone-0010004:
Bhaskar Das, Kellie McCartin, Ting-Chun Liu, and co-workers described a chemistry and embryo screen in PLOS ONE in 2010. Retinoids, a family of compounds related to vitamin A, guide key steps in early development. They also hold promise for therapy that pushes cells to mature in a controlled way.

The team made new retinoid compounds and tested them in zebrafish embryos, a common model for early growth. One retinoic acid derivative stood out for acting on a specific receptor rather than broadly. A selective compound like that could give researchers a sharper tool and, in time, a safer starting point for drugs.
plos-pone-0010104:
The authors were Lise Goltermann, Marie Larsen, Rajat Banerjee, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper tried a bold protein engineering trick. Changing every copy of one amino acid in a protein can reveal new biology. It can also create proteins with useful new properties, though misfolding is a real risk.

The team went further, removing an amino acid and its codons from use. Targeted libraries usually cover only a few amino acids, for practical reasons. Widening that reach could open new designs for enzymes and other engineered proteins. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010204:
Jacques Rizkallah and Don Sin proposed a fairer way to judge medical journals in 2010. Journals are often ranked by impact factor, a count of how often their papers get cited. Many doctors and scientists dislike that tool, since it has deep limits as a mark of quality. Their PLOS ONE paper sought an approach that combines several scores at once.

They added Eigenfactor and Article Influence scores to the mix. Each score captures a different side of a journal's reach and prestige. Combining them, they argue, gives a more balanced picture than any single number used alone.
plos-pone-0010304:
The authors were Tom Cattaert, Víctor Urrea, Adam Naj, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper presented a statistics tool for family gene studies. Epistasis, where genes interact to shape a trait, is hard to detect in related people. Their method, FAM-MDR, adapts a dimensionality reduction technique for use in small or extended family pedigrees, rather than unrelated samples.

It combines ideas from two earlier approaches to handle family structure. Flexible tools like this let researchers hunt gene interactions in the family data they already have. Gene interactions matter in many common diseases that single-gene scans explain poorly.
plos-pone-0010404:
Elsa Isingrini and colleagues built a mouse model of depression that resists standard drugs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Depression is common and often disabling, and many patients do not respond to treatment. Research suffers for lack of an animal model of that resistance. The team combined two pressures in mice: repeated mild stress that cannot be predicted, and a high-fat diet. They then tested a standard antidepressant, fluoxetine.

Mice under both pressures responded poorly to the drug. That pairing may mimic patients whose depression comes with metabolic problems. A workable resistance model lets labs screen new treatments that might succeed where old ones fail. It also invites study of how diet and stress interact in the brain. The model is the product here, ready for others to use.
plos-pone-0010504:
Malcolm Leissring and colleagues designed blockers of the enzyme that breaks down insulin in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin controls blood sugar, and its loss of control causes diabetes. The body clears insulin mainly by cutting it up with an enzyme called IDE. Blocking that enzyme should, in principle, let insulin act longer. The team designed inhibitors from scratch to fit the enzyme.

Their designed blockers did regulate insulin breakdown and activity in tests. A drug that boosts the body's own insulin could complement existing diabetes care. Design-first approaches show how far structural knowledge has come. The study also warns that IDE handles other proteins, so care is needed. Still, it proves a long-theorized strategy can work in practice.
plos-pone-0010604:
Marko Roblek and colleagues built precision tools for studying diseased lamin proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lamins form a mesh that supports the cell nucleus. Single-letter changes in lamin A can cause muscle and fat diseases that shorten life.

The team made antibodies that bind only the changed forms, named R453W and R482W. Normal lamin did not attract these antibodies. The tools let researchers spot the faulty protein inside real cells, mixed among healthy copies. Tracking the mutant alone should clarify how one small change damages whole tissues over time.
plos-pone-0010704:
Cecilia Seixas and colleagues tested parts of the cell's folding machine in a pond microbe, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tetrahymena swims and feeds using cilia, tiny beating hairs. Building cilia takes tubulin, a protein that must be folded by a machine called CCT, built from eight different subunits.

Knocking down the CCT alpha or delta subunits crippled cilia growth and upkeep. Cells swam poorly and showed faulty internal structure. Both subunits proved essential, not spare parts. The result ties general protein folding to one clear job, and it gives cilia researchers a clean system for testing folding drugs.
plos-pone-0010804:
Geoffrey Hall and colleagues scanned the brains of adults with autism viewing faint faces, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The amygdala, a small brain hub for emotion, works differently in autism according to many models. Debate remained over whether the difference means weaker or stronger response. Faces shown too briefly to notice offer a clean test of the first, automatic response.

Anxious faces flashed below awareness still engaged the amygdala in autistic adults. The pattern of engagement differed from that of non-autistic adults. Early results of this kind are preliminary by design. They suggest the social brain reacts differently from the very first instant, before thought can intervene.
plos-pone-0010904:
Francis Concepcion and Jeannie Chen published this eye study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rhodopsin is the light-sensing protein of rod cells in the retina. A human mutation called Q344ter cuts off its tail. That removes the signal that guides it to the right address inside the cell. People with this change slowly lose their vision.

The authors built mice carrying the faulty protein and bred them with mice lacking normal rhodopsin. Dark-raised mutant mice still lost retinal cells, proving that the misplaced protein itself kills photoreceptors. Light made the damage worse, and the stray protein stayed chemically active, switching on signaling partners in the wrong place. Concepcion and Chen show a case where a lost address label turns a working protein toxic, informing research on inherited blindness.
plos-pone-0011004:
Yaqin Xu, Anja Krause, Hiroko Hamai and co-authors published this cystic fibrosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The inflamed airways of cystic fibrosis were usually blamed on the defective CFTR channel in airway lining cells. Alveolar macrophages, the lung's resident immune cleaners, also carry CFTR, and the authors asked what happens to them when the channel is silenced.

Turning CFTR down in human macrophages by a hundredfold unleashed an inflammatory phenotype: more IL-8, a potent cell-summoning signal, driven by activation of its master switch, plus more cell death. A membrane protein called caveolin-1 also rose and was investigated as part of the mechanism. Xu and colleagues show the CF lung's inflammation is not only an epithelial problem. Faulty macrophages may fan the very inflammation that destroys CF lungs.
plos-pone-0011104:
Heinisch, Dupres, Wilk and colleagues used a fine imaging tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. With a microscope that can feel single molecules, they looked at a sensor protein in the outer wall of yeast cells. The sensor, called Wsc1, helps yeast detect stress on its surface.

The images showed the sensors gathered in clusters rather than spreading out evenly. Clustering may help the cell sense weak signals and respond as a group. The work shows how surface order shapes cell signaling in a simple organism. Such basic insight often carries over to more complex cells, including human ones.
plos-pone-0011204:
Tsai, Garcia-Gil, Van Haeften and colleagues studied pig sperm in PLOS ONE in 2010. Before a sperm can fertilize an egg, a cap like structure on its head must dock firmly against its outer membrane. The team examined that docking step as sperm become ready inside the female tract.

They showed the docking is stable, holding the cap in place until the right moment. That step is a key part of fertilization that had been hard to pin down. Knowing it informs animal breeding, where sperm quality decides success. It also marks a step that future contraceptive methods could target.
plos-pone-0011304:
Porter, Kelley, George and colleagues found an HIV assembly twist in PLOS ONE in 2010. A protein that normally boosts immune gene reading also interacts with HIV's main building protein. The team tested how this regulator affects the processing of that viral protein inside the cell's main compartment.

The regulator enhanced the cutting and handling of the virus building protein. That moonlighting role could change how much virus a cell produces. It gives HIV research a new host factor to consider as a drug target. Host factors interest drug makers because the virus cannot easily mutate them away.
plos-pone-0011404:
Tokuhiro Chano and colleagues showed in 2010 that a protein called RB1CC1 can switch a key growth brake back on in human cancer cells. The RB1 pathway normally stops cells from dividing without control, and cancers often disable it. Rather than adding a foreign drug, the team raised the level of this built-in activator.

With more RB1CC1, cancer cells grew more slowly and formed far fewer colonies, the lab sign of a tumor's power to spread from single cells. Reactivating a brake the cell already owns is an appealing strategy, since it works with normal control systems. The result names RB1CC1 as both a marker and a possible lever in cancer. Tumors that have lost it may be the ones most in need of drugs that restore the same braking effect.
plos-pone-0011504:
Federico Calboli and co-authors ran a genome-wide association study in 2010 hunting genes behind neuroticism. The trait, a tendency toward worry and emotional volatility, runs in families and predicts anxiety and depression, yet its genetic roots had stayed elusive. The team scanned DNA variants across the genome in a population-based sample and tested each for a link to the trait.

A genome-wide scan is a disciplined kind of hunt: it makes no guesses about which genes matter and corrects strictly for the huge number of tests. Whatever survives that discipline is a lead the field can trust and follow. Personality genetics needs such hard data, since candidate-gene stories in psychology have often failed to replicate. The study adds a firm, population-level footing to one of psychology's most studied traits.
plos-pone-0011604:
Kai Tang and colleagues rebuilt the family tree of Roseobacter bacteria from whole genomes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Roseobacters live in ocean surface waters worldwide and can make up a large share of all bacteria there. They help drive the ocean's chemical cycles, moving carbon and other elements through sea life.

With many new genome sequences in hand, the team compared them to chart how this group diversified. Their tree shows lineages spreading into varied roles across coastal and open waters. Understanding that split helps scientists predict how these abundant microbes respond as oceans warm and change.
plos-pone-0011704:
Bradley Schneider and co-authors looked at how mosquito spit shapes West Nile virus infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus enters the body during a mosquito bite, so the first host cells it meets sit in the skin, then in the nearest lymph node. Two cell types, macrophages and dendritic cells, are key early responders in the defence against this virus.

The team found that spit from Aedes aegypti changes how white blood cells are called in, and how the presenting cells send signals, once infection starts. In short, the bite itself tilts the early fight. Tests of vaccines that skip the spit may miss part of the real story.
plos-pone-0011804:
Juan Rodriguez-Paris and co-authors judged a screening chip for inherited hearing loss, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Testing a child born with hearing loss most often starts with one gene, GJB2. If the cause is not found there, more genes are checked one by one, which is slow and costly, since so many gene faults can play a part.

The team weighed an array that tests close to two hundred known faults at once, for its worth in real clinics. For clinics, the study answers a plain question: should this chip join routine testing or not? A sound panel could cut short the long hunt that deaf children and their families face.
plos-pone-0011904:
Jun Liu and co-authors traced in 2010 the evolution of tetherin, a primate protein that traps newly made viruses at the cell surface. Tetherin blocks HIV-1 particles from being released unless the virus's Vpu protein counters it. Similar host defenders, such as APOBEC3G and TRIM5a, carry signs of long arms races with viruses.

Comparing tetherin across primates shows how its sequence changed under that pressure. Fast change in the parts viruses touch is a signature of repeated attack and defense over millions of years. Reading that history in primates, our close relatives, helps explain why some animal viruses jump to humans more easily than others.
plos-pone-0012004:
Eric Weaver published in 2010 a detailed family tree of the cat AIDS virus across the United States. Feline immunodeficiency virus causes AIDS-like illness in cats and serves as a working model for HIV. Like HIV, it keeps diverging as it spreads, so isolates differ more with time and distance.

A detailed phylogenetic analysis sorts those isolates into their true relationships, showing how the virus entered and diversified within the country. Such trees guide the choice of strains for vaccine and diagnostic work, since a test built on one branch may miss another. They also give veterinarians a map of what is actually circulating in American cats.
plos-pone-0012104:
Daudi Simba, Marian Warsame, Deodatus Kakoko, and colleagues reported a community study from rural Tanzania in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria can be cured with modern combination drugs, but only when sick children get them fast. Tanzania had adopted those drugs as standard care, yet cost and supply problems kept them out of reach for many families in the countryside.

The team followed children in the Kilosa area to see who actually got the new treatment quickly, and who did not. Work like this shows the gap between a policy on paper and medicine in a child's hands. It points health programs at the real barriers, such as price, distance, and stock, that decide whether a cure arrives in time.
plos-pone-0012204:
Eleonora Dehlink, Alexandra Baker, Elizabeth Yen, and co-authors measured allergy antibody in children's blood for PLOS ONE in 2010. IgE, the antibody behind immediate allergic reactions, is usually measured free in the blood serum, and high levels flag allergy. But much of the body's IgE sits bound to receptors on cell surfaces, invisible to the standard test, so serum levels may not tell the whole story.

The team measured serum IgE, cell-bound IgE, and the receptors themselves in children, and mapped how the three relate. If bound IgE follows different rules, allergy testing may be missing part of the signal. A fuller picture could refine diagnosis in children whose symptoms and serum tests disagree.
plos-pone-0012304:
Iskandar Abdullaev, Alena Rudkouskaya, and Alexander Mongin tested ion channels in glioma brain tumors, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gliomas are among the most treatment-resistant cancers, and some evidence blamed two potassium channels, opened by calcium, for helping tumor cells multiply so relentlessly. Other studies disagreed, leaving the channels' guilt in doubt.

The team confirmed both channels do work in human glioma cells, yet blocking them did not govern the cells' proliferation. That negative result saves the field from chasing the wrong lever for growth, while leaving open other roles, such as movement, for the channels. In a cancer this desperate for targets, ruling one out cleanly is real progress.
plos-pone-0012404:
Meredith Shaffer, Yanping Huang, Evann Corbo and colleagues asked whether a plentiful T cell protein is truly needed, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ezrin links cargo to the cell's inner skeleton and is packed into young thymus cells that mature into T cells. Its abundance suggested a key job in T cell development, but presence alone does not prove need.

Mice lacking ezrin still built T cells normally, the team found. Backup proteins likely cover its absence in this setting. The negative result is valuable: it stops labs from chasing a dead end and redirects attention to the settings, such as cell movement, where ezrin may truly be required.
plos-pone-0012504:
Marika Olcott, Marcella Henkels, Kise Rosen and colleagues fed fruit fly larvae selected strains of a common soil bacterium, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Pseudomonas fluorescens strains live around plant roots and some are sold to protect crops. The fruit fly is a standard stand-in for probing how microbes affect animal bodies, and larvae offer a fast, sensitive test.

Some strains killed larvae or delayed their development, while others were far gentler. Strain-level differences mean a species name alone cannot vouch for safety. The fly assay gives regulators and growers a quick screen before bacterial products are spread widely on food crops.
plos-pone-0012604:
Wilkinson, Solan, Taylor and co-authors asked whether variety within one species matters for an ecosystem. Most biodiversity research counts species, not the genetic variety inside each one. Their 2010 study used fungi, which break down dead matter and release carbon as they grow.

They varied how much genetic diversity the fungi carried and then measured growth and breathing rate. Diversity inside the species changed both, so a single-species view can miss real effects. The lesson reaches beyond fungi, since microbes drive soil and carbon cycles everywhere. Protecting variety within species may matter as much as protecting species counts.
plos-pone-0012704:
Sun, Errami, Long and co-authors measured how alike full-text biomedical papers can be, beyond simple copying checks. Software had been used to find duplicate papers in the MEDLINE index, mostly from titles and summaries. Their 2010 study worked with complete articles, which are now widely available online.

They characterised text similarity across whole papers in a systematic way. Strong overlap can flag plagiarism, honest reuse of methods text, or duplicate publication, and the three need telling apart. Better measures help journals and indexers police the literature without false alarms.
plos-pone-0012804:
Zhao, Ayoub and Hayashi located the silk genes of widow spiders on their chromosomes. Spider dragline silk is famed for being both strong and tough for its weight. It is made of two proteins, MaSp1 and MaSp2, spun into the frame lines of webs and the spider's safety line.

Their 2010 mapping placed the genes for these proteins in the widow spider genome. Gene position helps explain how the pair is switched on together during spinning. The work supports efforts to copy spider silk for medical and engineering uses.  The mapping used labelled DNA probes on spread chromosomes.
plos-pone-0335304:
Kumlachew Geta and co-authors measured how often patients at an Ethiopian referral hospital needed a second abdominal operation after gut surgery, and what raised the odds. Reopening the abdomen carries real risks of harm and death, and it strains hospital budgets and staff. Their 2026 review examined more than twelve hundred patient charts from gastrointestinal procedures performed over two years.

One in ten patients underwent the second operation, a rate above several earlier reports. Prior abdominal surgery stood out as by far the strongest predictor, followed by finding starved, dying bowel during the first operation and needing circulation-supporting drugs during surgery. The authors say flagging these high-risk patients early could focus monitoring and resources where repeat surgery is most likely.
plos-pone-0340004:
Eihab Fathelrahman and his team ran a mock bird flu strike on the UAE. They fed facts from forty-six bird farms into a spread model tuned for the land. Then they played four paths. One had no steps at all. The rest used moves curbs, mass shots, or culls of sick farms.

Culls closed the mock strike in sixteen days. That was the shortest run and the least harm of all paths. No steps let it run for twenty-six days. Move curbs oddly stretched it most, to thirty-two days. The team says the dry run lets chiefs weigh cost and gain while calm holds.
plos-pone-0341404:
Anne Schlutt and co-workers build a kinder way to give lab mice repeated injections and blood draws. Handling stress burdens mice and can distort research, and tail handling frightens them most. Their 2026 study designs a short medical training course plus a small tunnel that holds the mouse gently during procedures, tested in a liver cancer model needing many weeks of injections.

Trained mice approached handlers sooner within a few sessions, and the change lasted the whole experiment. Tunnel-treated mice stayed more active after injections and bounced back to normal behavior faster than firmly held ones. Body temperature tracked room conditions more than training. Gentler routines promise better welfare and cleaner data for long studies.
plos-pone-0341704:
Michael Jones, Richard Dawson, and Jon Mills offer a new way to build fake populations in 2026. Such populations stand in for real people in models of transport, health, and disasters. Real survey microdata is scarce and locked away for privacy. Their method needs none of it.

A large language model invents one household at a time. After each step, the fake population is checked against published totals. Gaps guide the next prompts, so the result drifts toward the targets. No retraining is needed. Tested in many countries, the method matched basic totals closely. It could open population modelling to teams with no access to census files.
plos-pone-0342004:
Mohammed Hlayel and co-workers build a fast bridge between factory controllers and their cloud-based digital twins. A digital twin mirrors a real machine so engineers can test changes safely, but the link must answer within a strict timing standard. Their 2026 study connects a common brand of factory controller to cloud software through a live two-way web channel.

The bridge answered in well under the standard's limit on average. It beat three rival connection methods by wide margins on round-trip time. It also held its speed with many users at once in simulated loads. Factories moving toward more human-centered, resilient production could use such links to watch and steer machines from afar.
plos-pone-0344604:
Waqar Rauf Butt and co-workers turn an ordinary smartphone into a pothole measuring tool. Councils struggle to survey road damage because pro gear is costly and manual checks are slow. Their 2026 study pairs phone photos with the depth sensor built into newer phones, guided by a deep learning pipeline that outlines each pothole and refines its depth.

Training used twenty-five thousand photo and depth pairs gathered under mixed road and light conditions. The system beat existing methods on both depth accuracy and outline quality. Cleaner edges after extra processing helped too. A phone in a vehicle could feed cities a live damage map, letting repair crews start with the deepest, riskiest holes.
plos-pone-0346704:
Erika Z Chung, Belinda Curpen, and co-authors asked whether ultrasound measurements taken during the first weeks of chemotherapy can forecast how a breast tumor will finally respond. Chemotherapy before surgery is standard for several breast cancer types, but success is only confirmed afterward, too late to spare non-responders needless toxicity. Their 2026 study followed one hundred six patients with ultrasound at six points across treatment.

Patients whose tumors vanished completely showed steep shrinkage in width, area, and volume within the early weeks. Partial responders shrank steadily but less, weak responders barely moved, and non-responders stayed flat throughout. Statistical tests confirmed the early gap between complete responders and the rest. The authors conclude early size change carries real, if imperfect, predictive value for final response.
plos-pone-0347004:
Edna Judith Márquez leads a team of four uncovering hidden species inside a common Colombian river fish, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The fish, an Astyanax tetra from the Magdalena basin, has long been filed under one uncertain name. The stakes are practical: the Ituango dam now cuts the Cauca River, and conservation cannot protect what taxonomy cannot see. The team characterized seventeen genetic markers and sampled across the river's middle and lower reaches.

Genetics split the fish into two groups, and family tree analyses of two further genes backed the split as distinct lineages. Unexpectedly, one lineage clustered with relatives from the Maracaibo basin, not with its river mates. Body shape analysis agreed that the groups differ. Both carried genetic diversity alongside signs of recent population crashes and inbreeding. A fish treated as one widespread species is at least two, and each half needs its own protection plan.
plos-pone-0348204:
Waleed Kattan maps where Saudi Arabia's dentists actually work in this 2026 PLOS ONE health policy analysis, using the health ministry's 2023 yearbook across twenty health regions. He compares public against private practice and Saudi against foreign dentists, asking whether the spread matches the goals of the country's Vision 2030 reforms.

The workforce grew to nearly eight dentists per ten thousand people, yet the map is lopsided: small regions such as Al-Bahah are dentist-rich while crowded Makkah has barely half that density. Private practice employs about seventy percent of dentists and clusters in cities, showing the deepest regional inequality. The analysis gives planners hard numbers for steering dentists toward underserved regions.
plos-pone-0348404:
Akihiro Ito and co-workers check whether a planned trial comparing two oxygen levels during lung rehabilitation for chronic lung disease can actually be run. Extra oxygen during exercise training should help breathless patients train harder, but the better dose is unknown. Their 2026 pilot runs six patients through both programs in random order, blinded, using a high-flow nose tube.

The walk test could not anchor a sample size for the main trial. One program improved symptom scores more, while the stronger oxygen program built more muscle. Effect sizes now let the team size a full trial around symptom and muscle outcomes. Pilot work like this prevents a large, expensive trial from being built on the wrong yardstick.
plos-pone-0348504:
Haruka Nagaya and colleagues linked blood vitamin C levels with brain scans in just over two thousand older adults. Vitamin C in food has been tied to lower risk of thinking decline, yet direct links to brain structure were unclear. Scans measured grey and white matter volumes and the strength of a key resting brain network, with many health and habit factors counted.

Low vitamin C in blood went with a lower share of grey matter and weaker network links, even after age, schooling, illness, smoking, drinking, and activity were taken into account. A snapshot cannot prove that vitamin C protects the brain. Still, the tight link in a large group makes diet and brain ageing worth closer, longer study.
plos-pone-0348604:
Subeen Kim and co-workers look for frailty risk factors among older Koreans, separately for women and men. Frailty, a state of weakness that invites falls and illness, grows common with age. Their 2026 study draws on six years of national health survey data covering more than six thousand five hundred adults aged sixty-five and over, scored by a standard frailty checklist.

About one in five women was frail, against roughly one in nine men. Smoking and even sharing morning meals with family linked with higher frailty in women, a pattern the authors flag for care. For men, higher income and eating more were protective. Many chronic diseases and poor self-rated health raised risk in both sexes. Prevention, they argue, should be shaped by gender.
plos-pone-0348804:
Peter Persoon asks a quiet question with big consequences: does progress speed up when existing knowledge gets re-sorted into new categories? Ideas are not only created, he notes, but also reinterpreted, and patent offices record that reinterpretation whenever they move a patent into a different class. Using patent records as a stand-in for technical knowledge, he documents two patterns and builds an exact maths model around them.

Newer patents are reclassified more often, and bigger classes absorb a larger share of reclassified patents. The model's further predictions held across all major technology areas, pointing to a strong link between re-sorting and the pace of change. Persoon argues that the shape of technical growth can be explained from inside the knowledge system itself, not only by outside economic forces.
plos-pone-0349104:
Hagos T. Atalay, Victoria J. Kain, and Amanda G. Carter gauge how ready health workers in northern Ethiopia feel to support kangaroo care at home. Kangaroo care keeps small babies warm against a parent's chest and saves lives where incubators are scarce. Their 2026 study surveys close to six hundred professionals and also builds a questionnaire to measure readiness itself.

The new questionnaire held together well in testing. Readiness itself was shaky: few workers had read the national guideline, and most had never been trained in the method. More than half said their workplaces lacked support for it. Workers with past hands-on experience felt more positive. Training and backing, the authors argue, must come before home programs can spread.
plos-pone-0349204:
Cathy Yang and colleagues tested an unusual nerve repair in rats: gluing severed nerve fibers back together with a plastic-like compound called PEG. When a chunk of the sciatic nerve is lost, standard graft repairs regrow slowly and recovery is usually poor. Using grafts from genetically identical rats, the team compared the fusion treatment with ordinary grafting on gaps of two sizes.

The compound seals the cut membranes of nerve fibers almost instantly, which in principle preserves the fibers instead of letting them die back and regrow at a millimeter or two per day. Structure and walking behavior were then tracked to judge recovery. If fusion works reliably, it could change how surgeons treat the worst peripheral nerve injuries.
plos-pone-0349304:
Charlotte Jane Whiffin and a large team explored whether storytelling, guided by an approach called Life Threads, can help families after a relative suffers a traumatic brain injury. Such injuries change family life deeply, yet relatives get little support for their own grief and shock. Twenty family members joined group sessions, used threads and objects to lay out their stories over four weeks, and then spoke at length about the experience.

Most participants said the method let them tell their story in ways ordinary conversation had not, and many reported real benefits, from making sense of events to feeling heard. Success depended on a safe, well-held setting. The authors see promise in the approach and frame this early study as groundwork for larger trials.
plos-pone-0349404:
Ihssan S Masad and colleagues tested a jelly-like radiation detector designed to check that cancer radiotherapy delivers dose exactly where the plan says. Their hydrogel changes its magnetic properties where radiation lands, so an MRI scan can read the delivered dose in three dimensions. Gels were scanned, irradiated by a robotic radiotherapy system, then scanned again and compared against the treatment computer's calculations.

The gel's dose maps matched the plan closely, especially in the high-dose zone that matters most. A standard agreement test passed more than nine in ten points at every dose level and viewing plane checked. The authors conclude the new gel is a reliable tool for verifying complex treatments before or alongside patient care. A small targeting error there can mean a missed tumour or a burned organ.
plos-pone-0349504:
Qianqian Sun and colleagues checked a World Health Organization rehabilitation scoring set on more than a thousand Chinese cancer patients in 2026. No full scale existed for judging how such patients function during rehabilitation, so a trusted measure had to be proven locally.

Trained staff scored patients, and a smaller group was scored again for consistency checks. Scores held together well, matched other trusted measures of mood, daily living, and general condition, and separated patients sensibly. Factor checks supported the scale's structure. A validated common yardstick lets rehabilitation teams across China compare progress and plan care on shared terms.
plos-pone-0349604:
Maura De Coster, Lisette M Kootker, and co-authors read diet history from cremated bones at Nijmegen in the Netherlands, a Roman frontier town where local Batavian life met imperial supply networks. Strontium in bone reflects the geology behind a person's food, and its concentration can hint at salt-rich diets. Their 2026 study compared rural, urban, and military burials from before and during Roman rule.

Urban and military remains carried higher strontium concentrations, consistent with heavier use of salt-preserved foods from Roman provisioning. Northern rural contexts instead showed steady concentrations and narrowing isotope ranges, suggesting local food traditions, possibly including earlier salt habits, persisted. The authors argue dietary change under Rome was patchy and negotiated, not a simple swap of local for imperial food.
plos-pone-0349804:
Eric M Mortensen, Nkiruka Atuegwu, and Shane J Sacco tested whether fancy learning models beat plain regression at predicting return to hospital within thirty days after pneumonia. Records covered just over twenty seven hundred adults at one academic centre from 2018 to 2024, with full vital sign values kept as continuous inputs rather than cut into bands.

About ten percent returned within thirty days. Gradient boosting and neural nets scored about the same as plain regression on both accuracy scales. Drug abuse history and a kidney lab value emerged as underused predictors. Extra model complexity bought nothing here; better data and follow up design may matter more than smarter maths.
plos-pone-0350004:
Alexandra Gaal Kovalcikova and colleagues tested whether white cell nets drive kidney damage in a mouse model of chronic kidney disease. Nets are webs of DNA that immune cells cast out, suspected of harming tissue. Mice lacking the enzyme that enables net making were compared with normal mice, both dosed with a kidney harming chemical for two weeks.

Chemical dosing shrank body weight and worsened kidney markers sharply in normal mice. Knockout mice fared no better, and even showed an earlier rise in one kidney marker. Immune cells were clearly activated, yet net making itself did not drive damage in this model. Kidney researchers should look elsewhere for this models main harm path.
plos-pone-0350204:
Allison K White, Md Saydur Rahman, and Richard J Kline measured fish at a human-made reef off the Texas coast in 2026. The reef, built from recycled and shaped materials, covers a large area and draws fish, but its value needed numbers.

Using a sonar that splits its beam to size echoes, the team estimated fish weight at sites of different heights and worked out how much carbon those fish hold. Fish were far more plentiful than over bare sandy bottom. Counts like these help judge whether built reefs truly support fisheries, and whether the fish they hold store a meaningful share of carbon.
plos-pone-0350804:
Yongping Yu and fellow researchers in China tackled a practical fire safety problem in 2026: which factors matter most when a building catches fire. Many things can start or spread a blaze, and naming the few that drive the rest helps prevention work.

The team turned past fire cases into a network, where each factor was a node and links showed factors that appeared together. Their new method weighed a node's place in the core, its reach, and how hard it would be to replace. That ranking points safety teams toward the controls likely to cut risk most, rather than spreading effort thinly over every possible cause.
plos-pone-0351304:
Quick HIV viral load testing near the clinic, rather than at a distant central lab, returns results faster for children and young people. Perry Msoka and colleagues watched clinics and interviewed health workers in Tanzania to find where the near-site system jams, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

The work formed part of a four-country East African trial testing young people at three points across a year. Observations from 2023 into 2024 captured daily friction: machine downtime, supply gaps, staffing, and result hand-offs among the suspects. Naming the bottlenecks matters because the technology's speed only helps if samples, staff, and results actually flow, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0351404:
Zebrafish larvae are favorite stand-ins for studying the human heart, but labs measure them at different ages and conditions. Patricia Fiorino and colleagues charted how the larval heart changes hour by hour, in this 2026 PLOS One study, and tested how temperature and water acidity sway the readings.

Heart rate, output, and the fraction of blood pumped were measured at eight ages from one to just over three days after fertilization. Heart rate climbed until about three days, then leveled. Output rose in two bursts, while the pumped fraction mostly held steady with one brief dip. Small temperature and acidity shifts moved the numbers, so the authors urge standard settings.
plos-pone-0351504:
How people bond in close relationships shapes who they feel they are, and Cui Lyu and colleagues mapped those links in six hundred twenty-four Chinese college students. Their 2026 PLOS One study drew the connections as a network rather than simple pairs, and compared men's and women's maps.

Identity questions clustered tightly together. A feeling that time and selfhood are coming apart formed the main bridge between attachment and identity, followed by a scattered sense of self. Anxious attachment was the strongest single bridge on the relationship side. Overall network structure did not differ by gender, though women's connections ran slightly stronger in total.
plos-pone-0351704:
Making heart muscle cells from stem cells in the lab is slow and the cells stay immature. Agatha Ribeiro Kalthof and colleagues found that switching off a gene called IRX3 speeds the process, in this 2026 PLOS One study using human induced stem cells.

Cells lacking the gene turned into heart cells in greater numbers and switched on mature heart genes more strongly. Their electrical behavior improved, energy factories spread more evenly, and the striped muscle fibers organized better. Early in the process, partner genes that drive heart development rose, and young heart cells multiplied faster. The finding may help labs grow better heart tissue for disease models and repair research.
plos-pone-0352204:
Adams and colleagues, in a 2026 study, turn North Carolina residents into partners in tick research. Tick-borne disease is rising in the state, yet local data are thin. Working with twenty-two county health agencies, the team handed out kits so people could send in ticks they found, along with notes on where and what they were doing.

Over two years, more than four hundred ticks arrived. Testing checked them for several bacterial germs, including the one that causes Lyme disease. Species matched earlier records, with one surprise: a lone star tick turned up in the cool mountains, the first published record there, hinting at a push into higher ground. Recreation, such as hiking and yard leisure, was the activity most tied to encounters. How counties advertised the program affected returns, though numbers were small. The authors offer the project as a model for cheap disease tracking.
plos-pone-0352504:
Cherry Kim and seven colleagues evaluate this 2026 PLOS One imaging study on spotting anemia from CT scans that patients are already having for other reasons. A dual-energy CT technique can estimate the electron density of blood, which should fall as red cell mass drops. The team analyzed more than twenty-five hundred scans, with and without contrast dye, comparing blood-pool measurements against laboratory blood counts.

Electron density fell steadily as anemia worsened and correlated strongly with hemoglobin on scans without contrast, where it detected anemia accurately. On contrast scans the link survived while the ordinary brightness measure used by radiologists showed none. The authors frame contrast-scan detection as opportunistic, useful mainly for catching severe anemia incidentally, and say the approach needs testing on other scanner brands.
plos-pone-0352604:
Hong Yang and seven co-authors present a 2026 mouse study of pachymic acid, a compound from a medicinal fungus. They test its effects on body clocks disturbed by obesity. A high-fat diet upsets daily rhythms as well as weight and blood sugar. The compound had never been tested for rhythm effects.

Mice given the compound gained less weight, handled glucose and fats better, and recovered steadier daily patterns of melatonin and body temperature. Gene activity in the liver also fell back into a normal daily cycle. The team traces the benefit to a fat-signalling pathway in the liver. It involves a receptor called S1PR4. That pathway could become a target for treating rhythm problems linked with obesity.
plos-pone-0352804:
Reza Sharifi and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One analysis of cleft lip and palate in Iran, drawn from the Global Burden of Disease study.
