These birth conditions affect feeding, speech, and appearance across a lifetime, and Iran lacked an up-to-date national picture. The authors estimated new cases, existing cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost for the whole country and all thirty-one provinces between 1990 and 2023.

Deaths and disability from clefts fell dramatically over those three decades, dropping by roughly nine-tenths, while the share of people living with the condition stayed broadly steady. Tehran showed the highest prevalence and Isfahan the lowest, and children under five carried the greatest burden. Provinces with stronger social development generally had lower disability rates, and the authors call for sustained early detection and specialist care.
plos-pone-0352904:
Tigist Alemu and four colleagues analyse maternal deaths in an Ethiopian intensive care unit. Their 2026 study covers a tertiary hospital in the country's south. It follows three hundred seventy-eight obstetric patients admitted to intensive care over ten years. The question is not only how many mothers died, but how fast, and what predicted it.

One hundred twenty-six of the women died. More than seven in ten deaths came within the first five days. Half of all deaths had occurred by roughly the third day. Living in a rural area raised the risk. So did shock, multi-organ failure, and needing a breathing machine. Impaired consciousness was the strongest warning sign of all. The message is stark: survival is decided in the first days, so rural referral speed and early resuscitation matter most.
plos-pone-0353204:
Cai compared artery-clearing treatment for two kinds of severe stroke in a 2026 study. One kind blocks an artery at the back of the brain and often causes deep disability or death. Both groups had scans that map blood flow to guide treatment, drawn from a shared international registry.

Patients with the back-brain blockage arrived with worse symptoms than the comparison group. After careful matching of similar patients, recovery and death rates at three months looked much the same in both groups. The back-brain group even had faster reopening and fewer bleeding problems. Scan-guided selection may help these patients gain the same benefit as others.
plos-pone-0353504:
Soltanabadi and colleagues, in a 2026 review, ask how far neck movement relates to pain and disability in people with neck pain. Clinicians often measure how far a patient can turn or tilt the neck, assuming tighter movement means worse symptoms. The team gathered every study that linked that movement measure to patient-reported pain or disability.

Forty-five studies, with about three and a half thousand patients in total, were combined in statistical summaries. Movement in every direction showed a modest link with symptoms: less movement went with somewhat more pain and disability. The link was stronger for fresh injuries and for whiplash from crashes than for long-lasting or non-injury pain. Study quality varied a lot, and the authors rate the overall certainty as very low. They call for standard ways to measure neck movement and stronger studies before clinics lean too hard on this measure.
plos-pone-0353704:
Manish Barik and co-authors track chewing tobacco trends in 2026. They used three national family health surveys from India. The surveys span about fifteen years. All women were aged fifteen to forty nine. Such products raise oral cancer risk and harm health in other ways, and India holds most of the world's users. Each survey round was analysed apart, with layered models searching for who uses these products.

Use fell steadily across the rounds, from a high single digit share to a lower one. A flavoured chew mix stayed the most common form, and one northeastern state kept by far the highest rate. Low schooling, older age, caste, region, and smoking inside the home all linked to use.
plos-pone-0354204:
Konstantinos Karagiorgos and co-authors simulate how river flooding breaks a city's road network, hunting for failure patterns that simple damage counts miss. Roads are a city's lifelines, and floods cut them in tangled ways. Their method blends classic network measures of how connected and central streets are. It adds community detection. Then it floods the network twice: under a rare flood, and under an extreme near-worst-case flood drawn from Swedish planning practice.

Damage grew in jumps, not smoothly. The network split into a few large islands plus hundreds of small cut-off fragments. Average travel burden more than doubled under the larger flood. The analysis also named isolated high-risk nodes and streets that could serve as evacuation corridors. Karagiorgos and colleagues offer the framework to any flood-prone city.
plos-pone-0354304:
Raed M Ennab, writing alone in PLOS ONE in 2026, runs a fair race between four heart disease classifiers on synthetic data. The dataset is a large competition file of six hundred thirty thousand artificial patients, not real ones, built for model comparison. All four algorithms, from logistic regression to three boosted tree systems, faced identical cross validation splits. Preprocessing stayed locked inside each training fold. Traps were set to catch information leaking from the answers.

The race ended nearly in a dead heat. The best tree system edged the field by a hair; logistic regression trailed by only a few thousandths on the headline discrimination score. Calibration was excellent across the board, and the leakage traps came back clean. Ennab's point is the frame itself: synthetic benchmarks can rank algorithms honestly, but their scores say nothing about performance on real clinic patients, a caveat vendors prefer to skip.
plos-pone-0354604:
Wei Gou leads a team of seven reading the full length message molecules of artery cells exposed to cigarette smoke, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Using long read sequencing on human aortic smooth muscle cells, they captured complete RNA transcripts rather than fragments, letting them see edited and spliced variants that short reads miss. A puzzle framed the work: weak smoke extract slightly boosted cell survival in their tests, while stronger doses killed in proportion.

At the mid strength dose they catalogued more than eleven thousand previously unknown transcripts. Activated messages clustered in cell division and in ferroptosis, an iron driven death pathway, while energy production and antioxidant defense messages fell. Hundreds of splicing changes touched cell cycle regulators. The authors argue that smoke's damage is executed through coordinated rewriting of the cell's message library, an isoform level view of how smoking injures blood vessels.
plos-pone-0354704:
Noura Alsufyani, Sawsan Alowa, Hend Alrasheed, and Sakher Alqahtani published this 2026 forensic study of estimating legal age from dental X-rays. Whether someone is under or over eighteen matters in court, and wisdom teeth are still developing at that age. Using nearly six hundred panoramic images of teenagers and young adults, they trained machine learning to segment the tooth and classify age.

Their best model judged the age line with high accuracy, edging past manual expert scoring on several measures. Alsufyani suggests pixel-level analysis catches subtle cues that human readers miss.
plos-pone-0354804:
Yan Mou, Zhaolong Gao, and Jinjiang Li present in 2026 a vision system for picking out the main object in underwater scenes. The task supports tracking, editing, and recognition, but water muddies colour and depth readings. Their network fuses colour and depth data through attention steps that inject and embed features across both channel and space views.

By modelling how the two data types complete each other at wide and narrow scales, the system sharpens standout regions and quiets background noise. Layered fusion also lessens depth errors. Tests on several underwater sets beat leading methods, the authors report, showing the value of careful fusion.
plos-pone-0354904:
Jaime Banks, Jonathan Stromer-Galley, Samiksha Singh, and Collin Capano published this 2026 paper introducing DiSCoKit, free open-source software for survey research with live chatbots. Studies of how people interact with large language models need participants to chat with a real model inside a survey, which survey platforms make awkward.

DiSCoKit plugs live model sessions into tools like Qualtrics, logs the conversations, and lets researchers steer the model's behavior for experiments. Banks and colleagues walk through the design, a sample deployment, and the toolkit's limits. Their goal is to give social scientists a safer, roomier way to study human and AI interaction.
plos-pone-0355104:
Isaac Ogloblin Ramirez and six colleagues reconstruct daily work at an ancient industrial site in Israel, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Tel Shiqmona held a vast Iron Age works for purple dye, unmatched in size around the Mediterranean, and the Kingdom of Israel ran it as a state asset. Scholars often picture such workshops as fixed spaces with one job, and the team tested that assumption on the eighth century BCE level.

Using microscope scale soil analysis and chemical spectroscopy, they found the same rooms served different trades at different times of year. Olive pressing fit late autumn, sheltering livestock fit winter, and textile work fit spring, with dye making slotted into the gaps. Ash was spread to freshen floors between seasons. The pattern points to careful, scheduled management of a valuable royal facility.
plos-pone-0355204:
Susana Carvalho and a large team recorded bearded capuchin monkeys in northeastern Brazil hunting and eating small vertebrates across forty-five months, the most extensive record of its kind for these monkeys. Their 2026 study of two neighboring groups weighed how provisioning by humans, sex, age, fruit and insect supplies, and weather shaped how often the monkeys caught mammals and lizards.

Vertebrate eating proved habitual, not desperate. Males and adults hunted most, brains and organs were eaten first, and predation rose when fruit ran short while dropping when humans provisioned the monkeys. The authors argue such small-prey habits may have been the stepping stone that led early human ancestors toward larger game, and suggest re-examining fossil bone collections for overlooked small prey.
plos-pone-0355304:
Tianfu Huang builds in 2026 a learning system to forecast when smart meter sensors on a Chinese island will drift out of accuracy. Salt fog, damp air, and heating and cooling cycles corrode the parts that measure power. Six years of field records from hundreds of sensors trained a combined model that joins several network types with a swarm based weighting step.

The combined forecaster beat its best single part and explained most of the variation in drift. Two new indices captured salt build up and corrosion drive, and the clash of load current with temperature emerged as the top drift cause. In field use the system warned days ahead.
plos-pone-0355504:
Tianle Duan and co-authors linked the density of physical establishments in American counties with rates of hearing difficulty. Hearing research usually stops at body and income factors. Their 2026 study mapped shops, services, and similar establishments against hearing data across counties and over time.

Raw comparisons suggested denser counties hear better. Those counties also had denser roads, higher status, younger residents, and better schooling and insurance. Once road density and social factors were held constant, the link flipped: denser establishments then came with more hearing difficulty. The authors credit road networks, as a proxy for access and connectivity, with driving the reversal. They also flag specific establishment types as hearing-health risks.
plos-pone-0355604:
Le Huu Binh, Thuy-Van Duong, and Duc Huy Le present a learning-based method for organizing wireless sensor networks in this 2026 paper. In software-defined sensor networks for the Internet of Things, each node's radio range shapes the whole network's energy use and reliability. The goal is for every node to end up with a sensible number of neighbors. Their algorithm lets each node adjust its own range using reinforcement learning. A second learning model at the central controller picks which node learns next. The nodes share lessons without sharing raw data.

In simulations, the federated approach hit the target neighbor counts more accurately than well-known topology control algorithms, while also using less energy and delivering better transmission quality. The authors argue that splitting learning between nodes and controller suits networks too large and too privacy-sensitive for purely central control.
plos-pone-0356004: Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas and Enterobacterales are nightmare bacteria — but new drug combinations offer hope. This reference-laboratory study examined carbapenem resistance alongside susceptibility to ceftazidime/avibactam and ceftolozane/tazobactam. The susceptibility data guide last-resort antibiotic choices.
plos-pone-0356604:
Janny Mathieu and colleagues ran a randomized trial on a simple question. Does telling a spine surgeon what an expert triage clinician found change anything for back pain patients? Their 2026 study enrolled 101 adults referred for a surgical consultation. Everyone received a standardized assessment from a chiropractor. But for half the patients, the findings were shared with the surgeon beforehand.

Patients reported pain, disability, quality of life, and care paths over twelve months. The authors expected equal pain outcomes with smoother journeys through care. But proof of equivalence on the main pain measure was not established at the three-month check. The trial tests a practical reshaping of spine care. It uses spine experts as informed gatekeepers to scarce surgical time.
plos-pone-0356904:
Delia Akosua Bandoh and a Ghanaian team test stool from toddlers with diarrhea in a coastal district where rotavirus vaccine coverage is high, asking what germs fill the gap the vaccine left. Diarrhea still burdens young children, and its causes are shifting. A few dozen children under five at a district facility gave samples checked by rapid tests and a broad gene panel, with illness severity scored on a standard scale.

Rotavirus itself appeared in only a single case. Two bacterial types dominated instead, one in about half the children and a combined shigella-type signal in about three quarters, with norovirus the leading virus. Nearly every child carried more than one germ, and mixed bacterial-viral infections leaned more severe. Bandoh and colleagues urge routine pathogen surveillance to keep guiding treatment.
plos-pone-0357004:
Marion C Aichberger and five colleagues ask whether experiencing ethnic discrimination soured people on digital contact tracing, in PLOS ONE in 2026. App based tracing during COVID-19 only works if the public trusts the state behind it. The team surveyed a quota sample of seven hundred German residents in September 2020 and modeled how discrimination experiences flowed through privacy fears, trust, and solidarity into support for the tool.

The models confirmed the worry: discrimination predicted lower support and lower willingness to opt in, carried by privacy concerns and weaker trust in government. Solidarity, the hoped for bridge, did not explain the link. Among non users, fear that the government might turn tracing data against their own ethnic group specifically reduced future willingness. The authors say disease control tools must be designed with minority communities' justified mistrust in view.
plos-pone-0357104:
Nataly Rodríguez-Lugo and colleagues catalog the bacteria and fungi living inside the roots of an endangered bromeliad in Colombia's high páramo, a cold tropical ecosystem under climate pressure. Root microbes can make or break a rare plant's survival, and this species' partners were unknown. Using long-read gene sequencing on root tissue and surrounding soil, the team compared who lives where and what jobs they likely do.

Root communities were less diverse than soil but more tightly interwoven, rich in acid-loving and nitrogen-fixing partners, while soils carried the region's usual microbes and more nutrient cycling roles. Both held fungi that feed on dead matter plus some known plant pathogens. Rodríguez-Lugo and colleagues say conservation for this bromeliad should plan around its root partners, not just the plant.
plos-pone-0357404:
Stephanie Casey and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE reporting hard lessons from attempts to clean DDT out of old soil using white-rot fungi. DDT, a banned pesticide, lingers for decades; fungi such as the oyster mushroom can break down similar pollutants in labs. The team tried two realistic approaches: mixing spent mushroom-growing material straight into contaminated soil in pots, and adding fungus-grown substrate to soil at a field site.

Neither approach produced any measurable drop in DDT or its breakdown products. The fungi struggled to survive and spread through real, aged soil, unlike the freshly spiked soils used in many earlier lab successes. Rather than hiding a negative result, the authors map what limited performance: fungal survival, substrate quality, and poor colonization. The account gives future cleanup projects a realistic checklist of what must be fixed before mushroom-based treatment can work outside the lab.
plos-pone-0357904:
Justin Clements and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE measuring PCBs, the banned industrial chemicals that linger for decades, in wildlife across northern New Mexico. Animals were collected opportunistically over fifteen-plus years and grouped by diet: meat eaters, plant eaters, and omnivores. The team compared total contamination, chemical family profiles, and the dioxin-like fraction that drives much of the toxicity.

Carnivores carried the heaviest PCB loads and the highest toxic equivalents, consistent with the chemicals concentrating up the food chain. Mountain lions held more than their main prey, mule deer and elk, a direct demonstration of that magnification. Deer and elk sampled near developed areas were also more contaminated than rural counterparts. Production was banned in the nineteen seventies, so these are legacy pollutants from old equipment and materials still leaking into food webs, with top predators the clearest sentinels.
plos-pone-0359304: Kuchynka and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on signaling proteins filmed inside living cells. G proteins relay signals from the cell surface inward. The team tracked one form built from G-beta-1 and gamma-2 parts and found its movement differs by subtype. How fast these relays drift can change how long a signal lasts, a detail drug designers care about.
plos-pone-0359404:
Zongcheng Hu and Li Shao wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about the Chinese Baroque Historic Area, a district famous for its blend of Chinese and Western building styles. The authors trace how the narratives of place identity have evolved, the stories told about what the district is and means.

Their method follows long-term textual practices, how writing about the area has presented it across many years. Place identity guides tourism, preservation, and residents' pride, and it is built partly through repeated texts. Heritage managers and city marketers are the readers for a history of how one district's story has been written.
plos-pone-0360404:
Xingguang Li and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It traces HIV-1 CRF01_AE, one named strain family of the virus that causes AIDS. The authors follow how this strain has spread around the world and how it has changed over time.

Their evidence comes from phylogenetic analysis, which builds family trees from virus gene sequences to show how samples relate. Those trees reveal routes of spread and branching patterns in the strain's history. Public health researchers use such reconstructions to understand epidemics and to keep vaccine and testing work matched to the viruses actually circulating.
pmc-13238504:
Wang and colleagues devise a rapid strip test for African swine fever, a disease that empties pig farms. The virus is lethal, highly contagious, and causes severe bleeding in pigs. In China it has split into variant strains of differing strength, which complicates tracking and control, and lab testing can be slow where outbreaks strike.

Their strip targets the viral protein p72 and works like a home test: a sample flows along a gold-tagged strip and shows a line if the virus is present. No machines are needed, so checks can happen at the farm gate. Fast answers decide whether a herd is quarantined in time to save its neighbours.
pmc-13240904:
Mortensen and co-authors in Connecticut tested whether advanced machine learning beats logistic regression at foretelling pneumonia returns. Models usually ignore steady vitals or curved interactions. Records came from one teaching center between 2018 and 2024. 2,752 patients with first pneumonia stays were in the set.

About one in ten patients returned within thirty days. Gradient boosting and neural networks scored no better than plain logistic regression. Two missed clues surfaced instead: drug abuse history and blood urea nitrogen values. The authors suggest richer social data, not fancier algorithms, may lift the hit rate.
pmc-13241504:
Makalo at the University of The Gambia reviews fourteen years of children's heart care in a low-resource setting. Three Gambian studies between 2008 and 2022 chart congenital heart disease care. Early care leaned on overseas surgery referrals with long waits. Later cohorts reflect growing local echocardiography and specialist training.

Detected cases rose as diagnostics improved, with septal defects the commonest lesions. In-hospital mortality fell from about eleven percent to under seven percent. Fewer than five percent of children received any surgery, and none locally. Makalo calls for earlier detection, regional cardiac services, and prevention.
pmc-13242504:
Caya Hotstegs, Jose Llano, and Hans Kestler built a standard test set for researchers who model gene networks as on-off switches. Their dataset paper appeared in Scientific Data in 2026. Boolean network models simplify gene regulation into genes that are either active or silent, and they are widely used to study cell behavior. Yet new methods are usually tried on hand-picked or artificial models, which can bias the verdict.

The benchmark set covers four kingdoms of life: animals, bacteria, fungi, and plants. Each model was built from recurring patterns and motifs actually observed in real gene regulatory networks, rather than invented for convenience. That grounding aims to keep the models' structure and dynamics close to biology. With a shared, unbiased yardstick, groups can compare algorithms fairly and spot weaknesses earlier. The authors offer the set as common ground for the modeling community.
pmc-13244504:
Fiona Leggat and colleagues listened to the Filipino health workers who carry stroke care outside big hospitals. Their qualitative study appeared in Global Health Action in 2026. Seventeen providers, professional and volunteer, across five regions were interviewed in mid 2024 for the TULAY stroke project. The title quotes one participant's blunt summary: we don't know anything about stroke care. Rehabilitation, the team heard, is where the system thins out most.

Three themes organized the accounts. Services and rehabilitation are distributed inequitably, leaving provinces far behind the capital. Barriers stack at every level, from family costs to workforce gaps and fragmented referrals. Providers also named what they want: training, local programs, and support built with survivors rather than for them. Because the Philippines devolves health decisions locally, the authors favor community-rooted plans over one national template. Local design, they argue, is not a compromise but the mechanism.
pmc-13246904:
Slebioda and Zawieja taught a neural network to tell grass varieties apart in this 2026 Theory in Biosciences study. Red fescue is a widely planted grass with seventy-six closely related varieties that breeders must distinguish for registration, using just seven measured shape traits. Sorting that many similar classes at once is hard for a single model, so the authors split the problem into subsets.

Their best design used fifteen subsets of five or six varieties, each handled by its own small network. A strict confidence rule applied: a variety counted as identified only when the networks agreed strongly. That setup classified known varieties correctly and, importantly, flagged unfamiliar samples as unknown instead of forcing a wrong label. The method suits seed-testing and breeding programs.
pmc-13247104:
Li, Ngan, and Zhao measured children's faces against their throat anatomy in this 2026 Progress in Orthodontics study. Enlarged adenoids and tonsils obstruct breathing and are suspected of steering jaw growth, but studies disagree on the facial pattern. The team took side-view head X-rays of five hundred sixty-three children aged six to ten, computing each enlarged child's ratio of adenoid to tonsil size.

Children whose tonsils dominated showed a more forward, overgrown lower jaw pattern, while those whose adenoids dominated tended toward a downward-rotated jaw. The balance between the two tissues tracked with facial measurements across the group, and age modified some of the links. The authors urge timely airway assessment in orthodontic practice, since the growth pattern may depend on which tissue dominates.
pmc-13247304:
Lim and co-authors describe orthodontic treatment of a growing girl with a Class III bite, in this 2026 Case Reports in Dentistry article. In this pattern the upper jaw sits too far back, producing an underbite-like crossbite at the front teeth. The patient, ten and a half years old, also had a sideways functional jaw shift and a family history of prominent lower jaws.

Treatment began with a protraction facemask, worn to pull the upper jaw forward, started later than the conventional early window but timed to her growth stage, and without palate expansion. Fixed braces followed. The upper jaw moved forward, the crossbite and shift resolved, and her profile and smile improved, ending in stable, well-matched teeth. The authors argue biological timing can matter more than strict age rules in selected patients.
pmc-13248304:
Jia and colleagues mapped a family of genes in pepper plants, reported in BMC Genomics in 2026. The genes make ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes, proteins that tag other proteins for removal or control. Such enzymes shape plant growth, stress responses, and, the team suspected, the pigments that color pepper fruit.

The researchers found fifty-six family members and sorted them into eleven groups by ancestry. Many carried DNA switches that respond to light or stress. Two members tracked closely with a gene that builds chlorophyll, the green pigment. The authors present the catalog as groundwork for breeding peppers with chosen fruit colors and hardier growth.
pmc-13248404: Jung and colleagues issued this correction in BMC Geriatrics in 2026 for their study of digital health literacy in later life. A passage in the original paper pointed readers to the wrong place for the sample description. The corrected text states that sociodemographic and health details for the two thousand two hundred twenty-seven participants, aged sixty-five to ninety-one, are summarized in a table rather than in Figure 1. The study's data and conclusions are unchanged.
pmc-13248904:
Zhang and colleagues built a cell-based production line for an H5N1 flu vaccine, reported in 2026. Bird flu remains a pandemic threat, and growing vaccine virus in eggs is slow to scale. The team instead grew the virus in MDCK dog kidney cells floating freely in serum-free liquid, tuning infection conditions step by step.

In a seventy-five liter tank, the virus reached high levels within forty-eight hours. Filtering and two chromatography steps stripped out nearly all leftover cell protein and DNA. Two fifteen-microgram doses converted every test subject's blood to positive antibody status in early checks. The authors present the platform as ready groundwork for pandemic vaccine supply.
pmc-13250104:
Murchie and colleagues report that fossil droppings from ground squirrels in Yukon, Canada, hold ancient DNA spanning about 700,000 years. Their 2026 Nature Communications paper studies coprolites, preserved dung pellets, taken from burrows frozen in permafrost. The samples range from the recent Holocene back to the middle Pleistocene.

Using shotgun metagenomics, a method that reads all DNA in a sample at once, plus targeted enrichment, the team recovered DNA from plants, insects, microbes, and large animals. They assembled more than eighteen mitochondrial genomes, including steppe bison, horse, and mammoth. Damage patterns typical of old DNA supported the results as genuine. The pellets thus offer detailed records of past Arctic ecosystems and animal family histories.
pmc-13252704:
Alfonso Medela and colleagues test an AI helper for a rare skin disease in this 2026 study. Generalised pustular psoriasis is uncommon and easily confused with look-alike conditions, which delays correct treatment.

The device, trained on thousands of images across more than 200 skin conditions and fine-tuned with extra images of this disease, named it with high accuracy. Fifteen clinicians, most in primary care, then reviewed 100 images of similar conditions, first alone and then with the device's top five suggestions. Their accuracy at spotting the disease rose by about 23 percent with the help, and slightly more for primary care doctors. The authors back such tools where specialist access is thin.
pmc-13252804:
Ryo Tomemori and colleagues follow a drug switch for stubborn diabetic eye swelling in this 2026 real-world study. About four in ten cases of diabetic macular edema resist standard injections, and a newer antibody drug blocks two vessel-growth signals at once.

The study covered 28 eyes from 19 patients who switched to the drug faricimab after older treatments failed. A year later, retinal thickness had fallen by about 29 percent on average, and just over half the eyes reached a dry retina. Vision scores held steady rather than improving, and injections were needed more often than before the switch. Thickness of the deeper choroid layer stayed stable, which the authors read as a good sign.
pmc-13253704: Yuri Kato and co-authors issued a 2026 correction notice for their study of renalase knockdown in mouse satellite cells, the stem cells that repair muscle. The notice states that Figure 3 in the original paper appeared wrongly and has now been fixed. The sample shows the figure caption, covering signals such as STAT3 and p38 MAPK at day three, but not the study's full findings, so only the correction itself can be described here.
pmc-13254004:
Shirin Shahbazi Sighaldeh and co-authors explore why people in Iran decide to have children in a 2026 interview study. The team spoke face-to-face in 2025 with 64 people of reproductive age across seven cities, mostly women. Their answers were coded into 678 initial codes and then grouped into themes.

Six main categories emerged, from personal attitudes to social norms, modern lifestyle change, and religious and political beliefs. Money strength at home and government support also mattered. The same factor could help or hinder, depending on how people saw it. The authors urge broad policies that also build positive mindsets about childbearing.
pmc-13254404:
Theodora Manolakou and a large team find a new drug target in rheumatoid arthritis in a 2026 study. T cells drive the joint inflammation in this disease, and current drugs often fail to control it for long. The team traced a chain where a gene switch, NFATc1, turns on MTHFD2, an enzyme feeding one-carbon metabolism in active T cells.

A new small molecule, TH9619, blocks MTHFD1/2 and cut inflammatory cytokine output. It also raised protective regulatory T cells and guarded cartilage and bone in animal models. Its effects in patient T cells differed from current anti-folate therapy, mainly in poor responders.
pmc-13257504:
Qi Wang and colleagues ask whether resveratrol, a compound found in grape skins, can blunt liver scarring caused by arsenic. Their 2026 rat study centers on SIRT1, a protein that helps regulate metabolism. They track how arsenic disturbs bile acid handling in the liver over time.

Arsenic exposure built up harmful bile acids, inflamed the liver, and switched off genes that detoxify or export bile. It also lowered SIRT1 and changed a partner protein's chemical tagging. Resveratrol restored SIRT1, steadied bile acid balance, and cut arsenic stored in the liver. The result was visibly less fibrosis in treated animals.
pmc-13258004:
Naufal Nordin, Woi Pui Juan, and Nurul Umira Samsudin present a 2026 study of school children's visual-motor integration, the skill of coordinating what the eyes see with hand movement. They assessed 148 children, with a mean age of 9.94 years, from three urban schools in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Testing used a standard drawing-based test, and pencil grips were classed into five types from photos. School marks came from teacher-based classroom assessments.

Test raw scores were linked to performance in all four core subjects, Malay language, English, science, and mathematics. The links were strongest for science and mathematics. Age-adjusted scores stayed linked only to science and mathematics. Pencil grip type showed only a weak link to test scores, with the lateral quadrupod grip scoring highest. The authors say grip alone is a poor sign of visual-motor skill.
pmc-13260204:
Ziyi Chen and co-authors find a hidden editing pattern in the blood of lupus patients. In systemic lupus erythematosus, immune attack turns inward, and gene messages are trimmed at varying lengths. Their 2026 study scans several patient cohorts for shifts in this process, called alternative polyadenylation.

Across cohorts, immune gene messages ran longer at their tails in patients than in healthy people. The team distilled the pattern into an ImmAPA score that sorts patients into high and low groups. Bandage draws assembly graphs in an interactive way, so users can navigate them easily. Seeing the graph helps spot tangles, repeats, and possible errors that tables hide. recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: Louis Constant, Napoleon's valet, shares his private memories in volume four. He saw the emperor at table, at work, and at rest. Small details paint a human picture of the great man. An intimate backstage view of history.
reitzenstein-poimandres-1904:
Richard Reitzenstein published his study of the Poimandres in German in 1904. The Poimandres is the opening revelation of the Corpus Hermeticum, where Hermes receives a vision. Reitzenstein set that text inside its Graeco-Egyptian religious world.

He traced kinship between Hermetic writings, early Christianity, and Gnosticism. His method, the history-of-religions approach, treated texts as products of mixed cultures. The book founded a modern historical way of studying ancient mysticism. Scholars argued with his conclusions for decades, which proves his influence. Written for specialists, it changed how a whole field asked its questions.
reymont-peasants-1904:
Wladyslaw Reymont wrote The Peasants as a four-volume Polish epic, published in the first years of the 1900s. The Knopf English text of 1928 gathers the work in one volume. Life in the village of Lipce follows the four seasons. Land, faith, weddings, and feuds shape the peasants' year.

The Boryna family stands at the center, with land disputes and a tangled marriage plot. Reymont writes of soil and weather as forces in their own right. Village speech and custom fill the pages with color. The epic helped Reymont win the Nobel Prize in 1924. It remains Poland's great novel of rural life.
russell-new-creation-vol6-1904:
Russell closed his own series with The New Creation, the sixth Studies volume of 1904, written for the consecrated. The book treats the calling, holiness, and discipline of the new creature, the believer set apart for God's work. Church order, conduct, marriage, and daily duty all fall under its careful, detailed rules.

Where earlier volumes mapped history and prophecy, this one governs a daily life from waking to sleep. Russell writes as pastor and organizer, shaping a people fit for the kingdom he expected very soon. With it his six-volume set stands complete, the full system of the Bible Student movement in its founder's words.
rutherford-radio-activity-1904:
Ernest Rutherford published Radio-activity in 1904, only a few years after radioactivity itself was found. Rutherford, a New Zealand physicist working in Canada and England, was the field's boldest experimenter. His book was the first full textbook on the new science.

Rutherford explains rays from uranium and radium, and how one element can change into another. He sets out half-life, the steady rate at which active matter decays. The work helped turn a strange glow in the lab into nuclear science, the field Rutherford would lead for decades. It also gathers the lab methods used to trace rays and count particles.
scheible-das-kloster-vol04:
In 1846 Johann Scheible issued band four of Das Kloster, holding cells thirteen through sixteen. The German anthology had grown past its first year into a known fixture of the trade. Scheible, its editor and publisher, hunted down scarce print that libraries had long ignored.

What he found, he reprinted whole: grimoires, Faust books, and grim Höllenzwänge among them. Folk charms, some meant for love and some for healing, share the binding with popular tales. The worth of such a band lies in survival. Texts that lived in a handful of copies now sat in one sturdy volume on many shelves.
schiller-wilhelm-tell-1804:
William Tell was Schiller's last completed play, finished in 1804, and Theodore Martin translated it into English. Tell, a Swiss marksman and quiet family man, refuses to bow to the hat of the Austrian bailiff Gessler. Gessler's punishment is cruel: Tell must shoot an apple from his own son's head.

Tell succeeds, yet vows revenge, and the Swiss cantons rise against their rulers. Schiller turns the old legend into a broad drama of a people's freedom. The play made Tell a worldwide emblem of resistance to tyranny. Rossini's opera later carried the tale further still. Schiller wrote it without ever seeing Switzerland, working from chronicles and maps alone.
scott-elliot-lost-lemuria-1904:
The Lost Lemuria, printed in 1904, gives Scott-Elliot's account of the sunken southern continent. Lemuria, in theosophical teaching, preceded Atlantis as a home of early humanity. Scott-Elliot marshals geological and biological evidence for the lost land. The spread of fossils and living species across oceans anchors his case.

Two maps trace the continent and its shrinking remains. He joins the science of his day to the society's clairvoyant records. The Story of Atlantis is the companion volume to this one. Together they set out the Theosophical Society's lost continent doctrine in full. The Gutenberg text preserves the argument entire. It remains the movement's Lemuria in chief.
serge-panine-volume-04: The fourth volume of Serge Panine brings the drama to a head. The heartless villain's elaborate plots unravel toward exposure. Justice and outraged passion collide at last. A rousing close to a very popular novel.
smith-wealth-nations-cannan-1904:
Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations appears here in Edwin Cannan's 1904 edition. Smith, a Scottish philosopher, first published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in 1776. Cannan, an economist, edited the text with notes that scholars used for a century.

Smith argued that the division of labor makes nations rich, and that free trade beats the old mercantilist controls. His famous invisible hand pictured each person seeking gain yet serving the public good. He also warned about monopolies, dull factory work, and business plots against the public. The book founded modern economics, and Cannan's edition remains a careful way to read it in full.
spr-proceedings-vol18-1903-1904:
Volume eighteen binds parts forty six through forty nine, for 1903 and 1904. Two decades in, the SPR Proceedings keep their founding bargain. Print the evidence for telepathy, apparitions, and mediumship, and print the criticism too. Fresh experiments try to close the gaps critics had found.

Trance cases, with Piper still central, receive long verbatim reports. The census tradition shapes new surveys of spontaneous experiences. Physical wonders appear rarely, and then under heavy guard. Volume eighteen sustains the journal of record through its Edwardian years. It offers historians a dense, dated file of the debate. The society's patience is its signature here.
steiner-theosophy-1904:
Rudolf Steiner wrote his Theosophy in 1904, while he still led the German theosophists. Its full title calls it a first step to knowledge past the senses. The book sets out man as body, soul, and spirit. It is the root text of the school he later built, Anthroposophy.

Birth anew and karma frame the tale of the soul's long growth. Three worlds stack up: flesh, soul, and spirit, each with its own laws. Steiner then maps a path by which a pupil can gain sight of those worlds. The book asks for slow, keen thought, not blind faith.
stevenson-the-zuni-indians-1904:
Matilda Coxe Stevenson was among the first women to do serious fieldwork in the Southwest, and she spent years at Zuni Pueblo. Her report, published in 1904 in the Bureau of American Ethnology's annual report, is the fullest early study of Zuni religion.

Stevenson describes the rain priesthood, whose prayers served the whole pueblo, and the kachina cult with its masked dancers. She gives detailed accounts of the esoteric fraternities, the secret societies that ran ceremonies and healing. Her access to restricted rites raised questions even then. Whatever the disputes, the record she left is unmatched in detail.
suess-face-of-earth-vol1-sollas-1904:
W J Sollas published his translation of Volume 1 of Eduard Suess's Face of the Earth in 1904. Suess, a Viennese geologist, wrote Das Antlitz der Erde as a synthesis of the whole science. Sollas, an Oxford geologist, carried the great work into English over many years.

Volume 1 treats the structure of the continents and the history of the Mediterranean lands. Suess argued that mountains rise as the cooling Earth contracts and its crust crumples, the contraction theory of mountain building. He also named Gondwana, a lost southern continent pieced together from matching fossils and rocks. The volume began the English form of the most ambitious geology of its age.
swift-battle-of-the-books-1704:
Jonathan Swift wrote The Battle of the Books while working as secretary to Sir William Temple, a retired statesman. A loud quarrel then divided scholars: were modern writers the equals of the ancient Greeks and Romans? Swift published his mock-epic prose satire in 1704, alongside A Tale of a Tub.

In the royal library at St. James, the ancient and modern books come alive and go to war. Bees and spiders argue the same case in a famous fable: the spider spins from itself, the bee gathers from every flower. Swift mocks pedants on both sides but saves his sharpest cuts for modern pride. The piece remains the wittiest shot fired in the ancients-versus-moderns war.
swift-tale-of-a-tub-1704:
Jonathan Swift published A Tale of a Tub in 1704, his first major work, issued with The Battle of the Books. Swift was then an unknown Irish clergyman in his thirties. The book's wild energy and strange digressions startled readers and made his reputation.

The tale itself is an allegory of three brothers who inherit coats they must not alter, standing for the Catholic, Anglican, and dissenting churches. Around it Swift piles mock prefaces and digressions praising madness and modern learning. The satire cuts at religious corruption and empty scholarship alike. Many call it the most savage and brilliant prose satire of its age.
synge-riders-to-sea-1904:
J. M. Synge drew Riders to the Sea from his visits to the Aran Islands, where the sea took men from nearly every family. The one-act play was first performed in 1904. It lasts under an hour and is often called the summit of Irish tragedy.

Maurya, an old widow, has already lost her husband and four sons to the sea. The play opens as her daughters identify a drowned man's clothing from far up the coast. Her last surviving son, Bartley, insists on sailing despite her pleas. When his body is carried in, Maurya reaches a calm, terrible acceptance. Synge's language, shaped by Irish speech, gives the grief a biblical weight.
the-a-b-c-of-phrenology-1904: The A, b, c, of phrenology, 1904, the phrenological alphabet. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-comedy-of-errors-pg1504: Shakespeare's farce of two sets of twins in this edition: shipwrecked brothers and their servants cause joyful chaos in Ephesus. Mistaken beatings, mistaken wives, and a happy reunion. The shortest, silliest Shakespeare, and a perfect evening's fun.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The fourth volume of the Confessions brings young Rousseau to Paris. The unknown musician meets Diderot and the brilliant philosophes. Ambition and awkwardness mark his difficult early days. A rare genius struggling toward the light.
the-follies-of-science-at-the-court-of-r: The Follies of Science at the Court of Rudolph II, 1576-1612, 1904. The Prague follies. This book preserves that history. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
the-thirty-years-war-volume-04: The fourth volume carries Schiller's narrative through the later campaigns of the Thirty Years War, as exhaustion and diplomacy begin to shape the peace. Great commanders fall and empires bleed in prose of tragic grandeur. Essential for understanding how modern Europe was forged in suffering.
the-wandering-jew-volume-04: Eugène Sue’s fourth volume of the Wandering Jew gathers the heirs. The Rennepont family’s fate hangs in the balance. The great melodrama rolls ever onward. Suspense and sensation on every page, Eugène Sue.
the-works-of-samuel-johnson-in-sixteen-v: Volume four of Samuel Johnson's works: essays, criticism, and the great moralist's judgments on literature and life. The Rambler and Idler papers show his mind at its most vigorous. The foundation of English criticism. Johnson's Dictionary alone would immortalize him; these works show the rest.
thompson-devils-evil-spirits-babylonia-v:
The second volume of R. Campbell Thompson's Devils and Evil Spirits of Babylonia came out at London in 1904. Where volume one fought demons in general, this one turns to set sicknesses. Thompson again pairs English renderings with the cuneiform texts and full notes.

The chief series here are Asakki Marsuti, on fever sickness, Ti'i, and Luh-ka, plus mixed spells that fit no one series. Each spell treats illness as a spirit to be named and driven out. The volume rounds out the classic English source on Mesopotamian healing magic.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-04:
The fourth volume of Charles Thomson's Bible, from 1808, holds the New Testament. Thomson translated it from the Greek, as he had the Septuagint in the first three volumes. Jane Aitken printed the set at Philadelphia, and it counts as the first American translation of the whole Bible into English.

The four gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul and the other apostles, and Revelation stand in Thomson's plain, careful English. His renderings sometimes cut closer to the Greek than the King James text does. Thomson had been secretary of Congress through the war for independence. His Bible is both a work of faith and a monument of early American print culture.
thomson-electricity-matter-1904:
Lectures given at Yale in 1903 as the Silliman Lectures became J. J. Thomson's Electricity and Matter in 1904. Thomson had discovered the electron, a particle far lighter than any atom, in 1897. His lectures present the corpuscular theory, which treats electrons as the basic bits of matter. Cathode rays figure large in the evidence.

Thomson shows how his particles can explain electric charge, mass, and the build of atoms. He writes as a guide at the front of a new field. The lectures carry the excitement of a science remaking itself. Readers see theory built straight from lab results. The book fixed his views for a wide public.
tob-0004:
Presented in Edwin Arnold's English translation, the Bhagavad Gita is a Hindu scripture that forms part of the great epic Mahabharata. Tradition attributes the larger work to Vyasa. Its scene is a battlefield, just before fighting begins, where the warrior Arjuna must face relatives and teachers among the opposing army.

Arjuna hesitates, and his charioteer Krishna answers him. Krishna, revealed as divine, teaches duty, selfless action, and devotion, urging Arjuna to act without being ruled by the results. Readers meet questions about work, death, the self, and God in a tense conversation rather than a sermon, which helps explain its lasting place in Hindu life.
tob-0104:
Fifteenth-century Bavaria produced the Munich Manual of Demonic Magic, a working magician's handbook in Latin. Its unknown compiler cared little for theory. Conjurations, experiments, and lists of spirits fill the pages, aimed at plain results: treasure found, love won, enemies checked.

The raw, practical tone sets it apart from loftier grimoires that preach about angels. Scholars value it as a true picture of late medieval magic in daily use. The only English version is Richard Kieckhefer's modern translation, which remains under copyright, so no public-domain text is attached to this entry. The manual's fame rests on its blunt honesty.
tob-10804:
Lady Wilde, Oscar Wilde's mother, who wrote as Speranza, gathered Ireland's folk beliefs in Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms, and Superstitions of Ireland. She collected fairy legends, healing charms, omens, and keening songs from the peasantry she knew. The oral world she recorded was already vanishing in her lifetime.

Tales of the sidhe, banshees, sacred wells, and second sight sit beside practical charms for illness, love, and protection. Lady Wilde writes in vivid, sympathetic prose, treating storytellers as authorities rather than curiosities. Folklore collections like hers preserve, in print, what a culture once carried entirely in memory and voice.
tob-13504:
Henry Cornelius Agrippa, a German scholar and physician, issued his Three Books of Occult Philosophy in the 1530s. The work sums up the learned magic of the Renaissance in one system. The copy here follows the complete 1898 English edition.

Book one treats natural magic, the hidden powers of things; book two, the heavens and their numbers; book three, divine names and ceremony. Agrippa draws on Kabbalah, astrology, and ancient philosophy to argue that all levels of the world answer each other. The spurious fourth book often travels with it. Few occult books have been mined as long or as widely.
tob-4004:
Desiderius Erasmus published The Praise of Folly in 1509, and John Wilson's translation presents his mock-encomium in classic English. Folly herself takes the podium, robed and belled, to praise her own influence over human affairs. Monks, theologians, schoolmen, kings, courtiers, and lovers all owe their happiness, she explains, to her.

The joke sharpens as Folly grows earnest about war, corruption, and empty ritual, stinging the powerful while delighting the humanists who first passed the book hand to hand. Luther's generation weaponized its laughter; Erasmus himself stayed ironic. As satire that helped prepare a reformation while disowning one, The Praise of Folly remains sly, learned, and very funny.
tob-9047-62704:
Precious stones close Pliny's Natural History in volume six of Bostock's translation. Diamonds, emeralds, pearls, and lesser gems each get a history: where they are found, how they are cut, and what powers people claim for them. Pliny enjoys exposing fakes and frauds in the gem trade.

With the stones, the thirty-seven books come to an end. The survey began with the heavens and ends with the smallest bright things dug from the earth. No other Roman work attempts so much. Bostock's six volumes give English readers the whole of antiquity's great storehouse of fact, fable, and shrewd comment.
tob-9104:
Hume's thirteen Principal Upanishads stand here in a second record of the Harvard Sanskritist's one-volume classic. The Katha's dialogue with Death and the Chandogya's thou art that anchor the set. Students across a century have learned Hindu philosophy from Hume's translations and notes.

The texts range from brief verses to long prose dialogues between kings, wives, sons, and sages. All circle one claim: the self within and the ground of the world are the same. Verified from the 1919 edition scan, this copy keeps the standard student text in circulation. Few single volumes carry so much of a tradition's thought.
triumph-wagen-antimonii-fratris-basilii-: Triumph Wagen Antimonii, 1604. The German antimony chariot. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
troward-edinburgh-lectures-1904:
Thomas Troward gave his Edinburgh Lectures on Mental Science in 1904. Troward was a judge in India who turned to deep thought on mind. The talks give the strict case for New Thought. They are the most weighty of the mind science books.

Spirit and mind drive the growth of form in his scheme. The mind of man shares in the mind that made all things, he holds. Thought, thus, is a real force that shapes fate and flesh. The talks set the creed of a whole school on firm, clear ground.
un-ga-res-2504:
West New Guinea's fate was sealed in Resolution 2504, adopted by the General Assembly on 19 November 1969. The Dutch and Indonesia had settled their fight over the land in a 1962 deal. The UN ran the land for a short spell, then passed control to Indonesia. Under the deal, the people were to have an act of free choice on their future, with UN advice and help.

The Assembly now had the report on how that act was run in 1969, and on its result: a vote for life within Indonesia. The text takes note of the report and of the Secretary-General's role in the whole affair. Critics at the time, and since, have called the act far from free.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2504 (XXIV), adopted on 19 November 1969, closed the United Nations chapter on West New Guinea, also called West Irian. In 1962 the Assembly had noted the agreement between Indonesia and the Netherlands on the territory. It had backed the Secretary-General's role under it. A temporary United Nations authority had since run its handover.

The text takes note of the Secretary-General's report on the act of free choice held under the agreement. It thanks him and his staff for finishing their tasks. It also welcomes aid for the territory's growth. It notes Dutch help given with Indonesia, much of it through the Asian Development Bank and United Nations bodies.
un-sc-res-104: Resolution 104, adopted unanimously on 20 June 1954, took up Guatemala. The government had sent an urgent message to the Council. Foreign-backed forces had crossed into the country days earlier. Fighting had begun, and the government blamed outside help for the attack. The Council calls for an immediate end to any action likely to cause bloodshed. It asks every member state to give no assistance to such action, in the spirit of the Charter. The text is among the shortest the Council passed.
un-sc-res-1104: With a catalog date of 1997, Resolution 1104 records a decision of the UN Security Council. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1304: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 1304, which the catalog dates to 2000. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1404:
Angola brought the Council to Resolution 1404, adopted unanimously on 18 April 2002. A ceasefire signed on 4 April had just ended the long war. Sanctions on the UNITA rebels still needed watching during the peace. Civilians across the country faced hunger and ruin.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the sanctions monitoring team for six months, to 19 October 2002. Four experts will staff it. Within thirty days the team must file an action plan. The plan centers on rebel finances, the diamond trade, and the arms trade. States are told to cooperate fully with the team's work.
un-sc-res-1504: Resolution 1504, a Security Council act of 2003, is preserved here in official-record form through English Wikisource. Such decisions can renew missions, tighten sanctions, or call parties to account, and all of them share one format. The entry keeps that format intact, findings first and operative clauses after, exactly as the members voted it.
un-sc-res-1604: Kept as Resolution 1604, a Security Council decision survives in official-record form through English Wikisource. The body that issues these texts sits at UN headquarters and votes as fifteen national delegations. Their agreed words, preserved here without trimming, are what later arguments about the Council's intent always return to in the end.
un-sc-res-1704:
Timor-Leste, the small Southeast Asian country that won independence in 2002, fell into unrest in 2006 when its security forces split. Resolution 1704 answered by establishing a new United Nations mission there. The mission's core strength was police rather than soldiers.

Inside the text, UN police are tasked with restoring public safety while local officers are rebuilt and retrained. The mission also supports elections, courts, and government offices across the young state. The resolution shows the Council doing quiet nation-building work, years after the crisis that first brought peacekeepers to Timor.
un-sc-res-1904:
Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1904, adopted on 17 December 2009. Ten years had passed since the first sanctions text. Courts and listed people had raised fair-process complaints. The Council wanted the list kept accurate and the rules clearer.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on listed people and groups. Every new listing needs a detailed statement of case. A public summary of the reasons must be posted for each name. The text creates an Ombudsperson to review requests to come off the list. States are urged to propose new names and to share court rulings that touch old ones.
un-sc-res-2004:
The Security Council turned to Lebanon in Resolution 2004, adopted on 30 August 2011. Lebanon had asked for the peacekeeping force, UNIFIL, to stay one more year unchanged. Grave clashes had broken the calm in May and August 2011. Bomb attacks in May and July had struck the peacekeepers themselves.

The text extends UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2012. It condemns the attacks on peacekeepers in the strongest terms. All sides must honor the halt to fighting and respect the Blue Line in full. Israel should pull its army out of northern Ghajar without more delay. A careful review of the force, to fit it best to its tasks, is due before the year ends.
un-sc-res-204:
Senegal accused Portuguese troops of crossing its border in 1965. On 19 May 1965 the Security Council heard both governments. It deeply deplored any incursions into Senegalese territory. The Council restated its 1963 resolution on the same quarrel. Portugal ruled neighboring Guinea-Bissau at the time. Armed struggle for that colony's freedom was already under way.

Portugal had to take all effective steps to stop the violations. Senegal's sovereignty and borders had to be respected. The Secretary-General was told to follow events. The vote was unanimous. The text is one of several in which the Council pressed a colonial power over raids linked to liberation wars.
un-sc-res-404:
An armed raid on Benin's capital brought a Security Council mission on 8 February 1977. Benin's chargé d'affaires had written to the Council on 26 January. The attack had hit Cotonou on 16 January 1977, when foreign fighters landed and struck targets in the city before escaping. Benin's permanent representative addressed the Council on the events.

The Council affirmed that Benin's territorial integrity and political independence had to be respected. It decided to send a special mission of three of its members to Benin. The mission would investigate the events of 16 January at Cotonou and report by the end of February 1977. Its members would be named after talks between the Council's president and its members. The Secretary-General was asked to give the mission the help it needed. The Council stayed seized of the question while the inquiry ran.
un-sc-res-704:
Security Council Resolution 704, adopted on August 9, 1991, recommended the Marshall Islands for membership in the United Nations. The Pacific island nation had lately closed a long period under United States administration, first as a trust territory after the war. Full self-rule under its compact with Washington freed it to seek its own seat in the world body.

The Assembly admitted the Marshall Islands on September 17, in a batch of new members freed by the Cold War's end. For a land of low atolls with a small population, the seat mattered. It gave the islands a direct voice on oceans, fishing, and the nuclear tests once carried out on their soil.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Guatemala rushed a complaint to the Council in June 1954. Its government said foreign-backed forces were invading the country. The elected president, Jacobo Árbenz, faced a revolt armed and encouraged from abroad. Resolution 104 was adopted unanimously on 20 June 1954, after urgent debate.

The text is brief but pointed. It calls for the immediate end of any action likely to cause bloodshed. It also asks every UN member to give no help to such action. The words were aimed at halting outside support for the invasion. Events moved faster than diplomacy. Árbenz fell within days, starting decades of turmoil in Guatemala.

Security Council resolution 1104, adopted on 8 April 1997, is a routine step in staffing the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. The Council had decided to consider the names put forward for judges of the Tribunal, received by the Secretary-General by 13 March 1997. It forwards the list of nominees to the General Assembly, as article 13 of the Tribunal's Statute requires. The Assembly can then elect the judges from it.

Fighting in the Congolese city of Kisangani drives this text of 16 June 2000. Ugandan and Rwandan troops had clashed there again on 5 June, in the middle of Congo's wider war. Reports that Congo's natural wealth was being taken illegally also worried the Council.

The Council said it was outraged by the fighting and by both countries' failure to keep their promises to stop and pull back. It stood behind the Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement and pressed every party to honour it. It also backed the expert panel studying how Congo's resources were being looted, a trade the Council linked to the war dragging on.

Angola appears again in Resolution 1404, adopted unanimously on 18 April 2002. Two weeks earlier, the government and UNITA had signed a ceasefire. The war seemed finally over. Still, sanctions on the former rebels remained in force. A monitoring team was tracking how those measures worked.

The Council extended the team's mandate by six months, to 19 October 2002. Four experts would staff it. Within thirty days they owed a detailed plan for their work. Money, diamonds, and arms linked to UNITA topped the list. Periodic reports were required, with a further full report due by 15 October 2002.

A prosecutor is named for the Yugoslavia war crimes court on 4 September 2003. A week before, the Council had split the once-shared prosecutor post in two and set up its own post for the Rwanda court. Acting on the Secretary-General's choice, it named Carla Del Ponte to the Yugoslavia post, to start on 15 September 2003, for a four-year term.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 15 June 2005 for a further period ending 15 December 2005. A review of the operation had just been completed. The island stayed stable and the Green Line calm, with fewer incidents between the sides, and the Committee on Missing Persons had resumed its work in August 2004.

The mandate is renewed, and the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces are again called on to restore the military position at Strovilia to what it had been before July 2000. Both parties are again called on to treat the missing persons question with urgency and seriousness as a humanitarian matter, and a report on the mission's work is requested.

Timor-Leste gets a new, expanded United Nations mission on 25 August 2006, after the crisis of that year. Violence and political breakdown had displaced large numbers of people, and many weapons remained unaccounted for. A new government had been formed, but the security and humanitarian situation stayed fragile.

The United Nations Integrated Mission in Timor-Leste, UNMIT, is created for an initial six months. It would include up to 1,608 police personnel and a small initial group of 34 military liaison and staff officers, alongside a large civilian team. Its work centres on supporting the government, restoring public security through policing, and helping prepare for the 2007 elections. International security forces already in the country would work alongside it.

The Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions regime gets a fairness overhaul in Resolution 1904, adopted on 17 December 2009. Legal challenges to listings had grown, the Council was mid-way through reviewing every name on the Consolidated List, and Al-Qaida kidnappings for ransom were rising.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council continues the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo against listed individuals and entities, confirming the freeze covers ransoms and internet hosting that supports them. Its central reform creates an Office of the Ombudsperson for eighteen months: an independent figure who receives delisting requests from listed people and entities, replacing the Focal Point for this list. Listings must carry public narrative summaries of reasons, states must notify listed persons promptly, and the review of all Consolidated List names must finish by 30 June 2010. The Monitoring Team is extended for eighteen months, with the measures reviewed within eighteen months.

Lebanon's peacekeepers are kept in place by Resolution 2004, adopted on 30 August 2011 at Beirut's request. The mandate of UNIFIL, the UN Interim Force in Lebanon, was due to run out. The year had brought grave violations of Resolution 1701. They included terrorist attacks on UNIFIL patrols in May and July 2011. Marking of the Blue Line between Israel and Lebanon was still incomplete.

The Council extends UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2012 without amendment. It condemns the attacks on peacekeepers in the strongest terms and demands Lebanon finish its investigation and bring the perpetrators to justice. It orders a strategic review of UNIFIL before year's end to make sure the mission is configured for its tasks. It presses the parties to respect the Blue Line, stop all hostilities, and move toward a permanent ceasefire. Israel is again urged to withdraw from northern Ghajar without further delay.

Senegal accused Portuguese troops of crossing its border in 1965. Portugal still ruled neighboring Guinea-Bissau as a colony. Its forces were fighting independence guerrillas there. Raids and pursuits spilled into Senegalese villages. Resolution 204 was adopted unanimously on 19 May 1965, after both countries argued their cases.

The Council deeply deplored any incursions into Senegal. It repeated its 1963 warning on the same problem. Portugal was asked yet again to stop violating Senegal's sovereignty. The Secretary-General had to follow events and report. The text shows decolonization's wars straining borders across West Africa. Portugal's colonial wars lasted until its own revolution in 1974.

Seven Gulf sheikhdoms joined together as Britain withdrew in 1971. Their new federation, the United Arab Emirates, was proclaimed on 2 December. An application for UN membership followed immediately. Resolution 304 was adopted unanimously on 8 December 1971. The Council needed less than a week to respond.

Members recommended the Emirates' admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly seated the federation the next day. Few new states arrived with such wealth waiting underground. Oil income soon made the Emirates a major donor and investor. The one-line resolution captures the federation's first act of foreign policy: claiming a lawful seat among nations before its first month was out.

A mysterious attack on Benin's capital brings Resolution 404, adopted by consensus on 8 February 1977. Benin had written to the Council about events at Cotonou on 16 January, when an armed group had struck the city and then escaped. Its representative addressed the Council, and the text recalls every member's duty to respect the territory and independence of others.

The Council affirmed that Benin's territorial integrity and political independence must be respected. It decided to send a special mission of three of its own members to Benin to investigate what happened on 16 January, with a report due by the end of February. The Secretary-General was asked to supply whatever help the mission needed.

The Marshall Islands, a Pacific nation of low atolls, spent decades under United States administration. It moved to self-government under a compact with Washington. Full UN membership was the next step. Resolution 704, adopted without a vote on 9 August 1991, examined its application.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of the Marshall Islands. Some summaries pair this text with Micronesia's admission. In fact, the text covers the Marshall Islands alone. The Assembly admitted it that September. Membership mattered for a country of scattered islands. The Marshalls gained a platform for issues like nuclear testing's legacy and rising seas.
veblen-business-enterprise-1904:
Thorstein Veblen was a Norwegian-American economist famous for mocking the rich in his Theory of the Leisure Class. His 1904 Theory of Business Enterprise turns from manners to machines and markets. It asks who really runs modern industry, and for what ends.

Veblen sets the captain of industry, who chases profit and credit, against the engineer, who wants goods made well. Business, he argues, often profits by holding back output rather than by serving need. His clash of profit and workmanship became a founding charge of institutional economics. The book's dry wit makes its hard economics easier to take. It followed his Leisure Class by five years and deepened its attack.
wells-food-of-the-gods-1904:
H. G. Wells wrote The Food of the Gods in 1904. Two men of science brew a food that makes all life grow vast. They call it Herakleophorbia and test it on chicks and wasps at a farm. The food leaks to the wild, and rats and weeds grow to dread size.

A race of giant babes grows up in a world not made for them. Wells tells their tale with warmth as well as dread of scale. Crowds cheer the giants, then fear them and seek their end. The tale asks what growth means when it will not stop.
wood-n-rays-1904:
Robert W. Wood, an American physicist, paid a short call to Blondlot's lab at Nancy in 1904. The French lab claimed to show N rays, a new ray that most men outside France now doubted. Wood wrote this short letter to Nature on what he saw and did there.

In the dark, Wood took a key part from the ray tool and put it in his pocket. The lab men still read the ray's marks just as before, with the tool broke and blind. His letter, three hours of work in sum, burst the N ray craze at one blow.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol04:
By 1857 the Journal of Discourses had reached Volume IV, still printed at Liverpool for Saints on two continents. Shorthand men recorded Brigham Young, his counsellors, the Twelve Apostles, and others as they preached in Utah. The sermons range from first principles of the faith to sharp words on daily behavior.

Read as a whole, the volume shows a church settling doctrine while building towns in a hard land. The doctrinal record unfolds sermon by sermon, year by year, in the leaders' own phrasing. Scholars and Saints alike return to these pages when they want the era undiluted.
